title: wezterm.lua to frankenterm.toml migration tool
description:
# wezterm.lua → frankenterm.toml Migration Tool

## Why
Users migrating from WezTerm have existing wezterm.lua configs. We need a best-effort migration tool that converts Lua configs to TOML format.

## Scope: best-effort
Lua configs can contain arbitrary code (functions, conditionals, loops). We can't convert arbitrary Lua to TOML. What we CAN convert:
- Static assignments: `config.font_size = 14` → `font_size = 14`
- Color scheme references: `config.color_scheme = "Dracula"` → `color_scheme = "Dracula"`
- Simple key bindings: `config.keys = { {key="c", mods="CTRL", action=wezterm.action.Copy} }`
- SSH domains: static domain definitions
- String/number/boolean config values

What we CANNOT convert (user must port manually or use WASM):
- Dynamic configs: `if hostname == "work" then ... end`
- Custom functions: `wezterm.on("update-status", function(...) ... end)`
- Complex Lua tables with computed keys
- Plugin references

## Implementation approach
Two strategies, used together:
1. **AST parsing**: Use a Lua parser (full_moon or similar) to parse the Lua AST and extract simple assignments. This handles ~70% of configs.
2. **Runtime extraction**: Actually run the Lua config with mlua, capture the resulting config table, and serialize it to TOML. This handles dynamic configs but requires the `lua` feature.

## CLI command
```bash
# Convert wezterm.lua to frankenterm.toml
frankenterm migrate-config ~/.wezterm.lua -o ~/.config/frankenterm/frankenterm.toml

# Dry run (show what would be generated)
frankenterm migrate-config ~/.wezterm.lua --dry-run

# Verbose (show what couldn't be converted)
frankenterm migrate-config ~/.wezterm.lua --verbose
```

## Output format
```toml
# Migrated from ~/.wezterm.lua on 2026-02-10
# Some settings could not be automatically converted.
# See comments marked [MANUAL] below.

font_size = 14.0
color_scheme = "Dracula"

[keys]
# [MANUAL] Complex key binding with custom action — review manually:
# Original Lua: wezterm.action_callback(function(window, pane) ... end)

[ssh_domains]
[[ssh_domains.domains]]
name = "work"
remote_address = "work.example.com"
```

## Files
- frankenterm/config/src/migrate.rs (NEW — migration logic)
- Or: standalone binary frankenterm-migrate (if we want it separate)

## Testing
- Convert 10 representative wezterm.lua configs (from WezTerm docs examples)
- Verify round-trip: load original Lua, load migrated TOML, compare config values
- Test unconvertible constructs produce clear [MANUAL] comments
- Test --dry-run doesn't write files
- Test --verbose shows all unconverted items
- **proptest**: Property-based tests for migration roundtrip fidelity — generate random valid Lua config tables with known static assignments (font_size, color_scheme, boolean flags, string values, simple key bindings), migrate to TOML, parse the TOML back, and verify every convertible field matches the original Lua value; also verify that unconvertible constructs always produce [MANUAL] annotations rather than silent data loss

## Cross-references
- **wa-vv3h** (rename project): The migration tool must use the post-rename binary name and config paths — coordinate naming so that `frankenterm migrate-config` is the canonical invocation and output paths default to frankenterm.toml (not wezterm.toml)
close_reason: Implemented in 581caf5a. Migration tool converts dynamic Value to TOML with [MANUAL] comments for unconvertible constructs. 10 tests.

title: FrankenTerm Extension Package Format (.ftx)
description:
# FrankenTerm Extension Package Format (.ftx)

## Why
Extensions need a standard packaging format for distribution, installation, and loading. The .ftx format bundles everything an extension needs.

## Format specification

### .ftx file structure
A .ftx file is a ZIP archive with this structure:
```
my-extension.ftx (ZIP)
├── extension.toml          # Manifest (required)
├── main.wasm               # WASM module (required for WASM extensions)
├── main.lua                # Lua script (required for Lua extensions)
├── assets/                 # Optional: themes, icons, etc.
│   ├── theme.toml
│   └── icon.png
├── README.md               # Optional: documentation
└── LICENSE                  # Optional: license file
```

### extension.toml (manifest)
```toml
[extension]
name = "my-theme"
version = "1.0.0"
description = "A beautiful theme"
authors = ["Author <author@example.com>"]
license = "MIT"
homepage = "https://github.com/author/my-theme"
min_frankenterm_version = "0.2.0"

[engine]
type = "wasm"  # or "lua" or "both"
entry = "main.wasm"  # or "main.lua"

[permissions]
filesystem = []
environment = ["TERM"]
network = false
pane_access = false

[hooks]
on_config_reload = "handle_config_reload"
on_pane_focus = "handle_pane_focus"
on_color_scheme_change = "handle_color_scheme"

[assets]
themes = ["assets/theme.toml"]
```

### Extension types
1. **Theme extensions**: Color scheme + font config, no code needed (just TOML assets)
2. **Hook extensions**: React to events (config reload, pane focus, etc.)
3. **Content extensions**: Provide pane content (status bars, clocks, etc.) — future
4. **Transform extensions**: Modify terminal output (syntax highlighting, etc.) — future

## Loading and installation
```bash
# Install from file
frankenterm extension install my-theme.ftx

# Install from URL (future)
frankenterm extension install https://example.com/my-theme.ftx

# List installed
frankenterm extension list

# Remove
frankenterm extension remove my-theme

# Extension directory
~/.local/share/frankenterm/extensions/
  my-theme/
    extension.toml
    main.wasm
    assets/
```

## macOS fallbacks
On macOS, the default extension directory also checks:
- `~/Library/Application Support/FrankenTerm/extensions/`
Prefer XDG paths when set, but fall back to macOS-native Application Support when XDG_DATA_HOME is unset.

## Implementation
- Parse extension.toml using existing toml workspace dep
- Validate WASM module exports match declared hooks
- Validate permissions are minimal (warn on excessive permissions)
- Cache compiled WASM modules per extension version

## Files
- frankenterm/scripting/src/extension.rs (NEW — extension loading)
- frankenterm/scripting/src/manifest.rs (NEW — extension.toml parsing)
- frankenterm/scripting/src/package.rs (NEW — .ftx ZIP handling)

## Dependencies
- zip = "2" (for .ftx reading) — add to workspace
- Already have: toml, serde, anyhow

## Testing
- Create a minimal .ftx with just manifest + WASM
- Load and verify manifest parsing
- Load and instantiate WASM module from .ftx
- Test invalid manifests are rejected with clear errors
- Test permission validation
- Test extension install/list/remove CLI commands
- **proptest**: Property-based tests for package manifest parsing — generate random valid and invalid extension.toml manifests (varying field combinations, version strings, permission sets, hook declarations), verify that valid manifests parse correctly and all fields roundtrip through serialize/deserialize, and that invalid manifests produce clear error messages rather than panics
- **criterion benchmarks**: Measure package loading performance — benchmark .ftx ZIP extraction time for packages of varying sizes (1KB theme-only to 5MB WASM+assets), manifest parsing latency, and full load_extension() pipeline including WASM compilation; establish baselines for extension marketplace responsiveness
close_reason: Implemented .ftx package format, extension manager, and extended manifest. 46 tests pass. Commit 4229bc7b.

title: Extension API: keybindings, events, pane hooks, storage
description:
# FrankenTerm Extension API: Keybindings, Events, Pane Hooks

## Why
Extensions need a rich API to be useful. This bead defines the host functions, event system, and hooks that extensions can use.

## Event system

### Built-in events (extensions can hook into)
| Event | Payload | When |
|-------|---------|------|
| `config.reload` | `{path: String}` | Config file changed |
| `pane.focus` | `{pane_id: u32, prev: u32}` | Pane focus changed |
| `pane.created` | `{pane_id: u32, domain: String}` | New pane opened |
| `pane.closed` | `{pane_id: u32}` | Pane closed |
| `pane.output` | `{pane_id: u32, text: String}` | New output (throttled) |
| `pane.title_changed` | `{pane_id: u32, title: String}` | Pane title changed |
| `tab.created` | `{tab_id: u32}` | New tab created |
| `tab.closed` | `{tab_id: u32}` | Tab closed |
| `window.focus` | `{window_id: u32}` | Window focus changed |
| `key.pressed` | `{key: String, mods: String}` | Key press (if not consumed by binding) |
| `session.save` | `{path: String}` | Session being saved |
| `session.restore` | `{path: String}` | Session being restored |

### Custom events (extensions can fire)
Extensions can fire custom events that other extensions can hook:
```
ft_fire_event("my-extension.custom-event", payload_ptr, payload_len)
```

## Host function API (WASM)

### Core functions
```
// Logging
ft_log(level: i32, msg_ptr: i32, msg_len: i32)

// Config access (read-only for most extensions)
ft_get_config(key_ptr: i32, key_len: i32, out_ptr: i32, out_len: i32) -> i32
ft_set_config(key_ptr: i32, key_len: i32, val_ptr: i32, val_len: i32) -> i32

// Pane interaction (requires pane_access permission)
ft_get_pane_text(pane_id: i32, lines: i32, out_ptr: i32, out_len: i32) -> i32
ft_send_input(pane_id: i32, text_ptr: i32, text_len: i32) -> i32
ft_get_pane_info(pane_id: i32, out_ptr: i32, out_len: i32) -> i32
ft_list_panes(out_ptr: i32, out_len: i32) -> i32

// Event system
ft_register_hook(event_ptr: i32, event_len: i32, priority: i32, func_name_ptr: i32, func_name_len: i32) -> i32
ft_fire_event(event_ptr: i32, event_len: i32, payload_ptr: i32, payload_len: i32) -> i32

// Keybinding
ft_register_keybinding(key_ptr: i32, key_len: i32, mods: i32, func_name_ptr: i32, func_name_len: i32) -> i32

// Environment (requires environment permission)
ft_get_env(key_ptr: i32, key_len: i32, out_ptr: i32, out_len: i32) -> i32

// Timer (async callback after delay)
ft_set_timeout(ms: i32, func_name_ptr: i32, func_name_len: i32) -> i32
ft_set_interval(ms: i32, func_name_ptr: i32, func_name_len: i32) -> i32
ft_clear_timer(timer_id: i32)

// Extension storage (per-extension key-value store)
ft_storage_get(key_ptr: i32, key_len: i32, out_ptr: i32, out_len: i32) -> i32
ft_storage_set(key_ptr: i32, key_len: i32, val_ptr: i32, val_len: i32) -> i32
```

## Lua API (equivalent)
The Lua engine exposes equivalent APIs through Lua tables:
```lua
frankenterm.log("info", "Hello from extension")
frankenterm.get_config("font_size")
frankenterm.on("pane.focus", function(event) ... end)
frankenterm.register_keybinding("ctrl+shift+t", function() ... end)
```

## Extension SDK (for WASM extension authors)
Provide a Rust crate `frankenterm-extension-sdk` that wraps raw host functions:
```rust
use frankenterm_extension_sdk::*;

#[ft_hook("pane.focus")]
fn on_pane_focus(event: PaneFocusEvent) -> Result<()> {
    ft::log::info!("Pane {} focused", event.pane_id);
    Ok(())
}

#[ft_hook("config.reload")]  
fn on_config_reload(event: ConfigReloadEvent) -> Result<()> {
    let theme = ft::config::get("color_scheme")?;
    ft::log::info!("Config reloaded, theme: {}", theme);
    Ok(())
}
```

## Files
- frankenterm/scripting/src/host_api.rs (NEW — host function implementations)
- frankenterm/scripting/src/events.rs (NEW — event system)
- frankenterm/scripting/src/keybindings.rs (NEW — keybinding registration)
- frankenterm/scripting/src/storage.rs (NEW — per-extension KV store)
- frankenterm-extension-sdk/ (NEW crate — Rust SDK for extension authors)

## Testing
- Test each host function individually
- Test event dispatch through extensions
- Test keybinding registration and triggering
- Test extension storage persistence
- Test permission enforcement (pane_access denied → ft_get_pane_text fails)
- Test timer/interval scheduling
- End-to-end: load an extension that registers a keybinding and fires on keypress
- **criterion benchmarks**: Measure event dispatch latency — benchmark fire_event() for each built-in event type with 1, 10, and 50 registered hooks, measure ft_register_hook() and ft_register_keybinding() registration throughput, and benchmark ft_storage_get/set latency; target <50μs for single-hook event dispatch and <500μs for 50-hook fan-out
- **proptest**: Property-based tests for event ordering — generate random sequences of hook registrations with varying priorities, fire events, and verify that hooks always execute in priority order; also generate interleaved register/unregister/fire sequences and verify no hooks are called after unregistration and no events are lost
- **LabRuntime DPOR**: Model concurrent hook execution with LabRuntime's dynamic partial-order reduction — verify that concurrent event dispatch (multiple events fired simultaneously from different panes) correctly serializes hook execution per-extension while allowing cross-extension parallelism, and that timer callbacks interleaved with event dispatch maintain consistent extension state
close_reason: Event bus (tiered dispatch), keybinding registry, per-extension KV storage. 83 tests, clippy clean. Commit 245a2da1.

title: Create SubprocessBridge base template for CLI tool integrations
description:
## SubprocessBridge Base Template

Create a reusable SubprocessBridge<T> struct that standardizes the pattern for invoking /dp CLI tools from FrankenTerm. Every Wave 1 integration repeats: binary discovery, timeout, JSON parsing, fail-open fallback.

### What to Build
In `subprocess_bridge.rs`:

```rust
pub struct SubprocessBridge<T> {
    binary_name: String,
    search_paths: Vec<PathBuf>,
    timeout: Duration,
    _phantom: PhantomData<T>,
}

impl<T: DeserializeOwned> SubprocessBridge<T> {
    pub fn new(binary: &str) -> Self;
    pub fn is_available(&self) -> bool;
    pub fn invoke(&self, args: &[&str]) -> Result<T, BridgeError>;
    pub fn invoke_with_env(&self, args: &[&str], env: &[(&str, &str)]) -> Result<T, BridgeError>;
}

pub enum BridgeError {
    BinaryNotFound(String),
    Timeout(Duration),
    ParseError(String),
    ExitCode(i32, String),
}
```

### Features
- Binary discovery: check PATH, then /dp/<project>/target/release/
- Configurable timeout (default 10s)
- JSON output parsing with serde
- Fail-open: BridgeError is non-fatal, callers decide whether to propagate
- Feature-gated: each bridge behind its own feature flag

### Unit Tests (30+)
- test_bridge_discovers_binary_in_path
- test_bridge_discovers_binary_in_dp
- test_bridge_is_available_true_when_found
- test_bridge_is_available_false_when_missing
- test_bridge_invoke_parses_json_output
- test_bridge_invoke_timeout_returns_error
- test_bridge_invoke_exit_code_error
- test_bridge_invoke_invalid_json_returns_parse_error
- test_bridge_invoke_with_env_passes_vars
- test_bridge_fail_open_pattern
- (+ 20 more edge cases: empty output, very large output, binary permission denied, etc.)

### E2E Script
```bash
# scripts/test_subprocess_bridge.sh
cargo test -p frankenterm-core -- subprocess_bridge --nocapture
echo 'PASS: SubprocessBridge tests complete'
```

### Logging
- debug!(bridge = %binary, available = %bool) on discovery
- debug!(bridge = %binary, args = ?args, timeout_ms = %timeout) on invoke
- warn!(bridge = %binary, error = %err) on failure

title: [EPIC] Performance Optimizations: Lazy Loading, Caching, Pooling
description:
# [EPIC] Performance Optimizations

## Mission
Make wa **fast and efficient** without sacrificing safety or correctness.

## Why This Matters
wa runs continuously in the background. Performance impacts:
- CPU usage (battery life on laptops)
- Memory footprint
- Latency of operations
- Scalability to many panes

Optimizations must be:
- Measurable (benchmarks prove value)
- Safe (no correctness regressions)
- Conditional (only apply when beneficial)

## Components

### 1. Lazy Pattern Compilation
Do not compile regex/Aho-Corasick engines until first use:
```rust
static PATTERN_ENGINE: Lazy<PatternEngine> = Lazy::new(|| {
    PatternEngine::compile(load_packs())
});
```

Benefits:
- Faster startup time
- Memory saved if patterns not used
- Hot-reload ready

### 2. Bloom Filter Pre-Filter
Before running Aho-Corasick, check Bloom filter:
```rust
if !bloom_filter.possibly_contains(&text) {
    return vec![]; // Quick reject
}
// Only then run full pattern matching
```

Budget: < 1µs for Bloom check

### 3. Connection Pooling for WezTerm CLI
Keep warm connections to WezTerm mux server:
```rust
struct WezTermPool {
    connections: Vec<MuxConnection>,
    max_size: usize,
}
```

Benefits:
- Avoid process spawn overhead
- Reduce socket churn
- Enable connection reuse

Note: Only beneficial if vendored mode or mux protocol direct access.

### 4. Memory-Efficient Output Cache
Already exists as `wa-4vx.4.12` - enhance with:
- LRU eviction by memory pressure
- Rolling hash for dedup detection
- Configurable cache size limits

### 5. Background Segment Compression
Already gated by `wa-4vx.3.11` decision - if needed:
- Compress segments older than N days
- Use zstd for good ratio and speed
- Transparent decompression on read
- Background compaction thread

### 6. Incremental FTS Sync
Ensure FTS index only processes new content:
- Track last-indexed segment per pane
- Batch index updates
- Avoid full reindex on restart

## Benchmarks
All optimizations must be validated by Criterion benchmarks:
- Baseline before optimization
- Result after optimization
- Regression tests to prevent backsliding

## Testing
- Benchmark suite for each optimization
- Memory profiling under sustained load
- No correctness regressions (same outputs)

## Success Criteria
- Startup time < 100ms (no feature flags)
- Pattern quick-reject < 1µs for non-matching text
- Memory usage < 100MB for typical workload
- CPU usage < 5% when idle

## Acceptance Criteria
- Each optimization yields measurable latency or memory improvement.
- Performance budgets are enforced in CI.
- Regression thresholds and baselines are documented.

title: Bloom filter pre-filter: quick reject non-matching text before regex
description:
# Bloom Filter Pre-Filter

## Purpose
Use a Bloom filter to quickly reject text that definitely doesn't match any pattern, avoiding expensive regex evaluation.

## How It Works
1. Build Bloom filter from all pattern keywords
2. For each incoming text segment:
   a. Hash key substrings through Bloom filter
   b. If Bloom returns "definitely not present" → skip
   c. Only if Bloom says "possibly present" → run full patterns

## Implementation
```rust
use bloomfilter::Bloom;

pub struct PatternEngine {
    bloom: Bloom<str>,          // Quick reject filter
    aho_corasick: AhoCorasick,  // Actual pattern matcher
}

impl PatternEngine {
    pub fn matches(&self, text: &str) -> Vec<Match> {
        // Quick reject: < 1µs
        if !self.bloom_possibly_contains(text) {
            return vec![];
        }
        // Full match: ~10-100µs
        self.aho_corasick_match(text)
    }
}
```

## Bloom Filter Parameters
- Size: ~10KB for 1000 patterns
- False positive rate: ~1%
- Hash functions: 3

## Benchmark Targets
- Bloom check: < 1µs
- Typical text (no matches): ~1µs total
- Text with matches: ~10-100µs (unchanged)
- 90%+ of segments rejected by Bloom

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Bloom filter built from pattern keywords
- [ ] Quick reject path < 1µs
- [ ] False positive rate verified < 5%
- [ ] Benchmark shows improvement for non-matching text

## Testing
- Criterion benchmarks with budgets and baseline comparison.
- Microbenchmarks for the specific optimization.
- CI regression guard with perf logs.

title: Connection pooling for WezTerm: reuse mux connections when available
description:
# Connection Pooling for WezTerm

## Purpose
Reduce overhead of WezTerm CLI calls by pooling connections to the mux server.

## Current Behavior
Each WezTerm CLI call spawns a new process, connects to mux, executes, and disconnects.

## Proposed Behavior
When using vendored mode (direct mux protocol):
```rust
pub struct WezTermPool {
    connections: Vec<MuxConnection>,
    max_size: usize,
    idle_timeout: Duration,
}

impl WezTermPool {
    pub async fn execute<T>(&self, cmd: MuxCommand) -> Result<T> {
        let conn = self.acquire().await?;
        let result = conn.execute(cmd).await;
        self.release(conn);
        result
    }
}
```

## Benefits
- Avoid process spawn overhead (~10ms per call)
- Reduce socket churn
- Enable connection keepalive
- Batch multiple operations efficiently

## Prerequisites
- Requires vendored mode (wa-nu4.4.1)
- Direct mux protocol access

## Fallback
CLI mode: No pooling possible, but can batch commands.

## Benchmark Targets
- With pooling: ~1ms per operation
- Without pooling: ~10-20ms per operation
- 10x improvement for high-frequency operations

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Connection pool implemented for vendored mode
- [ ] Idle connection cleanup
- [ ] Graceful fallback for CLI mode
- [ ] Benchmark proves improvement

## Testing
- Criterion benchmarks with budgets and baseline comparison.
- Microbenchmarks for the specific optimization.
- CI regression guard with perf logs.

title: Incremental FTS sync: avoid full reindex, track per-pane progress
description:
# Incremental FTS Sync

## Purpose
Ensure FTS index only processes new content, avoiding expensive full reindex operations.

## Current Challenge
On restart, wa might need to determine what's already indexed and what's new.

## Solution
```rust
pub struct FtsIndexState {
    /// Last indexed segment seq per pane
    per_pane_progress: HashMap<PaneId, SegmentSeq>,
    /// Global index version for schema changes
    index_version: u32,
}
```

## Sync Process
1. On startup: Load `per_pane_progress` from DB
2. For each pane: Query segments where `seq > last_indexed_seq`
3. Index only new segments
4. Update progress after successful batch

## Batching Strategy
- Batch size: 100 segments or 1MB text
- Commit progress after each batch
- Resume from last batch on crash

## Performance Impact
- Full reindex: O(total segments)
- Incremental: O(new segments)
- Startup overhead: O(1) - just load progress

## Recovery
If index corrupt or schema changed:
- Detect via `index_version` mismatch
- Trigger full rebuild
- Show progress indicator

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Per-pane progress tracked in DB
- [ ] Only new segments indexed on restart
- [ ] Batch processing with progress commits
- [ ] Full rebuild triggered on version mismatch
- [ ] Benchmark shows startup improvement

## Testing
- Criterion benchmarks with budgets and baseline comparison.
- Microbenchmarks for the specific optimization.
- CI regression guard with perf logs.

All 10 new tests pass.

title: Performance benchmarks and budgets: Criterion suite with regression guards
description:
# Performance benchmarks and budgets (Criterion)

## Goal
Establish benchmarks for all performance-critical paths and prevent regressions with explicit, documented budgets.

This system sits on the hot path of “every command the user runs” (watch loop, pattern matching, policy checks). Performance regressions are user-visible.

## Benchmark suite (Criterion)
Benchmarks must target *real* hot paths and be runnable locally:

```rust
// benches/pattern_engine.rs
criterion_group!(
    pattern_benchmarks,
    bench_bloom_check,
    bench_aho_corasick_match,
    bench_full_pattern_pipeline,
);

// benches/ingest.rs
criterion_group!(
    ingest_benchmarks,
    bench_delta_extraction,
    bench_segment_persistence,
    bench_fts_indexing,
);
```

## What we benchmark (minimum set)
- Quick reject / prefilter:
  - `memchr`/bloom/no-match fast paths
  - worst-case “near match but reject” path
- Pattern pipeline:
  - no-hit text (must be very fast)
  - one-hit typical text
  - extraction path with captures
- Ingest/deltas:
  - delta extraction on typical scrollback
  - gap detection path
- Storage:
  - write queue throughput (bounded queue)
  - FTS indexing cost for typical segment sizes
- Query surfaces:
  - typical FTS query latency (scoped)
  - worst-case query guardrails (bounded)

## Performance budgets (absolute ceilings)
Budgets are set as “this must feel snappy to users” ceilings. Exact numbers may be tuned after first implementation, but budgets must exist before optimization work is called done.

| Operation | Budget (target ceiling) | Notes |
|-----------|--------------------------|-------|
| Bloom filter check | < 1µs | hot path prefilter |
| Pattern match (no hit) | < 10µs | must be cheap for most text |
| Pattern match (with hit) | < 100µs | includes extraction |
| Delta extraction | < 1ms | per pane per tick typical |
| FTS insert (single) | < 5ms | typical segment size |
| FTS query (typical) | < 50ms | scoped query; “feels instant” |
| Startup (no patterns) | < 100ms | CLI responsiveness |

## Regression detection strategy (CI realities)
Perf measurement is noisy on shared runners. The plan must be robust:

- Local dev loop:
  - `cargo bench` is the source of truth for tuning.
  - Provide a short “budget check” summary line per benchmark so developers can self-serve.

- CI loop (two-tier):
  1) **PR job (warn-only by default)**
     - Run benches and upload `criterion` output + a short summary artifact.
     - Fail only on catastrophic regressions (e.g., >2x slower OR exceeding a hard ceiling by a large margin).
  2) **Main/perf job (enforce budgets)**
     - Prefer a stable environment (self-hosted runner if available).
     - Enforce budgets strictly and record historical trend artifacts.

- Baselines:
  - Store a baseline artifact from main (or a tagged commit) and compare PR results against it.
  - Comparisons must ignore obviously-noisy fields and focus on timing deltas.

## Reporting
Example (desired UX):
```
$ cargo bench --bench pattern_engine

bloom_check         time:   [0.8 µs 0.9 µs 1.0 µs]  ✓ (budget: 1µs)
aho_corasick_match  time:   [8.2 µs 8.5 µs 8.8 µs]  ✓ (budget: 10µs)
full_pipeline       time:   [45 µs 48 µs 51 µs]     ✓ (budget: 100µs)
```

On regression, the report must include:
- which benchmark regressed
- old vs new timings
- which budget was exceeded (if any)
- where to find the artifacts (CI URL/path)

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Criterion benchmarks exist for the minimum hot paths listed above.
- [ ] Budgets are documented and checked by an automated “budget check” step.
- [ ] CI produces artifacts for every run (raw criterion + summarized results).
- [ ] CI regression detection works (warn-only on PR; enforced on stable perf job).

## Testing
- Benchmark harness self-checks:
  - benches compile and run on supported platforms.
  - the budget-checking logic is covered by unit tests (parsing/threshold evaluation).
- CI regression guard tests:
  - include a small synthetic “known regression” fixture in test mode to verify:
    - the budget checker fails when it should
    - output includes the expected summary fields

description:
# Unify TUI Stack for FrankenTerm Dashboard

## Skills: /idea-wizard, /extreme-software-optimization

## Available TUI libraries (all ours)
1. **charmed_rust** (bubbletea Elm architecture, lipgloss styling, 16+ widgets)
2. **frankentui** (minimal kernel, diff-based rendering, SIMD, inline mode)
3. **rich_rust** (output formatting, tables, panels, syntax highlighting)
4. **opentui_rust** (low-level foundation, deterministic rendering)

## Integration plan

### Architecture
- **frankentui** as the rendering kernel (diff-based, RAII cleanup, inline mode)
- **charmed_rust** widgets for interactive components (lists, tables, text input)
- **lipgloss** for consistent styling across all UI elements
- **rich_rust** for formatted output in non-interactive contexts (CLI, robot mode)

### Dashboard components
1. **Pane picker**: Browse active panes, filter by status/age/CPU, select to focus
2. **Event feed**: Real-time stream of pattern detections, workflow triggers, alerts
3. **Stats panel**: Live metrics — pane count, memory, CPU pressure, FD usage
4. **Cost tracker**: Per-provider spending, quota bars, rate limit alerts (from caut)
5. **Session history**: Recent cass search results, relevant past solutions
6. **Bead progress**: Current bead work items, dependency graph visualization

### Inline mode (killer feature)
FrankenTerm TUI uses frankentui's inline mode:
- Status bar at bottom: pane count, alerts, CPU/memory pressure
- Agent output scrolls above naturally
- UI chrome never disrupts scrollback

### Performance (/extreme-software-optimization)
- Rendering: <16ms per frame (60fps capable)
- Diff-based: only redraw changed cells
- SIMD: accelerated color computation and layout calculation

## Tests
- Visual regression tests for each dashboard component
- Performance: measure render time under 200-pane load
- Inline mode: verify scrollback not disrupted

## Acceptance criteria
- Dashboard renders all 6 components
- Inline mode works correctly
- <16ms render time per frame
- Consistent styling via lipgloss
- Graceful degradation on small terminals

## Test Framework Requirements
- **Criterion benchmarks**: TUI render frame time benchmarks targeting <16ms for 60fps:
  - Full dashboard render: benchmark rendering all 6 components with realistic data (200 panes, 50 events, 16 providers). Target <16ms per frame.
  - Diff-based render: benchmark incremental render when only 1 component changes. Target <2ms per frame.
  - Individual component render: benchmark each of the 6 components individually. Identify the most expensive component.
  - Terminal size scaling: benchmark render at 80x24, 120x40, 200x60 terminal sizes. Verify render time scales sub-linearly.
  - SIMD color computation: benchmark lipgloss color blending with and without SIMD. Verify >2x improvement.
- **Proptest for widget layout invariants**: Property-based tests for layout correctness:
  - Generate random terminal dimensions (width 20-300, height 10-100), verify all widgets fit within bounds (no overflow, no negative sizes)
  - Generate random data sizes (0 to 10000 items in lists, 0 to 200 panes), verify layout remains valid (no overlapping widgets, no gaps)
  - Generate random resize sequences, verify layout recalculation produces consistent results (same final size = same final layout, regardless of intermediate sizes)
  - For each widget: generate random content, verify the rendered output has the correct number of lines and columns (matches the allocated space)

## Cross-References
- **wa-3kxe.5** (Operational telemetry): The dashboard's stats panel displays telemetry data collected by the operational telemetry pipeline. The telemetry system produces histograms, counters, and resource metrics; the dashboard consumes and visualizes them. Coordinate the data format — the telemetry pipeline should emit data in a structure the dashboard can directly render without transformation.

## Test and Observability Plan
1. Add comprehensive unit tests covering happy path, boundary/edge cases, and explicit failure/error behavior for logic introduced or changed by this bead.
2. Add deterministic integration and end-to-end scenario scripts that exercise full workflow behavior, including at least one negative/failure scenario and one recovery scenario.
3. Emit detailed structured logs during tests and e2e runs (timestamp, subsystem, correlation_id, scenario_id, inputs, decisions, outcomes, reason_code/error_code).
4. Persist triage artifacts for failed runs (stdout/stderr, structured logs, snapshots/fixtures, and concise failure summaries) so regressions can be root-caused quickly.
5. Ensure test commands and evidence locations are documented in the bead implementation notes and wired into normal validation/CI paths.

## User Impact
1. Specify the concrete operator/agent workflow pain this bead removes (speed, reliability, safety, or clarity).
2. Define measurable user-facing outcomes (for example p95 latency, failure/timeout rate, time-to-recovery, or reduction in manual intervention steps).
3. Define no-regression UX guarantees and explicit rollback/degradation behavior if those outcomes are not met.

3. Require structured diagnostics/logging and artifact bundles for decision points, data flows, and failure signatures.
4. Heavy compile/test/lint/benchmark runs must execute via rch and be recorded as evidence.

title: Epic: Memory Safety and Legacy Cleanup
description:
# Background
The project integrates legacy code from Rio and WezTerm. The UBS scan found critical memory safety hazards in these legacy areas, including `mem::transmute` and `mem::forget`. Additionally, there are `mem::forget` calls in `crates/frankenterm-core/src/session_restore.rs`.

# Reasoning
`mem::transmute` bypasses the compiler's type safety checks and can easily cause Undefined Behavior (UB) if the types have different sizes or layouts. `mem::forget` deliberately leaks memory or prevents destructors from running, which is dangerous in a long-running daemon unless strictly necessary for FFI.

# Goals
1. Remove or safely encapsulate `mem::transmute` usages in `legacy_rio` and `legacy_wezterm`.
2. Refactor `mem::forget` in `session_restore.rs` to use safe ownership transfer or `ManuallyDrop` if FFI is involved, ensuring no actual memory leaks occur in pure Rust code.

title: [EPIC] Fork Hardening — Fix WezTerm mux server root causes
description:
## Goal
Fix root causes in the forked WezTerm mux server that cause it to die under agent swarm load, moving beyond client-side workarounds to true reliability.

## Background & Motivation
From the user's X post: "I'm just so tired of WezTerm dying horribly under the extreme load of my agent swarm sessions and losing time and work. It just wasn't built for these assumptions."

The wa-3cyp performance epic focuses on CLIENT-side optimizations (polling, pooling, compression). This epic goes INTO THE WEZTERM CODE ITSELF to fix the root causes:
1. Memory leaks in the mux server (76GB RSS after 23 days observed)
2. No memory limits or OOM prevention
3. No incremental snapshot capability
4. Lock contention in hot paths

The user decided "I want to rename it to FrankenTerm and control the entire stack all the way for full control." This epic delivers on that promise by making the fork genuinely more reliable than upstream WezTerm for agent swarm workloads.

## Design Philosophy (Extreme Software Optimization)
Every change follows the ESO loop:
1. BASELINE — Measure current behavior (hyperfine, heaptrack)
2. PROFILE — Identify actual hotspots (not guesses)
3. PROVE — Golden outputs + isomorphism proof per change
4. IMPLEMENT — Only changes with Opportunity Score ≥ 2.0
5. VERIFY — sha256sum -c golden_checksums.txt
6. REPEAT — Re-profile (bottlenecks shift)

## Scope
This epic covers 5 targeted changes to the forked WezTerm mux server:
1. Memory leak root cause analysis and patches
2. cgroups memory budget and OOM prevention
3. Differential snapshots for continuous saving
4. Lock-free capture pipeline
5. Operational telemetry pipeline

## Relationship to Existing Beads
- Extends wa-3cyp (performance) — but focuses on WezTerm server code, not wa client
- Enables wa-rsaf (session persistence) — differential snapshots enable continuous saving
- Complements wa-2cha (watchdog) — OOM prevention adds another layer of protection

## Dependencies
- FrankenTerm rename (wa-vv3h) should ideally complete first (we're modifying forked code)
- No hard blockers — can start profiling immediately

## Acceptance Criteria
- Memory leak root causes identified and patched with isomorphism proofs
- cgroups memory budget prevents OOM with proactive save triggers
- Differential snapshots reduce save time to sub-100ms
- Lock-free capture eliminates contention in hot path
- Telemetry pipeline provides full observability
- All changes follow ESO loop (profile → prove → implement → verify)
- Comprehensive benchmark suite for regression detection

## Success Criteria
1. The complete epic scope is delivered across child beads with no unresolved critical blockers and no loss of declared capability.
2. Every child feature/task in this epic includes comprehensive unit tests plus deterministic integration/E2E scenarios.
3. The epic includes an end-to-end validation matrix covering happy paths, failure injection, recovery behavior, and sustained/soak execution where applicable.
4. Structured logging and artifact standards are enforced across epic deliverables (timestamp, correlation_id, scenario_id, decision path, reason_code/error_code) with triage-ready evidence bundles.
5. Verification demonstrates stable, repeatable outcomes across reruns and confirms policy/safety invariants for all touched subsystems.

## User Impact
1. Specify the concrete operator/agent workflow pain this bead removes (speed, reliability, safety, or clarity).
2. Define measurable user-facing outcomes (for example p95 latency, failure/timeout rate, time-to-recovery, or reduction in manual intervention steps).
3. Define no-regression UX guarantees and explicit rollback/degradation behavior if those outcomes are not met.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Resolve identified fork-level reliability root causes (memory leaks, resource/lock pathologies, snapshot resilience) with no user-visible feature regression.
2. Require ESO evidence discipline: baseline/profile/patch/verify cycle documented for each major change with before/after metrics and invariants.
3. Require comprehensive validation: unit tests, integration tests, end-to-end scripts, benchmarks, and soak scenarios covering failure injection and recovery workflows.
4. Require structured diagnostics/logging for leak signatures, contention metrics, snapshot operations, and degradation/rollback events with reproducible artifacts.
5. Enforce production-safety gates: rollback readiness, kill-switch behavior, and residual risk ownership before closure.

title: Memory leak root cause analysis and patches (ESO methodology)
description:
## Goal
Systematically profile the WezTerm mux server under agent swarm load to identify and fix the root causes of memory leaks, using the ESO (Extreme Software Optimization) methodology with isomorphism proofs for every patch.

## Background & Motivation
The user observed 76GB RSS after 23 days of agent swarm operation. The mux server was never designed for this workload (50+ panes, continuous output, long-running). The leaks are likely in:
- Terminal state accumulation (cursor history, attribute stacks)
- Scrollback buffer growth (even with limits, internal fragmentation)
- Notification subscriber accumulation (Screen::set_dirty notifies ALL subscribers)
- Codec/parser state accumulation (incomplete escape sequences held in memory)
- Tab/pane metadata that grows but never shrinks

## Technical Approach (ESO Loop)

### Phase 1: Baseline
```bash
# Start mux server with 50 panes simulating agent output
hyperfine --warmup 1 --runs 3 'wezterm cli list-clients'

# Record baseline RSS over time
while true; do ps -o rss= -p $MUX_PID >> /tmp/rss_baseline.csv; sleep 60; done
```

### Phase 2: Profile
```bash
# Heap profiling (find allocations that never get freed)
heaptrack wezterm-mux-server --daemonize=false

# DHAT for allocation patterns
valgrind --tool=dhat wezterm-mux-server --daemonize=false

# Custom allocator with tracking
MALLOC_CONF="prof:true,prof_prefix:/tmp/jeprof" wezterm-mux-server
```

### Phase 3: Identify Top Allocators
From heaptrack output, identify:
- Top 5 allocation sites by total bytes (leaks)
- Top 5 allocation sites by count (fragmentation)
- Allocations that grow monotonically with time (unbounded growth)

### Phase 4: Patch with Isomorphism Proof
For each leak source:
```
## Change: Cap terminal attribute stack at 256 entries
- Ordering preserved:     yes — FIFO stack semantics unchanged
- Tie-breaking unchanged: yes — no ordering affected
- Floating-point:         N/A
- RNG seeds:              N/A
- Golden outputs:         sha256sum -c golden_checksums.txt ✓
```

### Phase 5: Verify
```bash
# Run same workload, compare RSS curve
# Must be within 10% of baseline at t=0h
# Must not grow faster than 1MB/hour with 50 active panes
```

## Expected Leak Sources (Hypotheses)
1. **Screen::set_dirty subscribers**: Each subscriber registration may not be cleaned up when panes are dropped
2. **Terminal::parser_state**: Incomplete escape sequence buffers may accumulate
3. **Scrollback internal fragmentation**: Vec<Line> with small allocations creating fragmentation
4. **TabState metadata**: Per-tab state that grows with pane operations
5. **Mux notification channels**: Unbounded channel buffers for pane events

## Implementation Location
- WezTerm source: wezterm-mux-server/ and mux/ crates
- Profiling scripts: scripts/profiling/
- Golden outputs: tests/golden/

## Configuration
N/A — this is analysis and patching work, not a runtime feature.

## Dependencies
- FrankenTerm fork (bd-20fw) should be set up first
- Profiling needs a Linux machine (heaptrack, DHAT) → trj or css

## Acceptance Criteria
- Top 5 memory leak sources identified with heaptrack evidence
- Each leak patched with isomorphism proof documenting behavior preservation
- RSS growth rate < 1MB/hour with 50 active panes (down from ~130MB/hour)
- Golden output tests pass before and after patches
- Profiling scripts committed for future regression detection
- Results documented: before/after RSS curves, allocation profiles

## macOS Compatibility (Leak Detection Tools)
On macOS, Valgrind and heaptrack are not available (or poorly supported). Use macOS-native alternatives:
- **`leaks` tool** (built-in): `leaks --atExit -- wezterm-mux-server` — reports all leaked allocations at process exit. Use `leaks --groupByType` for categorized output.
- **Instruments.app**: Use the "Leaks" and "Allocations" instruments for interactive profiling. Instruments provides allocation flame graphs, leak detection, and memory growth tracking equivalent to heaptrack.
- **`malloc_history`**: Track allocation history for specific addresses identified by `leaks`.
- **`vmmap`**: Analyze virtual memory regions to understand fragmentation and large allocations.
- **jemalloc prof on macOS**: jemalloc's profiling (`MALLOC_CONF="prof:true"`) works on macOS. Use `jeprof` to analyze heap profiles — this is the cross-platform option that works on both Linux and macOS.
- **Recommended workflow**: Use `leaks` + Instruments on macOS for initial triage, jemalloc prof for cross-platform profiling, and Valgrind/heaptrack on Linux (trj/css) for deep analysis. Compare results across platforms to catch platform-specific leaks.

## Test Framework Requirements
- **Criterion benchmarks**: Memory usage over time benchmarks:
  - Benchmark RSS growth rate: run mux server with 50 mock panes for 1000 capture cycles, measure RSS at start and end. Target <1KB/cycle growth.
  - Benchmark per-pane memory footprint: create panes with varying scrollback sizes (1K, 10K, 100K lines), measure memory per pane. Track this as a regression metric.
  - Benchmark allocation rate: measure allocations/sec during steady-state capture. Identify allocation-heavy code paths.

## Cross-References
- **wa-3axa** (Custom allocator): The custom allocator (jemalloc + per-pane arenas) is designed to mitigate the leaks this bead identifies. Root cause analysis here informs allocator arena design — if leaks are primarily in scrollback buffers, per-pane arenas should isolate scrollback allocations. If leaks are in shared state (subscribers, notification channels), the allocator needs a different strategy.

## Test and Observability Plan
1. Add comprehensive unit tests covering happy path, boundary/edge cases, and explicit failure/error behavior for logic introduced or changed by this bead.
2. Add deterministic integration and end-to-end scenario scripts that exercise full workflow behavior, including at least one negative/failure scenario and one recovery scenario.
3. Emit detailed structured logs during tests and e2e runs (timestamp, subsystem, correlation_id, scenario_id, inputs, decisions, outcomes, reason_code/error_code).
4. Persist triage artifacts for failed runs (stdout/stderr, structured logs, snapshots/fixtures, and concise failure summaries) so regressions can be root-caused quickly.
5. Ensure test commands and evidence locations are documented in the bead implementation notes and wired into normal validation/CI paths.

## User Impact
1. Specify the concrete operator/agent workflow pain this bead removes (speed, reliability, safety, or clarity).
2. Define measurable user-facing outcomes (for example p95 latency, failure/timeout rate, time-to-recovery, or reduction in manual intervention steps).
3. Define no-regression UX guarantees and explicit rollback/degradation behavior if those outcomes are not met.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Complete memory-leak RCA with attributable root causes and validated patches for targeted leak sources under agent-swarm workloads.
2. Produce before/after memory-growth evidence under representative load profiles with deterministic measurement harnesses.
3. Require comprehensive validation: unit tests, integration tests, end-to-end scripts, and long-run leak regression tests with explicit pass/fail thresholds.
4. Require structured diagnostics/logging for allocation classes, leak candidates, patch impact deltas, and residual anomalous signals with replay artifacts.
5. Closure requires auditable proof that leak-growth budgets are met and no critical regressions were introduced.

title: cgroups v2 memory budget and OOM prevention
description:
# cgroups v2 Memory Budget and OOM Prevention

## Skills: /extreme-software-optimization

## Goal
Use cgroups v2 on Linux (and equivalent macOS mechanisms) to enforce per-pane memory budgets, preventing the mux server from being OOM-killed.

## Linux: cgroups v2
Create a cgroup hierarchy for FrankenTerm:
- /sys/fs/cgroup/frankenterm/ — top-level cgroup for mux server
- /sys/fs/cgroup/frankenterm/pane-<id>/ — per-pane child cgroups
- Set memory.max per pane cgroup (configurable, default 1GB)
- Set memory.high as soft limit (triggers throttling, not kill)
- Monitor memory.current for per-pane RSS tracking

## macOS Alternative
macOS lacks cgroups. Use advisory memory management:
- Jetsam priority adjustment via memorystatus_control (if available)
- Per-pane jemalloc arena with budget tracking (from wa-3axa)
- If pane arena exceeds budget: warn, pause captures, suggest cleanup
- OOM prevention: protect mux server via lower OOM score (Jetsam priority)
- Memory pressure monitoring via os_proc_available_memory() and vm_statistics64

## Implementation
```rust
#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]
mod cgroup {
    pub fn create_pane_cgroup(pane_id: PaneId, budget_bytes: u64) -> Result<()> { ... }
    pub fn destroy_pane_cgroup(pane_id: PaneId) -> Result<()> { ... }
    pub fn read_memory_current(pane_id: PaneId) -> Result<u64> { ... }
}

#[cfg(target_os = "macos")]
mod memory_budget {
    pub fn create_pane_budget(pane_id: PaneId, budget_bytes: u64) -> Result<()> { ... }
    pub fn check_pane_usage(pane_id: PaneId) -> Result<u64> { ... }
}
```

## Tests
- **Linux**: Create cgroup, set memory.max, verify enforcement
- **Linux**: Pane exceeding budget triggers throttling (memory.high)
- **macOS**: Arena budget tracking matches expected usage
- **macOS**: Memory pressure detection triggers warnings
- **Criterion benchmarks**: cgroup stat read <50μs per pane
- Test cleanup: all cgroups destroyed on pane close

## Acceptance criteria
- Per-pane memory budgets enforced (cgroups v2 on Linux, advisory on macOS)
- Mux server protected from OOM kill
- Per-pane RSS tracking without /proc parsing (via cgroup stats or arena stats)
- Graceful handling when cgroups v2 not available (fall back to advisory)
- Works on both Linux and macOS
close_reason: Implemented memory_budget.rs with cgroups v2 per-pane hierarchy (Linux) and advisory budget tracking (macOS). BudgetLevel tiers, MemoryBudgetConfig, PaneBudget state, MemoryBudgetManager with lock-free worst-level reads, OOM score protection, cgroups v2 availability check. 35 tests all passing. Committed and pushed to main.

title: Differential snapshots for continuous background saving
description:
# Differential Snapshots for Continuous Background Saving

## Skills: /extreme-software-optimization

## Goal
Implement differential (incremental) snapshots that capture only CHANGED state since the last snapshot, reducing I/O and CPU overhead for continuous background saving.

## How it works
1. Maintain a "dirty set" of pane IDs whose state changed since last snapshot
2. On snapshot:
   - Only capture panes in the dirty set
   - Write diff records (old_value → new_value) for changed fields
   - Store diffs as a chain: base_snapshot → diff1 → diff2 → ...
3. Periodically compact: merge diff chain into new base snapshot

## Dirty tracking
- Mark pane dirty on: output received, resize, title change, process exit
- Mark clean after: pane is successfully captured in a diff snapshot
- Track at field granularity: scrollback dirty vs metadata dirty

## Diff record format
```rust
pub enum SnapshotDiff {
    PaneScrollbackChanged { pane_id: PaneId, new_lines: Range<usize> },
    PaneMetadataChanged { pane_id: PaneId, fields: Vec<(String, DynValue)> },
    PaneCreated { pane_id: PaneId, snapshot: PaneSnapshot },
    PaneClosed { pane_id: PaneId },
    LayoutChanged { tab_id: TabId, new_layout: Layout },
}
```

## Restore from diff chain
1. Load base snapshot
2. Apply diffs in order
3. Result: complete state at the time of last diff

## Relationship to WAL (wa-283h4.2)
Differential snapshots are the SIMPLER version of continuous persistence:
- Diff snapshots: periodic (every 5 min), captures changed state
- WAL: continuous, captures every mutation
- If WAL is implemented, diff snapshots become redundant
- Implement diff snapshots first (simpler), WAL later (optimal)

## Tests
- Create base snapshot, modify 3 panes, take diff → verify only 3 diffs recorded
- Restore from base + diff chain → verify identical to current state
- **proptest**: Random sequence of modifications + snapshots → restore always matches current state
- **Criterion benchmarks**: diff snapshot with 200 panes, 5 dirty → target <50ms
- Compaction: chain of 10 diffs compacts into single base → restore still works
- Edge case: pane created after base, closed before next snapshot

## Acceptance criteria
- Dirty tracking at field granularity
- Diff-only snapshots for changed panes
- Restore from diff chain produces correct state
- Compaction reduces chain length without data loss
- <50ms for diff snapshot with 5 dirty panes out of 200
close_reason: Differential snapshot module complete: DirtyTracker, SnapshotDiff, DiffChain, DiffSnapshotEngine with auto-compaction. 36 tests (33 unit + 3 proptest) all passing. Added Criterion benchmarks with 5 groups (capture/restore/compact/tracker/scrollback). All acceptance criteria met.

title: Lock-free SPSC ring buffer for capture pipeline
description:
# Lock-Free SPSC Ring Buffer for Capture Pipeline

## Skills: /alien-artifact-coding (concurrency correctness), /extreme-software-optimization

## Goal
Replace the current capture pipeline buffering (Mutex-protected Vec) with a lock-free single-producer single-consumer (SPSC) ring buffer for zero-contention data flow from capture thread to processing thread.

## Why SPSC (not MPMC)
The capture pipeline is strictly producer→consumer:
- Producer: capture thread writes pane output
- Consumer: processing thread reads and indexes
- No contention needed — SPSC is optimal for this pattern
- MPMC (wa-1sm78) is for the event bus where multiple producers exist

## Design
```rust
pub struct SpscRingBuffer<T> {
    buffer: Box<[MaybeUninit<T>]>,
    head: CachePadded<AtomicUsize>,  // Write position (producer)
    tail: CachePadded<AtomicUsize>,  // Read position (consumer)
    capacity: usize,
}
```

Key properties:
- Cache-line padded head/tail to prevent false sharing
- Power-of-2 capacity for fast modulo (bitwise AND)
- No allocations after construction
- Wait-free: both push and pop are O(1)

## Formal Verification (/alien-artifact-coding)
SPSC ring buffer MUST be proven:
- **Linearizable**: Each push/pop appears atomic
- **No data races**: Producer never writes where consumer is reading
- **No lost elements**: Every pushed element is eventually poppable
- **Bounded**: Buffer never exceeds capacity

## Tests
- **Criterion benchmarks**: Push/pop throughput, target >100M ops/sec
- **LabRuntime DPOR**: Schedule exploration for producer/consumer interleavings
- **Loom**: Verify memory ordering correctness under TSO and weaker models
- **proptest**: Random push/pop sequences → verify every pushed element eventually popped
- Stress test: sustained 1GB/sec throughput for 60 seconds
- False sharing test: verify via perf stat that cache misses are near-zero

## Acceptance criteria
- Zero-contention SPSC ring buffer
- Cache-line padded to prevent false sharing
- >100M ops/sec throughput
- Formally verified correctness
- No allocations in steady state
- LabRuntime + Loom verification passes

title: Operational telemetry pipeline — structured tracing, histograms, resource tracking
description:
# Operational Telemetry Pipeline — Structured Tracing, Histograms, Resource Tracking

## Skills: /extreme-software-optimization

## Goal
Build a unified telemetry pipeline that collects structured metrics, traces, and resource observations from all FrankenTerm subsystems.

## What it collects
1. **Structured tracing**: spans for every operation (capture, process, store) with timing and context
2. **Histograms**: latency distributions for key operations (capture, PDU encode/decode, storage write)
3. **Resource tracking**:
   - RSS, virtual memory, FD count for mux server process
   - Per-pane CPU and memory (via process tree)
   - Disk I/O rates (SQLite write throughput)
   - Network stats (mux connection health)

## Platform-specific resource collection
- **Linux**: /proc/<pid>/status (VmRSS, VmSize), /proc/<pid>/fd/ (FD count), /proc/<pid>/io (read/write bytes)
- **macOS**: proc_pidinfo(PROC_PIDTASKINFO) for RSS/CPU, proc_pidinfo(PROC_PIDLISTFDS) for FD count, no direct /proc/*/io equivalent — use getrusage() for I/O approximation
- Abstract behind a `SystemMetrics` trait with platform-specific impls

## Storage
- In-memory circular buffer for recent metrics (last 1 hour, 30s resolution)
- SQLite table for long-term storage (hourly aggregates)
- Prometheus-compatible exposition endpoint (optional feature)

## Integration points
- Survival model (wa-1qz1.1): consumes RSS observations
- Conformal prediction (wa-1qz1.4): consumes resource time series
- Auto-tuning (wa-ssm4): uses metric distributions
- MuxWatchdog (wa-2cha): consumes health metrics
- Memory pressure engine (wa-2ahu0): consumes RSS per-pane

## Tests
- **Criterion benchmarks**: metric recording overhead <100ns per metric point
- Verify structured tracing spans nest correctly
- Verify histogram quantile accuracy (p50, p95, p99 within 5%)
- **Test both Linux and macOS metric collection paths**
- Verify circular buffer eviction at capacity
- Integration: metrics flow from collection to storage to API

## Acceptance criteria
- Unified metric collection across all subsystems
- Platform-specific resource collection (Linux + macOS) behind SystemMetrics trait
- <100ns per metric recording (no hot-path overhead)
- Histogram quantiles accurate to within 5%
- Optional Prometheus exposition endpoint
- In-memory + SQLite storage with configurable retention

title: Fork Hardening benchmark and test suite (ESO methodology)
description:
## Goal
Comprehensive benchmark and test suite for Fork Hardening changes, following the ESO methodology: golden outputs, isomorphism proofs, before/after measurements.

## Test Categories

### 1. Memory Leak Regression Tests
- Start mux with 50 simulated panes
- Run for 1 hour with continuous output
- Measure RSS at start, every 5 minutes, and at end
- PASS criteria: RSS growth < 1MB/hour (down from ~130MB/hour)
- Golden outputs: RSS curve must be within 10% of baseline

### 2. Lock-Free Buffer Tests
- Concurrent push/pop correctness (no data loss, no corruption)
- Overflow behavior (gap emission after threshold)
- Performance: P99 capture latency < 5ms under 50 panes

### 3. Differential Snapshot Tests
- Dirty tracking accuracy (only changed panes serialized)
- Diff chain application (base + N diffs = correct state)
- Continuous saving loop stability (24-hour stress test)
- Sub-100ms save time for typical diffs

### 4. cgroups Integration Tests (Linux only)
- Memory limit enforcement (mux stays within budget)
- Proactive save trigger at threshold
- Alert generation at critical threshold
- Fallback behavior on macOS (monitoring-only)

### 5. Telemetry Accuracy Tests
- Histogram accuracy vs known latency distribution
- Resource tracking accuracy vs /proc values
- Span hierarchy correctness (parent-child relationships)

### 6. Isomorphism Proofs (per patch)
Each mux server patch includes:
```
## Change: [description]
- Ordering preserved:     [yes/no + why]
- Tie-breaking unchanged: [yes/no + why]
- Floating-point:         [identical/N/A]
- Golden outputs:         sha256sum -c golden_checksums.txt ✓
```

### Implementation Location
- crates/wa-core/tests/fork_hardening_tests.rs
- crates/wa-core/benches/fork_hardening_benchmarks.rs
- scripts/profiling/ (heaptrack scripts, RSS monitoring)

## Dependencies
- Depends on all Fork Hardening beads being implemented
- Memory leak tests require Linux machine (trj or css)

## Acceptance Criteria
- Memory leak regression test passing (< 1MB/hour growth)
- Lock-free buffer correctness and performance tests
- Differential snapshot accuracy and speed benchmarks
- cgroups integration tests (Linux) and fallback tests (macOS)
- Telemetry accuracy validation
- All ESO isomorphism proofs documented per patch
- CI integration for regression detection

## Test Framework Requirements
- **Criterion benchmarks**: Comprehensive benchmarks for ALL hardening improvements:
  - Memory leak regression: benchmark RSS growth rate per 1000 capture cycles (target <1KB/cycle)
  - Lock-free SPSC buffer: benchmark push/pop throughput under contention (target >10M ops/sec)
  - Differential snapshot: benchmark diff computation time for varying pane counts (10, 50, 200) and dirty ratios (1%, 10%, 50%)
  - Snapshot save latency: benchmark full save cycle (dirty detection + diff + serialize + write). Target <100ms for typical diffs.
  - Telemetry overhead: benchmark the cost of tracing instrumentation. Target <1% overhead vs uninstrumented code.
  - Before/after comparison: each benchmark must record a baseline (before hardening) and improved (after hardening) measurement for the ESO isomorphism proof.
- **Proptest for regression detection**: Property-based tests that catch regressions:
  - Generate random pane output sequences, apply all hardening patches, and verify output is bit-identical to unhardened path (behavioral isomorphism)
  - Generate random capture schedules (varying timing, ordering), verify all pane data is captured correctly regardless of schedule
  - Generate random memory pressure scenarios, verify eviction decisions are deterministic and reproducible
  - For each ESO patch: generate random inputs, verify the golden output checksum matches (automated isomorphism verification)

title: Replace reqwest HTTP client with asupersync::http
description:
# Replace reqwest HTTP client with asupersync::http

## Background
reqwest is the primary HTTP client library, used for outbound API calls. It transitively depends on tokio, so it must be replaced.

## asupersync HTTP client
asupersync provides its own HTTP client built on its reactor:
- No tokio dependency
- Supports HTTPS via rustls integration
- JSON request/response bodies
- Connection pooling built-in

## Affected code
- Any module making outbound HTTP requests
- Feature-gated behind web/MCP features

## Migration pattern
```rust
// Before
let client = reqwest::Client::new();
let resp = client.get(url)
    .header("Authorization", token)
    .json(&body)
    .send().await?
    .json::<Response>().await?;

// After
let client = asupersync::http::Client::new();
let resp = client.get(cx, url)
    .header("Authorization", token)
    .json(&body)
    .send().await?
    .json::<Response>().await?;
```

## Acceptance criteria
- reqwest removed from Cargo.toml
- All HTTP requests use asupersync::http
- TLS works for HTTPS endpoints
- JSON serialization/deserialization works
- Timeout/retry behavior preserved

## Benchmark requirements
- **Criterion benchmarks for HTTP request latency**: Add `benches/http_client.rs` measuring:
  - HTTP GET request latency to localhost (minimal network overhead)
  - HTTPS GET request latency (includes TLS handshake)
  - JSON POST request latency with body serialization (varying body sizes: 1KB, 10KB, 100KB)
  - Connection reuse: first request vs subsequent request latency (connection pooling benefit)
  - Concurrent request throughput: requests/sec with N=1,2,4,8 concurrent requests
  - Comparison with reqwest for equivalent operations (same endpoints, same payloads)

## Property-based testing
- **Proptest for HTTP response parsing**: Use proptest to generate arbitrary HTTP response bodies and verify:
  - JSON deserialization correctly handles all valid JSON structures (nested objects, arrays, unicode, escapes)
  - Malformed JSON produces appropriate error variants (not panics)
  - Content-Length header matches actual body length for generated payloads
  - Response status codes are correctly mapped to Outcome variants (2xx → Ok, 4xx/5xx → Err)
  - Timeout responses correctly produce Cancelled outcome
close_reason: Completed: reqwest runtime HTTP path migrated to asupersync and validated with local builds/tests

title: Cross-Pane Correlation Engine
description:
# Cross-Pane Correlation Engine

## Goal
Detect simultaneous or causally-related events across multiple panes using statistical correlation analysis (chi-squared co-occurrence testing).

## How it works
When events occur across multiple panes within a configurable time window:
1. Build a co-occurrence matrix of (pane_i, event_type) pairs
2. Apply chi-squared test for statistical significance
3. Report correlated events with p-values

## Use cases
- Rate limit hits across multiple agents → shared API key exhaustion
- Error cascades: one agent failure triggers others
- Build coordination: multiple agents hitting same compilation
- Pattern: "whenever pane A errors, pane B errors within 30s"

## Integration
- Receives events from pattern detection engine (patterns.rs)
- Publishes correlation events to event bus
- Feeds into wa-283h4.1 (Causal DAG) which adds directionality

## Relationship to other beads
- **wa-283h4.1 (Causal DAG)**: This bead detects CO-OCCURRENCE (events happen together). The causal DAG detects CAUSATION (event A causes event B, with direction and lag). This is the prerequisite.
- **wa-283h4.11 (LSH error clustering)**: This detects SIMILAR errors across panes. Cross-pane correlation detects SIMULTANEOUS events (which may be different events).
- **wa-1l2o (Circuit breaker)**: Uses correlation output to detect cascades.

## Tests
- Synthetic event streams with known correlations → verify detection
- Chi-squared test correctly identifies significant vs spurious correlations
- **Criterion benchmarks**: correlation check for 50 panes × 10 event types (<5ms)
- **proptest**: random event streams never produce false positives above expected rate
- Integration: inject correlated events, verify correlation event published

## Acceptance criteria
- Co-occurrence matrix maintained incrementally
- Chi-squared significance test with configurable p-value threshold
- Correlation events published to event bus
- <5ms per correlation check for 50 panes
- False positive rate below 5% at p=0.01 threshold
close_reason: Cross-pane correlation engine implemented with chi-squared co-occurrence testing, 23 tests passing

title: SQLite tables for snapshot storage and scrollback dedup
description:
## Goal
Extend wa's existing SQLite database (schema v20+) to store mux snapshots persistently, with efficient querying and retention management.

## Background
wa already has a mature SQLite storage layer with WAL mode, schema versioning, 13+ tables including panes, output_segments, events, agent_sessions, etc. The snapshot storage should follow the same patterns: epoch-ms timestamps, proper indexing, and retention policies.

## Design
1. New table `mux_snapshots`:
   - id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY
   - snapshot_id TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE (UUID)
   - created_at INTEGER NOT NULL (epoch ms)
   - trigger TEXT NOT NULL ('periodic', 'manual', 'pre_restart', 'pre_upgrade')
   - mux_server_pid INTEGER
   - wezterm_version TEXT
   - wa_version TEXT
   - window_count INTEGER
   - tab_count INTEGER
   - pane_count INTEGER
   - snapshot_json TEXT NOT NULL (full MuxSnapshot as JSON)
   - snapshot_size_bytes INTEGER
   - checksum TEXT (SHA-256 of snapshot_json for integrity)

2. New table `snapshot_scrollbacks`:
   - id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY
   - snapshot_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES mux_snapshots(snapshot_id)
   - pane_id INTEGER NOT NULL
   - content_hash TEXT NOT NULL (for dedup across snapshots)
   - content TEXT NOT NULL (escaped terminal output)
   - line_count INTEGER
   - byte_count INTEGER
   - UNIQUE(snapshot_id, pane_id)

3. Content-addressed scrollback dedup:
   - If two consecutive snapshots have the same scrollback hash for a pane, only store it once
   - Reference by content_hash to avoid duplicating multi-MB scrollback buffers

4. Retention policy:
   - Keep last N snapshots (configurable, default 10)
   - Keep all snapshots from last 24 hours
   - Keep at least 1 snapshot per day for last 7 days
   - Configurable via wa.toml [snapshots] section

5. Schema migration:
   - Increment schema version to 21 (or next available)
   - Add migration in storage.rs following existing patterns

## Acceptance Criteria
- Tables created on schema upgrade
- Insert and query snapshots with proper indexing
- Scrollback dedup verified (same content only stored once)
- Retention cleanup works correctly
- Migration from v20 to v21 is clean

## Benchmark & Property Testing Requirements

### Criterion Benchmarks
Add `benches/snapshot_sqlite.rs` using criterion:
- **insert_latency**: Benchmark inserting a full MuxSnapshot (50 panes, 5000 lines each) into the mux_snapshots and snapshot_scrollbacks tables. Measure wall-clock time and I/O bytes. Target: <500ms for a typical 50-pane snapshot.
- **query_latest_snapshot**: Benchmark querying the most recent snapshot by created_at. Target: <5ms with proper indexing.
- **query_by_trigger**: Benchmark querying snapshots filtered by trigger type. Target: <10ms.
- **dedup_savings**: Benchmark insert time when content_hash matches an existing row (dedup path) vs fresh insert. Measure storage savings for 10 consecutive snapshots where 80% of panes have unchanged scrollback.
- **retention_cleanup**: Benchmark the retention cleanup query (DELETE old snapshots) with 100, 500, 1000 snapshots in the table.

### Proptest
Add `tests/proptest_snapshot_sqlite.rs`:
- **schema_migration_correctness**: For any arbitrary initial database state (proptest generates random existing rows in pre-migration tables), assert that migration to v21 preserves all existing data and creates new tables without errors. Run the migration, then verify all pre-existing rows are intact and new tables exist with correct schema.
- **retention_policy_invariants**: For any sequence of snapshot inserts with arbitrary timestamps and trigger types (proptest generates), assert that after cleanup: (a) at most N snapshots remain, (b) all snapshots from the last 24 hours are retained, (c) at least 1 snapshot per day for the last 7 days is retained.
- **dedup_correctness**: For any sequence of (snapshot_id, pane_id, content) triples where some share the same content, assert that only one copy of each unique content exists in storage, and all references resolve correctly.

## Cross-References
- **wa-283h4.2** (WAL snapshots): The WAL (Write-Ahead Log) snapshot system provides a complementary persistence mechanism. While wa-3q7q stores discrete point-in-time snapshots, WAL snapshots capture a continuous log of state changes. The two systems should share the same SQLite database and coordinate schema versions. WAL snapshots can reference wa-3q7q's snapshot_id as a "checkpoint" -- the WAL only needs to store deltas since the last full snapshot, dramatically reducing WAL size.
close_reason: Implemented: storage.rs schema v21 with mux_sessions, session_checkpoints, mux_pane_state tables. Includes cascade deletes, constraint validation, BLAKE3 dedup, multi-host support.

title: Scrollback memory pressure mitigation — evict old content under pressure
description:
## Goal
Implement wa-side scrollback eviction that reduces memory consumption by trimming captured scrollback data under memory pressure, while preserving recent and search-indexed content.

## Background & Motivation
WezTerm's scrollback is 100% in-memory (VecDeque<Line> in term/src/screen.rs). With 50+ panes and default 10,000 line scrollback, this consumes significant RAM. wa captures this scrollback into SQLite (output_segments table), which means the data exists in BOTH WezTerm's memory AND wa's SQLite.

While we can't reduce WezTerm's in-memory scrollback without forking, we CAN:
1. Trim wa's captured scrollback based on age/size policies
2. Request WezTerm to reduce scrollback_size via configuration
3. Detect memory pressure and aggressively trim

This reduces the total memory footprint and keeps wa's SQLite database manageable.

## Technical Design

### MemoryPressureMonitor
```rust
// Location: crates/wa-core/src/cleanup.rs (extend existing)

pub struct ScrollbackTrimmer {
    storage: Arc<StorageManager>,
    config: TrimConfig,
}

pub struct TrimConfig {
    pub max_lines_per_pane: usize,       // default: 10000
    pub idle_pane_max_lines: usize,      // default: 1000
    pub dormant_pane_max_lines: usize,   // default: 100
    pub memory_pressure_max_lines: usize, // default: 500
    pub trim_interval_seconds: u64,      // default: 300
    pub memory_high_watermark_gb: f64,   // default: 200.0 (on 256GB machine)
}
```

### Trim Logic
```rust
pub async fn trim_scrollback(&self) -> Result<TrimReport> {
    let system_memory = self.get_available_memory()?;
    let under_pressure = system_memory.available_gb < 
        (system_memory.total_gb - self.config.memory_high_watermark_gb);
    
    let mut report = TrimReport::default();
    
    for pane in self.storage.get_all_panes().await? {
        let tier = self.classify_pane_tier(pane.id);
        let max_lines = if under_pressure {
            self.config.memory_pressure_max_lines
        } else {
            match tier {
                PaneTier::Dormant => self.config.dormant_pane_max_lines,
                PaneTier::Idle => self.config.idle_pane_max_lines,
                _ => self.config.max_lines_per_pane,
            }
        };
        
        let trimmed = self.storage.trim_output_segments(pane.id, max_lines).await?;
        report.total_trimmed += trimmed;
    }
    
    Ok(report)
}
```

### Integration with Cleanup Engine
wa already has a cleanup engine (cleanup.rs) with retention policies and batch deletion. The scrollback trimmer integrates as an additional cleanup policy:
```rust
// In cleanup engine's periodic run:
async fn run_cleanup_cycle(&self) {
    self.run_retention_cleanup().await;  // existing
    self.trimmer.trim_scrollback().await; // new
    self.run_fts_optimize().await;       // existing
}
```

## Existing Code References
- cleanup.rs: Existing cleanup engine with retention policies
- storage.rs: output_segments table with content_hash
- backpressure.rs: Memory pressure detection (Green/Yellow/Red/Black tiers)

## Expected Impact
- 60-80% reduction in wa's SQLite storage for idle panes
- Faster FTS5 searches (less data to index)
- Prevents wa itself from becoming a memory hog
- Under memory pressure, aggressively frees space

## Dependencies
None — standalone improvement. Benefits from bd-9dp (tiered rates) for tier classification.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Active panes retain full scrollback (max_lines_per_pane)
- Idle panes trimmed to idle_pane_max_lines
- Memory pressure triggers aggressive trimming
- FTS5 index updated after trimming
- Trim report shows lines removed per pane
- No data loss for content that's been snapshotted (session persistence)

## Estimated Effort
2-3 hours implementation, 1 hour testing

## macOS Platform Note
Memory pressure detection must be platform-aware:
- **Linux**: reads `/proc/meminfo` for `MemAvailable` or uses PSI (`/proc/pressure/memory`) for fine-grained pressure stall information.
- **macOS**: use `vm_statistics64` via `host_statistics64(mach_host_self(), HOST_VM_INFO64, ...)` to obtain `free_count`, `active_count`, `inactive_count`, `wire_count`, and `compressor_page_count`. Compute available memory as `(free_count + inactive_count - compressor_page_count) * page_size`. For pressure-level detection, use the `dispatch_source_create(DISPATCH_SOURCE_TYPE_MEMORYPRESSURE, ...)` API which provides `DISPATCH_MEMORYPRESSURE_NORMAL`, `DISPATCH_MEMORYPRESSURE_WARN`, and `DISPATCH_MEMORYPRESSURE_CRITICAL` levels — a direct macOS equivalent of Linux PSI.

## Benchmark Requirements
- **criterion benchmarks** with target `benches/scrollback_eviction.rs`:
  - `eviction_decision_latency`: measure time to classify all panes and compute eviction targets for a 50-pane workload. Target: <1ms total decision time.
  - `trim_output_segments`: measure SQLite DELETE + VACUUM for trimming 10K segments down to 1K. Target: <50ms per pane.
  - `memory_pressure_detection`: measure platform-specific memory query latency. Target: <100us per query.

## Property-Based Testing (proptest)
- **Eviction ordering invariant**: dormant panes are always trimmed more aggressively than idle panes, which are always trimmed more aggressively than active panes. For any pane set with mixed tiers, `remaining_lines(dormant) <= remaining_lines(idle) <= remaining_lines(active)`.
- **No over-eviction**: trimming never removes more lines than exist; `trimmed_count <= original_count - min_lines`.
- **Pressure monotonicity**: higher memory pressure levels result in equal or more aggressive trimming. If `pressure_a > pressure_b`, then `max_lines(pressure_a) <= max_lines(pressure_b)`.
- **Idempotency**: running trim twice with unchanged conditions produces zero additional trims on the second pass.

## Cross-References
- **wa-2ahu0** (Memory pressure engine): provides the centralized memory pressure signal that drives eviction urgency; this bead consumes pressure levels from wa-2ahu0 rather than re-implementing pressure detection.
- **wa-1c2u** (Smart scrollback with importance weighting): complementary approach — wa-1c2u scores individual lines by importance while wa-3r5e makes pane-level eviction decisions. Together they ensure high-value lines survive even aggressive eviction.
close_reason: Implemented: ScrollbackEvictor with EvictionConfig, EvictionPlan, EvictionReport, SegmentStore/PaneTierSource traits. Tier-based limits (Active 10K → Dormant 100), pressure scaling (Green/Yellow/Orange/Red), min_segments floor. 25 tests all passing.

## Goal

## Goal
Validate the accounts/usage integration end-to-end without network access:
- `wa robot accounts refresh` invokes `caut` via wrapper, updates DB mirror
- `wa robot accounts` shows deterministic account state + recommended pick
- logs/artifacts remain secret-safe and actionable

This protects a high-risk integration surface (external CLI drift + error handling).

## Scenario
Run in an isolated temp workspace with a stubbed `caut` executable on `PATH`.

### Setup

- Create a temp `bin/` dir with a **fake caut** script that:
  - supports `caut refresh --service openai --format json`
  - supports `caut usage --service openai --format json`
  - returns fixture JSON for a few accounts
  - can be toggled to return:
    - non-zero exit + stderr message
    - invalid JSON

### Steps
1. Run: `wa robot accounts refresh --service openai`

2. Run: `wa robot accounts --service openai`
   - Assert: deterministic ordering, `recommended` matches policy.
3. Negative path:
   - Make fake caut fail (exit != 0) and re-run refresh
   - Assert: actionable error + remediation hint; no secrets leaked.

## Assertions
- Output stability:
  - Both commands validate against robot schemas.
  - Ordering is deterministic.
- Correctness:
  - DB mirror reflects fixture values.
  - recommended selection matches selection policy (threshold + LRU).
- Safety:

title: [Human command] `wa backup export` (database + config archive with checksum)
description:
# Task: wa backup export

## Goal
Create portable backup archives that users can store, copy, and restore from.

## Command Design
```bash
# Basic export
$ wa backup export
Backup saved: ~/.local/share/wa/backups/wa_backup_2026-01-18_143015.wa

# Custom output
$ wa backup export --output /path/to/backup.wa

# With compression
$ wa backup export --compress

# Include specific workspaces only
$ wa backup export --workspace /project/a --workspace /project/b

# Exclude large transcript data (config/events only)
$ wa backup export --metadata-only
```

## Output Format
Archive structure (tar + optional zstd):
```
backup.wa/
├── manifest.json      # Version, timestamp, checksums
├── schema_version     # Plain text: "3"
├── database.sql       # SQLite dump
├── config.toml        # Effective configuration
├── patterns/          # Custom pattern packs
│   └── custom.toml
└── checksums.sha256   # Per-file checksums
```

manifest.json:
```json
{
  "wa_version": "0.1.0",
  "schema_version": 3,
  "created_at": "2026-01-18T14:30:15Z",
  "workspaces": ["/project/a", "/project/b"],
  "stats": {
    "segments": 12345,
    "events": 567,
    "panes": 8
  },
  "checksum": "sha256:abc123..."
}
```

## Implementation Notes
- Use SQLite `.dump` for portability
- Acquire read lock during export (snapshot isolation)
- Stream large exports to avoid memory issues
- Verify checksum immediately after write

## Testing
- Unit tests: archive format validation, manifest generation
- Integration: export with active watcher, verify no corruption
- E2E: export + import round-trip preserves all data

## Acceptance Criteria
- Export creates valid, portable archive
- Checksum included and verified on write
- Progress shown for large databases
- Metadata-only mode for quick config backup
