# Replace smol with asupersync in FrankenTerm codec crate

## Why
The codec crate (frankenterm/codec/) handles PDU serialization and async I/O for the mux wire protocol. Uses smol for async read/write. Must be migrated before mux.

## Current state
- Uses smol::io::AsyncRead/AsyncWrite traits
- PDU framing with async read/write
- Compression (zstd) in the I/O pipeline

## What to change
1. Replace smol async I/O traits with asupersync equivalents
2. Update async read/write implementations
3. Feature flag: `async-smol` vs `async-asupersync`
4. Ensure PDU framing is identical regardless of runtime

## Testing
- PDU round-trip tests pass with both runtimes
- Compression/decompression works correctly
- Large PDU handling (>64KB) works
- Connection drop handling is correct

## Test framework requirements

### criterion benchmarks — encode/decode throughput
Benchmark with criterion:
- PDU encode throughput for typical message sizes (target: >500MB/s)
- PDU decode throughput for typical message sizes (target: >500MB/s)
- Compression ratio and throughput for zstd pipeline (target: >200MB/s with >2x compression)
- Large PDU handling (64KB, 256KB, 1MB) encode/decode latency
- Async framing overhead vs synchronous encode/decode

### proptest — codec roundtrip invariants
Use proptest to generate arbitrary PDU payloads and verify:
- encode followed by decode produces the original PDU (roundtrip identity: encode->decode = identity)
- Corrupted bytes in the stream produce Err, never panics or garbage data
- Partial reads (incomplete frames) are handled correctly and resume after more data arrives
- All PDU type variants round-trip correctly, including edge cases (empty payload, max-size payload)
- Compression is transparent: compressed and uncompressed PDUs decode identically
notes: Closed via commit e2dda5d (2026-02-11): frankenterm/codec supports mutually-exclusive features async-smol (default) and async-asupersync with compile-time guards; async leb128 reader uses read_exact for asupersync compatibility; workspace chrono enables serde so mux builds under codec checks. Verified: cargo fmt -p codec --check; cargo check, clippy, and test for codec in both feature modes.

title: Replace async-io with asupersync in async_ossl and wezterm-uds
description:
# Replace async-io in async_ossl and wezterm-uds

## Why
These two crates provide async I/O primitives used by the mux and SSH systems:
- async_ossl: Async OpenSSL wrapper (TLS for mux connections)
- wezterm-uds: Async Unix domain socket handling

## Current state
- async_ossl/src/lib.rs: Uses async-io for polling OpenSSL BIO
- wezterm-uds/src/lib.rs: Uses async-io for Unix socket polling

## What to change
1. Replace async-io polling with asupersync I/O polling (Cx-based)
2. OpenSSL BIO integration: map SSL_read/SSL_write to asupersync futures
3. Unix socket: map connect/accept/read/write to asupersync
4. Feature flag both crates: `async-io` vs `async-asupersync`

## Key consideration
These crates deal with raw file descriptors and system calls. The asupersync I/O reactor must support registering arbitrary FDs for read/write readiness, similar to what async-io provides via Async<T>.

## macOS platform note
On macOS, the I/O notification backend must use **kqueue** instead of Linux's epoll. The asupersync I/O reactor should abstract over this via a platform-specific poller:
- Linux: epoll_create1 / epoll_ctl / epoll_wait
- macOS/BSD: kqueue / kevent
- Both async_ossl and wezterm-uds must be tested on macOS to ensure kqueue-based FD registration works correctly for OpenSSL BIOs and Unix domain sockets
- Note: macOS Unix domain socket paths are limited to 104 bytes (vs 108 on Linux)

## Testing
- TLS handshake works with asupersync
- Unix socket connection and data transfer works
- Verify no FD leaks after connection close
- Test with real mux server connection

## Test framework requirements

### criterion benchmarks — I/O throughput
Benchmark with criterion:
- TLS handshake latency with asupersync vs async-io baseline (target: <5ms)
- Unix domain socket throughput (target: >1GB/s for local IPC)
- OpenSSL BIO read/write throughput through async wrapper (target: >500MB/s)
- FD registration/deregistration overhead in the I/O reactor

### LabRuntime DPOR — concurrent I/O operations
Use LabRuntime with DPOR exploration to verify:
- Concurrent TLS connections never deadlock on BIO polling
- Concurrent Unix socket accept + read/write is linearizable
- FD close during pending read/write produces clean errors, no use-after-close
- Multiple tasks sharing an I/O reactor do not starve each other
notes: Closed via commit 6940bc0 (2026-02-11): async_ossl and frankenterm-uds now feature-gate async-io vs async-asupersync. async-io dependency is optional; IoSafe impls are cfg-gated; compile-time guards require exactly one backend. Verified: cargo fmt; cargo check and clippy for both feature modes (per crate).

title: Replace smol with asupersync in mux crate
description:
# Replace smol with asupersync in FrankenTerm mux crate

## Why
The mux crate is the largest consumer of smol. It uses async for: domain management, pane I/O, tab management, mux server communication, and task spawning. This is the most complex migration.

## Current state
- Uses smol::spawn for background tasks
- Uses smol channels for pane I/O
- Uses smol::Timer for timeouts
- Uses promise crate (which wraps smol)
- Domain trait has async methods

## What to change
1. Replace all smol::spawn with asupersync structured concurrency
2. Replace smol channels with asupersync channels
3. Replace smol::Timer with asupersync time (via Cx)
4. Update Domain trait async methods for asupersync
5. Feature flag: `async-smol` vs `async-asupersync`

## Dependencies
- promise crate must be migrated first (wa-brc7d.1)
- codec crate must be migrated first (wa-brc7d.2)
- async_ossl must be migrated for TLS domains (wa-brc7d.3)

## Testing
- All mux tests pass with both runtimes
- Domain connection/disconnection works
- Pane I/O (read/write) works
- Tab creation/destruction works
- Concurrent multi-pane operation works
- No task leaks after tab close

## Test framework requirements

### LabRuntime DPOR — mux concurrency
Use LabRuntime with DPOR exploration to verify:
- Concurrent pane read/write across multiple tabs never deadlocks
- Domain disconnect during active pane I/O produces clean errors, no orphaned tasks
- Tab close while pane I/O is in-flight cancels all pending operations
- Channel send/receive ordering is preserved under concurrent multi-producer scenarios
- Task spawning and structured concurrency scopes do not leak tasks on cancellation

### criterion benchmarks — mux operation throughput
Benchmark with criterion:
- Pane I/O throughput: bytes read/written per second through mux layer (target: >500MB/s local)
- Tab creation/destruction latency (target: <500us per tab)
- Domain connection establishment latency (target: <10ms local, <100ms remote)
- Channel throughput for pane I/O pipeline (target: >1M messages/sec)

### Loom model checking — shared state
Use Loom to exhaustively verify the mux crate's shared state synchronization:
- Arc<Mutex<Tab>> access patterns are deadlock-free
- Domain registry (shared HashMap) concurrent access is safe
- Pane ID generation (AtomicU64) is monotonic and unique under contention
- No data races in the pane I/O buffer management

## Cross-references
- **wa-2dd4s.5** — FrankenMux integration: the mux crate provides the async runtime foundation that FrankenMux's unified tab model builds upon; this migration must complete before FrankenMux integration can use asupersync
- **wa-brc7d.1** — promise crate migration: must complete first as mux depends on promise
- **wa-brc7d.2** — codec crate migration: must complete first as mux depends on codec for wire protocol
- **wa-brc7d.3** — async_ossl/wezterm-uds migration: must complete first for TLS domain connections

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Implement the full scope described in this bead Objective/Details/Goals with no functional regressions in adjacent behavior.
2. Add comprehensive unit tests covering happy-path behavior, edge/boundary conditions, and explicit error/failure paths for the touched logic.
3. Add integration/E2E scenario scripts that validate real workflow behavior end-to-end, including at least one failure-injection path and one recovery path.
4. Ensure E2E scenarios emit detailed structured logs (timestamp, component, correlation_id, scenario_id, input, decision/outcome, reason_code/error_code) and retain artifacts for triage.
5. Validate determinism and policy/safety constraints for this change, including repeat-run stability and contract-level assertions on touched interfaces.
6. Wire new/updated tests into the project test workflow and document exact execution commands/log locations in implementation notes.

## User Impact
1. Specify the concrete operator/agent workflow pain this bead removes (speed, reliability, safety, or clarity).
2. Define measurable user-facing outcomes (for example p95 latency, failure/timeout rate, time-to-recovery, or reduction in manual intervention steps).
3. Define no-regression UX guarantees and explicit rollback/degradation behavior if those outcomes are not met.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Replace smol-dependent mux async execution paths with asupersync equivalents while preserving mux correctness, domain behavior, and protocol semantics.
2. Validate channel/timer/spawn conversions with explicit cancellation and backpressure guarantees (no lost messages, no orphan loops).
3. Require comprehensive unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end scripts that exercise mux lifecycle, pane I/O, domain management, timeout paths, and feature-flag fallback behavior.
4. Require structured diagnostics/logging for task lifecycle, domain events, timeout/deadline behavior, and migration-specific error classes with replay artifacts.
5. Heavy compile/test/lint/perf checks must be executed via rch and recorded as evidence before closure.

title: Replace tokio refs in wezterm-ssh with asupersync
description:
# Replace tokio in wezterm-ssh with asupersync

## Why
wezterm-ssh is the hardest migration. It wraps libssh2 (C library) with Rust async via tokio. The C library has its own event loop expectations.

## Current state
- Uses tokio::spawn, tokio::time, tokio channels
- SSH session runs on dedicated tokio thread
- libssh2 session callbacks drive async I/O
- Complex state machine for SSH connection lifecycle

## What to change
1. Replace tokio primitives with asupersync equivalents
2. The dedicated SSH thread may need to become an asupersync task
3. libssh2 polling integration: need asupersync I/O reactor FD registration
4. Feature flag: `async-tokio` vs `async-asupersync`

## Key risk
libssh2 expects specific threading and polling behavior. Changing the async runtime may break subtle timing assumptions. Extensive testing needed.

## Testing
- SSH connection to real server works
- SCP file transfer works
- Port forwarding works
- Connection timeout works
- Graceful disconnect works
- Stress test: 10 concurrent SSH connections

## Test framework requirements

### criterion benchmarks — SSH channel throughput
Benchmark with criterion:
- SSH channel data throughput (target: >100MB/s over localhost)
- SSH session establishment latency (target: <500ms including key exchange)
- SCP file transfer throughput for various file sizes (1KB, 1MB, 100MB)
- Channel multiplex overhead: N channels over 1 SSH connection vs N separate connections

### LabRuntime DPOR — concurrent SSH sessions
Use LabRuntime with DPOR exploration to verify:
- Concurrent SSH session establishment never deadlocks on libssh2's internal locks
- Concurrent channel open/close on the same session is linearizable
- Session disconnect during active channel I/O produces clean errors in all channels
- Multiple SSH sessions sharing the asupersync I/O reactor do not starve each other
- libssh2 callback re-entrancy is safe under asupersync's task scheduling

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Implement the full scope described in this bead Objective/Details/Goals with no functional regressions in adjacent behavior.
2. Add comprehensive unit tests covering happy-path behavior, edge/boundary conditions, and explicit error/failure paths for the touched logic.
3. Add integration/E2E scenario scripts that validate real workflow behavior end-to-end, including at least one failure-injection path and one recovery path.
4. Ensure E2E scenarios emit detailed structured logs (timestamp, component, correlation_id, scenario_id, input, decision/outcome, reason_code/error_code) and retain artifacts for triage.
5. Validate determinism and policy/safety constraints for this change, including repeat-run stability and contract-level assertions on touched interfaces.
6. Wire new/updated tests into the project test workflow and document exact execution commands/log locations in implementation notes.

## User Impact
1. Specify the concrete operator/agent workflow pain this bead removes (speed, reliability, safety, or clarity).
2. Define measurable user-facing outcomes (for example p95 latency, failure/timeout rate, time-to-recovery, or reduction in manual intervention steps).
3. Define no-regression UX guarantees and explicit rollback/degradation behavior if those outcomes are not met.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Migrate the scoped async/runtime surface to asupersync-compatible semantics without user-visible behavior regressions.
2. Require comprehensive validation: unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end scripts for happy path, cancellation, timeout, and failure/recovery behavior.
3. Require structured diagnostics/logging for runtime-path selection, cancellation/deadline outcomes, error classes, and performance impact metrics with reproducible artifacts.
4. Execute heavy compile/test/lint/benchmark checks through rch and capture evidence in bead comments.
5. Closure requires auditable command/artifact evidence plus residual-risk notes.

title: Extension sandboxing: WASM or Lua runtime for safe custom code execution
description:
# Extension Sandboxing

## Purpose
Run custom extension code safely without risking system security.

## Options Evaluated

### 1. WASM (Recommended)
- Pros: Strong isolation, multi-language, proven
- Cons: Larger binary, more complex
- Libraries: wasmtime, wasmer

### 2. Lua
- Pros: Simple, fast, battle-tested (Neovim/WezTerm)
- Cons: Single language, needs careful sandboxing
- Libraries: rlua, mlua

## Recommendation: WASM via wasmtime
- Better isolation guarantees
- Supports Rust, Go, C, AssemblyScript
- WASI for controlled system access

## Sandbox Capabilities
```rust
pub struct ExtensionSandbox {
    engine: wasmtime::Engine,
    linker: wasmtime::Linker<SandboxState>,
    capabilities: SandboxCapabilities,
}

pub struct SandboxCapabilities {
    pub read_pane_output: bool,
    pub send_notifications: bool,
    pub http_requests: bool,
    pub file_access: FileAccessScope,
}
```

## Capability Levels
- Level 1: Read-only (patterns only)
- Level 2: Read + notify (most workflows)
- Level 3: Read + notify + HTTP (integrations)
- Level 4: Full (admin extensions)

## Extension Manifest
```toml
[extension]
name = "my-patterns"
capabilities = ["read_pane_output"]
```

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] WASM runtime integrated
- [ ] Capability-based permissions
- [ ] Extensions cannot access system without permission
- [ ] Untrusted extension cannot crash wa

## Testing
- Unit tests for sandbox policy enforcement and resource limits.
- Integration tests running a restricted extension in a sandbox.
- Security checks: verify no filesystem/network escape.

title: E2E script: workspace isolation (no cross-project DB leakage; --workspace honored)
description:
# Task: E2E script — workspace isolation

## Goal
Prove that wa honors workspace scoping and does not leak data across projects.

This is a critical UX property:
- users run multiple projects in parallel
- agents should not read/write the wrong DB
- debugging depends on knowing which workspace you are looking at

## Scenario
- Spawn a dummy pane that prints a unique token: WORKSPACE_TOKEN.

Steps
1) Start wa watch with --workspace <A>.
2) Wait until WORKSPACE_TOKEN is persisted (wa robot search --workspace <A>).
3) Run wa robot search --workspace <B> for WORKSPACE_TOKEN.

Assertions
- In workspace A: the token is found.
- In workspace B: the token is NOT found.

Optional extension
- Start wa watch in workspace B and ensure it creates a distinct DB.

## Artifacts
- effective config for both workspaces
- wa watch logs
- wa robot search outputs for A and B

## Registry
- Register this case in the E2E case registry (`wa-4vx.10.20`), including prerequisites and default inclusion status.
- Ensure `./scripts/e2e_test.sh --all` includes this case (or mark non-default with justification).

## Logging
- Follow the standard E2E harness logging contract (`wa-4vx.10.6`) and runner (`wa-4vx.10.11`).
- Emit per-step start/end markers with timestamps + durations.
- Include case name and pane ids in every log line.
- Redact secrets (device codes, tokens) in logs and artifacts.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Test is deterministic.
- Failures make it obvious whether the bug is:
  - workspace resolution
  - DB path derivation
  - CLI flag propagation


## Testing
- Meta-validation:
  - Assert the two workspaces produce distinct DB/log paths (not just search behavior).
  - Add a control assertion that workspace B can find a different token once it has ingested something.

- Artifact validation:

title: [EPIC] Phase 2: Workflow Engine & Automation
description:
# Phase 2: Workflow Engine & Automation

## Overview
This epic builds the workflow automation system that responds to detected patterns. The workflow engine is what makes wa "active" rather than just a passive monitor - it can take corrective actions when agents hit limits, experience compaction, need authentication, etc.

## Strategic Importance
The workflow system transforms wa from a "monitoring tool" into an "automation platform". This is where the real value emerges:
- Automatic context recovery after compaction
- Automatic account rotation on usage limits
- Automatic authentication renewal
- Foundation for more sophisticated multi-agent coordination

## Key Components

### 1. Workflow Engine Architecture
- Trait-based workflow definition: \`Workflow\` trait with name, description, handles, steps, execute_step
- Step results: Continue, Done, Retry, Abort, WaitFor
- WaitCondition: Pattern, PaneIdle, External
- Per-pane workflow locking (prevent conflicting workflows)
- Idempotent, recoverable, audited execution

### 2. Handle Usage Limits Workflow (Codex First)
Steps:
1. Exit current session gracefully (Ctrl-C twice for Codex)
2. Parse session info for resume (session ID, token usage)
3. Select next available account
4. Perform account authentication
5. Resume previous session
6. Send continue prompt

This is the most complex workflow and proves out the architecture.

### 3. Handle Compaction Workflow
Steps:
1. Wait for compaction to complete (stabilization window)
2. Send agent-specific context refresh prompt
   - Claude Code: "Reread AGENTS.md so it's still fresh in your mind."
   - Codex: "Please re-read AGENTS.md and any key project context files."
   - Gemini: "Please re-examine AGENTS.md and project context."

### 4. Browser Automation Skeleton
- Playwright integration structure
- Browser profile persistence
- OpenAI device auth flow (skeleton)
- Anthropic OAuth flow (skeleton)
- Google auth flow (skeleton)
- Semi-automated fallback (open browser for human when automation fails)

### 5. CAUT Integration
- Shell out to \`caut\` for usage tracking
- get_usage(service) - current usage for OpenAI/Anthropic/Google
- refresh_usage(service) - refresh from APIs
- Account selection logic based on percent_remaining

## Workflow Design Constraints
Every workflow must be:
- **Idempotent**: Re-running doesn't make a mess
- **Recoverable**: Can resume after a crash
- **Audited**: Every step recorded (what was observed, what was sent)
- **Guarded**: Each step validates state before action

## Workflow Execution Model
Each step follows: Observe → Decide → Act → Verify

Step can return:
- \`Continue\` - proceed to next step
- \`WaitFor(condition)\` - pause until condition met
- \`Retry(after)\` - retry same step after delay
- \`Abort(reason)\` - stop workflow with error
- \`Done(result)\` - workflow completed successfully

## Data-Driven Workflow Descriptors
In addition to compiled Rust workflows, support YAML/TOML descriptors for simple prompt injection sequences:

\`\`\`yaml
# ~/.config/wa/workflows/custom_compaction.yaml
name: custom_compaction_prompt
trigger:
  event: session.compaction
  agent: claude_code
steps:
  - wait_stable: 2s
  - send: |
      Please re-read AGENTS.md and the project's README.md.
  - wait_for: "❯"
\`\`\`

## Success Criteria
- [ ] Workflow engine can execute multi-step workflows
- [ ] handle_compaction workflow works end-to-end for Claude Code
- [ ] handle_usage_limits workflow works end-to-end for Codex (at least skeleton)
- [ ] Browser automation structure is in place (can be extended in Phase 3)
- [ ] CAUT integration returns account usage data
- [ ] Workflows are audited and recoverable

## Dependencies
- Depends on Phase 1 (Foundation) - needs pattern engine, storage, watcher

## Technical Notes

### Why Codex First for Usage Limits?
- Codex has the clearest device auth flow
- Resume mechanism is well-documented
- Good test case for the complexity

### Semi-Automated Browser Auth
If Playwright can't complete auth (MFA, CAPTCHA, password):
1. Open non-headless browser
2. Request human to complete auth
3. Persist browser profile for future sessions
4. Notify when auth complete

This provides graceful degradation.

title: User pattern packs: load custom rules from ~/.config/wa/patterns/
description:
# User pattern packs

## Purpose
Allow users to define custom pattern packs that load alongside built-in packs.

## User Pack Location
```
~/.config/wa/patterns/
├── my-org-patterns/
│   ├── pack.toml        # Pack metadata
│   └── rules.toml       # Rule definitions
└── custom-agent/
    ├── pack.toml
    └── rules.toml
```

## Pack Format
```toml
# pack.toml
[pack]
name = "my-org-patterns"
version = "1.0.0"
description = "Custom patterns for internal agents"
extends = "core.codex"  # Optional: inherit from built-in

# rules.toml
[[rules]]
id = "my-org.custom_warning"
name = "Custom Warning Pattern"
pattern = "\\[INTERNAL\\] Warning: (.+)"
severity = "warning"
extract = { message = "$1" }
agent_types = ["codex", "custom-agent"]
```

## Loading Priority
1. Built-in packs (highest priority)
2. User packs in order found
3. Workspace-local packs (.wa/patterns/)

For conflicts, later packs override earlier ones unless `extends` is used.

## Implementation
```rust
pub fn load_all_packs(config: &Config) -> Result<Vec<PatternPack>> {
    let mut packs = vec![];
    
    // Load built-in
    packs.extend(load_builtin_packs()?);
    
    // Load user packs
    let user_dir = config.patterns_dir();
    if user_dir.exists() {
        for entry in fs::read_dir(user_dir)? {
            let pack = PatternPack::load(entry?.path())?;
            packs.push(pack);
        }
    }
    
    // Load workspace packs
    if let Some(workspace_dir) = config.workspace_patterns_dir() {
        // Similar loading
    }
    
    // Resolve inheritance and conflicts
    resolve_pack_inheritance(&mut packs)?;
    
    Ok(packs)
}
```

## Validation
User packs are validated on load:
- Valid TOML syntax
- Required fields present
- Regex patterns compile
- No duplicate rule IDs (within pack)

## Testing
- Unit tests for pack loading
- Tests for inheritance resolution
- Tests for conflict handling
- Tests for invalid pack rejection

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] User packs load from ~/.config/wa/patterns/
- [ ] Pack format documented
- [ ] Inheritance (extends) works
- [ ] Conflict resolution is predictable
- [ ] Invalid packs rejected with clear errors
- [ ] Tests cover all scenarios

title: Criterion benchmarks + budgets (pattern detect, delta extraction, FTS query)
description:
# Task: Benchmarks + budgets

## Goal
Prevent performance regressions on hot paths.

This is the “performance test suite” complement to unit/E2E tests: it ensures wa stays fast enough to run continuously.

## Bench targets (must exist)
- Overlap/delta extraction (hot ingest path)
- Pattern engine quick reject (typical no-match)
- Pattern detection on “typical pane output”
- FTS query latency for common queries on representative DB size
- Watcher loop overhead when idle (per-pane check cost)

## Initial budgets (PLAN §13.4 + Appendix G.7)
These are v0 targets; we can tune later, but they must be explicitly recorded so regressions are real failures, not vibes.

- Quick reject no-match: **< 1µs** for typical non-matching text.
- Pattern detection (typical corpus): **p50 < 1ms**, **p99 < 5ms**.
- FTS query common patterns (DB ~100k captures):
  - **p50 < 10ms**, **p99 < 50ms** (hard cap: < 50ms for common queries).
- Watcher loop overhead (idle): **< 100µs per pane check**.

Notes:
- Budgets should be reported with machine metadata (OS/CPU/rustc/features).
- CI should enforce budgets in a non-flaky way (relative threshold vs baseline, or dedicated perf runners).

## CI integration
- Local-only initially is acceptable if CI is too noisy, but the harness must produce machine-readable artifacts.
- Once stable, integrate into CI (tracked by `wa-nu4.3.4.4`) with:
  - clear pass/fail thresholds
  - artifact upload of benchmark results on failure

## Artifacts & logging
Bench runs must produce debuggable artifacts:
- raw Criterion JSON output
- a short summary (top regressions, top slowest benches)
- build/machine metadata:
  - OS, CPU model, rustc version, enabled features
  - git commit hash when available

## Testing
- Bench harness self-check:
  - Add a small “sanity bench” guaranteed to run so the harness failing to execute is caught early.

- Budget enforcement tests:
  - If budget checks are implemented as code, include a unit test that feeds a fake benchmark JSON and asserts:
    - regression triggers failure
    - outputs include which benchmark regressed and by how much

## Acceptance Criteria
- Bench suite runs locally and produces a baseline.
- Budgets above are documented and emitted in summaries.
- CI enforcement can come later if early CI is too noisy, but the artifacts/logging are in place.
notes: Progress (2026-01-21): added bench metadata/budget emission (JSONL) via benches/bench_common.rs; each bench now emits budgets + machine metadata and writes target/criterion/wa-bench-meta.jsonl.

title: Design MuxSnapshot schema for full mux state serialization
description:
## Goal
Design and implement the core data structures that represent a complete, serializable snapshot of the WezTerm mux server state. This is the foundational data model for the entire session persistence feature.

## Background & Motivation
When the wezterm-mux-server process dies or needs to be restarted (e.g., due to memory leaks, protocol corruption after extended runtime, or upgrades), ALL running processes in all panes are killed because the mux server owns the PTY file descriptors. The kernel sends SIGHUP to all child processes. There is currently no way to save and restore session state across restarts.

WezTerm's Lua API provides building blocks (get_lines_as_escapes, inject_output, process/directory introspection, mux hierarchy enumeration) but no native serialization. The resurrect.wezterm plugin does this via Lua but is approximate and limited.

wa (wezterm_automata) already has: SQLite storage with WAL mode, pane tracking (PaneRecord), delta extraction, agent session correlation (AgentSessionRecord), and a vendored mux client. We can leverage all of this.

## Design Requirements
1. Define MuxSnapshot struct containing:
   - snapshot_id: String (UUID)
   - created_at: i64 (epoch ms)
   - mux_server_pid: Option<u32>
   - wezterm_version: String
   - wa_version: String
   - windows: Vec<WindowSnapshot>
   - workspaces: Vec<WorkspaceSnapshot>
   - active_workspace: Option<String>

2. Define WindowSnapshot containing:
   - window_id: u64
   - workspace: String
   - title: Option<String>
   - tabs: Vec<TabSnapshot>
   - active_tab_index: usize

3. Define TabSnapshot containing:
   - tab_id: u64
   - title: Option<String>
   - pane_tree: PaneNode (recursive tree for splits)
   - active_pane_id: u64

4. Define PaneNode enum:
   - Leaf(PaneSnapshot) for single panes
   - VSplit { left: Box<PaneNode>, right: Box<PaneNode>, ratio: f64 } for vertical splits
   - HSplit { top: Box<PaneNode>, bottom: Box<PaneNode>, ratio: f64 } for horizontal splits

5. Define PaneSnapshot containing:
   - pane_id: u64
   - domain: String
   - title: Option<String>
   - cwd: Option<String> (working directory)
   - foreground_process: Option<ProcessInfo>
   - dimensions: PaneDimensions (rows, cols, scrollback_rows)
   - cursor_position: Option<CursorPosition>
   - is_alt_screen: bool
   - user_vars: HashMap<String, String>
   - scrollback_hash: Option<String> (hash of scrollback content, for dedup)
   - agent_session: Option<AgentSessionRef> (link to wa's agent session tracking)

6. Define ProcessInfo:
   - name: String
   - argv: Option<Vec<String>>
   - pid: Option<u32>
   - is_whitelisted_for_restore: bool

7. Define AgentSessionRef:
   - agent_type: String (claude_code, codex, gemini)
   - session_id: Option<String>
   - wa_agent_session_id: Option<i64>

8. All structs must derive Serialize, Deserialize, Clone, Debug
9. All structs must be roundtrip-safe through JSON and potentially TOON format
10. Include schema version field for forward compatibility

## Implementation Location
New file: crates/wa-core/src/snapshot_schema.rs
Re-export from crates/wa-core/src/lib.rs

## Acceptance Criteria
- All structs compile and pass serde roundtrip tests
- Schema can represent arbitrary pane split topologies via recursive PaneNode
- JSON serialization produces human-readable output
- Schema version is included for migration support
- Integration with existing PaneRecord and AgentSessionRecord types

## Property Testing Requirements

### Proptest
Add `tests/proptest_snapshot_schema.rs`:
- **schema_versioning_compatibility**: For any MuxSnapshot with schema_version N (proptest generates versions 1..=current), assert that a deserializer for version current can read it (forward compatibility). For any MuxSnapshot with schema_version current, assert that fields not present in version N-1 are handled gracefully with defaults (backward compatibility). This ensures that snapshots created by older wa versions can always be read by newer wa versions.
- **pane_node_roundtrip**: For any arbitrary PaneNode tree (proptest generates random trees with 1-50 leaves), assert JSON roundtrip produces identical trees.
- **snapshot_completeness**: For any arbitrary MuxSnapshot (proptest generates), assert that every pane_id referenced in the PaneNode trees appears exactly once (no orphans, no duplicates).
- **optional_fields_resilience**: For any MuxSnapshot, randomly set optional fields to None (proptest generates a bitmask), serialize to JSON, deserialize, and assert all non-optional fields survive and optional fields are correctly None.

## Cross-References
- **wa-29k1** (SnapshotEngine orchestrator): wa-29k1 is the primary consumer of the MuxSnapshot schema. It populates the structs defined here during the capture pipeline. Any schema changes must be coordinated with the SnapshotEngine's capture logic.
- **bd-nz6** (SQLite tables for snapshot storage): wa-nz6 stores MuxSnapshot as JSON in the snapshot_json column. The schema must remain JSON-serializable, and any schema version bumps must be accompanied by migration logic in bd-nz6's storage layer. The snapshot_size_bytes column in wa-nz6 depends on the serialized size of the structs defined here.

title: Define Outcome<T,E> error handling strategy
description:
# Define Outcome<T,E> error handling strategy

## Background
Asupersync uses Outcome<T,E> instead of Result<T,E>. Outcome has four variants:
- Ok(T) — success
- Err(E) — application error
- Cancelled(CancelReason) — task was cancelled (user, timeout, fail-fast, race-loss, parent, shutdown)
- Panicked(PanicPayload) — task panicked

The severity lattice for composition: Ok < Err < Cancelled < Panicked (worst wins in joins).

## What needs to happen
1. Decide whether to adopt Outcome throughout the codebase or create adapter layers
2. If adapting: create From<Outcome<T,E>> for Result<T,E> and vice versa
3. If adopting: plan the gradual migration of return types
4. Handle the ? operator — Outcome implements Try trait differently than Result

## Recommendation
Start with adapter layer approach:
- Internal async code uses Outcome natively
- Public API boundaries convert to/from Result
- This minimizes blast radius while gaining cancel-correctness internally

## Key patterns to establish
- How to convert existing anyhow::Result → Outcome
- How to handle Cancelled at module boundaries
- How to propagate CancelReason through the call stack
- How to use cx.checkpoint()? for explicit cancellation points

## Acceptance criteria
- Error handling strategy document/module with conversion utilities
- Outcome adapter traits implemented
- Example migration of one simple async function showing the pattern

## Property-based testing
- **Proptest for Outcome composition laws**: Verify that Outcome's monadic operations obey algebraic laws:
  - `map`: identity law (`outcome.map(|x| x) == outcome`), composition law (`outcome.map(f).map(g) == outcome.map(|x| g(f(x)))`)
  - `and_then`: left identity, right identity, associativity
  - `or_else`: error recovery ordering, Cancelled vs Err priority respects severity lattice
  - Use `proptest!` with `prop::sample::Index` to generate arbitrary Outcome variants and verify laws hold across all variant combinations.

## Benchmark requirements
- **Criterion benchmarks for Outcome vs Result overhead**: Measure that Outcome operations (map, and_then, or_else, ?) have zero-cost overhead compared to equivalent Result operations. Add `benches/outcome_vs_result.rs` comparing: construction, pattern matching, chaining 10 operations, and error propagation with ?. Target: identical codegen (verify with `--emit=asm` if needed).
close_reason: Implemented Outcome<T,E> error handling strategy: Cancelled/Panicked error variants, OutcomeExt/ResultExt traits, pub re-exports, outcome_adapter benchmark. 60 tests pass.

title: Integrate streaming tailers: prefer subscription when available; fallback to polling
description:
# Task: Integrate streaming tailers

## Goal
Teach the ingest system to choose between:
- polling tailers (CLI get-text)
- streaming tailers (vendored subscribe)

The objective is reduced CPU/latency without changing downstream semantics.

## Capability detection
At runtime, decide per workspace/domain:
- if subscription is supported and healthy → use streaming
- otherwise → use polling

The decision should be:
- deterministic
- observable in logs/health snapshot

## Semantics must match polling mode
Regardless of tailer type:
- segments are written with seq
- gaps are emitted on discontinuity
- pattern detection and workflows behave the same

## Failure & fallback behavior
- If streaming connection drops:
  - record a diagnostic event
  - fall back to polling with backoff

- If polling is too slow or misses data:
  - record explicit GAP events (existing invariant)

## Performance expectations
- Vendored streaming mode should show significantly lower polling load and better latency.
- Add counters to compare:
  - messages/sec
  - dropped events
  - gap rate

## Testing strategy
- Unit tests with a fake stream:
  - normal ordered stream → segments
  - dropped/out-of-order stream → GAP behavior
  - stream disconnect triggers fallback

## Acceptance Criteria
- In vendored mode, ingest runs with significantly lower polling load.
- In non-vendored mode, behavior remains unchanged.
- Streaming failures degrade gracefully (no crashes, clear diagnostics).

# Task: Sync exported DB snapshots (immutable artifacts)

## Goal
Make it easy to move **database snapshots** between machines for debugging or continuity, without ever touching the live DB file.

## Safety model
- Only sync snapshots created via `wa export` / `wa diag bundle` (explicit export paths).
- Never sync the live DB file or WAL/SHM.
- Treat snapshots as immutable artifacts:
  - versioned filenames
  - no in-place overwrite
  - optional compression (if/when supported by export)

## Naming & versioning
- Filenames should encode enough metadata to be self-describing:
  - wa version
  - created timestamp (UTC)
  - workspace key (hashed/short)
  - optional host

## Push/pull behavior
- `push` uploads snapshot(s) to the target under an artifacts directory.
- `pull` downloads snapshots and places them under a local artifacts directory.
- Default behavior is additive (no overwrites).

## UX expectations
- Plans should clearly distinguish:
  - “syncing snapshots” (safe)
  - “syncing live DB” (forbidden; should never appear)

## Testing
- Covered by `wa-nu4.3.8.5` (sync tests):
  - live DB paths are rejected
  - snapshot filenames are stable and never overwritten
  - push/pull round-trips via local-directory backend

## Acceptance Criteria
- `wa sync push` can push an exported snapshot to a target without overwriting existing files.
- `wa sync pull` can pull the same snapshot back and preserves the filename.
- Attempts to sync live DB paths are rejected by the planner.

title: Integrate FrankenSearch into FrankenTerm — replace DIY search with production library
description:
# Integrate FrankenSearch into FrankenTerm

## Vision
Replace FrankenTerm's current hand-rolled search module (`search/mod.rs` with its own embedder, chunking, hybrid_search, reranker) with the production-grade `frankensearch` library. FrankenSearch provides two-tier progressive delivery (fast results in ~15ms, quality-refined in ~150ms), FSVI vector format with f16 quantization and SIMD, Tantivy BM25, RRF fusion, and an embedder stack with automatic fallback — all battle-tested across three production codebases.

## Current State
FrankenTerm already has a `search/` module with its own hybrid search, chunking, embedder, and reranker code. This is a parallel implementation of what FrankenSearch does better and more robustly. The integration replaces the DIY version with the library.

## Key Integration Challenge
**Runtime mismatch**: FrankenSearch uses `asupersync` (structured concurrency, no Tokio), while FrankenTerm uses Tokio. A runtime bridge adapter is required. FrankenTerm already has an epic (`ft-brc7d`) for asupersync migration, so this integration should use feature-gated adapters that work with either runtime.

## Integration Surface
- Replace `crates/frankenterm-core/src/search/` internals with frankensearch facade
- Wire `TwoTierSearcher` progressive callbacks into TUI search overlay
- Index terminal scrollback, session recordings, and agent output
- Expose via robot mode CLI and IPC status API
- Feature-gate behind `frankensearch` feature flag

## Success Criteria
- All existing search functionality preserved or improved
- Progressive delivery visible in TUI (fast results appear, then refine)
- Search latency p50 < 20ms for fast tier across 10K+ indexed documents
- Zero regression in pane rendering performance (search runs off hot path)
- Graceful degradation when search index unavailable

## Test and Observability Plan
1. Add comprehensive unit tests covering happy path, boundary/edge cases, and explicit failure/error behavior for logic introduced or changed by this bead.
2. Add deterministic integration and end-to-end scenario scripts that exercise full workflow behavior, including at least one negative/failure scenario and one recovery scenario.
3. Emit detailed structured logs during tests and e2e runs (timestamp, subsystem, correlation_id, scenario_id, inputs, decisions, outcomes, reason_code/error_code).
4. Persist triage artifacts for failed runs (stdout/stderr, structured logs, snapshots/fixtures, and concise failure summaries) so regressions can be root-caused quickly.
5. Ensure test commands and evidence locations are documented in the bead implementation notes and wired into normal validation/CI paths.

## User Impact
1. Specify the concrete operator/agent workflow pain this bead removes (speed, reliability, safety, or clarity).
2. Define measurable user-facing outcomes (for example p95 latency, failure/timeout rate, time-to-recovery, or reduction in manual intervention steps).
3. Define no-regression UX guarantees and explicit rollback/degradation behavior if those outcomes are not met.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Replace FrankenTerm search internals with frankensearch-backed implementations while preserving existing public API contracts and user-visible search workflows.
2. Deliver progressive two-tier behavior across TUI and robot mode (fast initial + refined follow-up) with no regressions in correctness or operator ergonomics.
3. Preserve/extend compatibility guarantees: feature-gated fallback behavior, backward-compatible output schemas, and deterministic rollback path for cutover incidents.

title: asupersync↔Tokio runtime bridge adapter
description:
## Context
FrankenSearch uses `asupersync` for all async operations (every method takes `&Cx`), while FrankenTerm uses Tokio. A runtime bridge adapter is needed to call frankensearch APIs from Tokio task contexts.

**Related prior work:**
- `ft-e34d9` (IN_PROGRESS): Epic to replace Tokio with asupersync across all of FrankenTerm
- `ft-1j0ye` (CLOSED): Dual-runtime scaffold — `runtime_compat.rs` already exists with feature-flagged Mutex/RwLock/channel/spawn abstractions

## Scope
Create a `search_bridge.rs` module in frankenterm-core that:
1. Wraps `TwoTierSearcher` methods with Tokio-compatible async interfaces
2. Manages an asupersync `Cx` (capability context) lifecycle within a Tokio task
3. Handles cancellation propagation between Tokio CancellationToken and asupersync structured cancellation
4. Provides a `SearchBridge` struct that owns the searcher and exposes `async fn search()` returning Tokio futures
5. Uses existing `runtime_compat.rs` (from ft-1j0ye) abstractions where applicable

## Key Design Decision
Use `tokio::task::spawn_blocking` to run asupersync's event loop on a blocking thread, with channel-based result passing back to the Tokio runtime. This avoids nested runtime issues and keeps the integration clean.

## Alternative: Feature-gated dual path
When ft-e34d9 (asupersync migration) completes, the bridge becomes unnecessary — frankensearch can be called directly via native asupersync Cx. Design the bridge as a thin shim behind `#[cfg(not(feature = "asupersync-runtime"))]` that gets compiled out when the migration is done. The `#[cfg(feature = "asupersync-runtime")]` path calls FrankenSearch directly without the bridge.

## Testing Requirements
- `test_bridge_round_trip`: spawn_blocking correctly passes query and returns results
- `test_bridge_cancellation_forward`: Tokio CancellationToken → asupersync Cx cancellation
- `test_bridge_cancellation_reverse`: asupersync cancel → Tokio task cancelled
- `test_bridge_timeout`: search exceeding deadline returns error, never hangs
- `test_bridge_concurrent_searches`: 10 parallel searches, no deadlocks
- `test_bridge_overhead`: bridge adds < 1ms beyond raw FrankenSearch latency
- All tests use structured JSON logging with `test_name`, `phase`, `duration_ms`, `result`

## Acceptance Criteria
- FrankenSearch `TwoTierSearcher::search()` callable from Tokio async context
- Progressive callbacks (`SearchPhase::Initial`, `Refined`, `RefinementFailed`) propagated to caller
- Cancellation works in both directions
- No deadlocks under concurrent search + pane rendering
- Bridge adds < 1ms overhead beyond the search itself
- Bridge compiles out cleanly when asupersync-runtime feature is enabled (direct path used instead)
- All unit tests pass with structured logging output

title: Replace existing search module with FrankenSearch backend
description:
## Context
FrankenTerm's existing `search/` module is a substantial implementation (~200KB across 12 files) with its own hybrid search, chunking, embedder stack, reranker, vector index, and background daemon. FrankenSearch provides all of this more robustly. The migration must be careful, incremental, and regression-tested — this is NOT a trivial swap.

## Existing search/ module inventory (what's being replaced)
- `mod.rs` (1.6KB) — orchestration
- `hybrid_search.rs` (25KB) — RRF fusion, multi-signal search
- `embedder.rs` (11KB) — embedder trait + dispatch
- `hash_embedder.rs` (14KB) — locality-sensitive hashing
- `fastembed_embedder.rs` (1.1KB) — fastembed wrapper
- `model2vec_embedder.rs` (1.1KB) — model2vec wrapper
- `model_registry.rs` (1.3KB) — model catalog
- `chunk_vector_store.rs` (52KB) — HNSW vector index with persistence
- `chunking.rs` (60KB) — text chunking with overlap strategies
- `reranker.rs` (7.8KB) — FlashRank cross-encoder reranking
- `vector_index.rs` (19KB) — FSVI-like vector storage
- `daemon/` — background indexing service

## Scope
Replace internals of these files while preserving their public API contracts:
- `search/mod.rs` — replace orchestration with `TwoTierSearcher` delegation via SearchBridge
- `search/hybrid_search.rs` — replace with frankensearch-fusion RRF
- `search/embedder.rs` — replace with frankensearch-embed `EmbedderStack`
- `search/chunk_vector_store.rs` — replace with frankensearch-index FSVI
- `search/chunking.rs` — evaluate overlap with frankensearch-storage; keep FrankenTerm-specific chunking strategies (terminal output has different structure than prose)
- `search/reranker.rs` — replace with frankensearch-rerank (FlashRank cross-encoder)
- `search/vector_index.rs` — replace with frankensearch FSVI format
- `search/daemon/` — adapt to use frankensearch background indexing APIs

The existing `SearchConfig` in `config.rs` should be extended to support FrankenSearch-specific settings (rrf_k, quality_weight, quality_timeout_ms, fast_only mode, embedder tier selection).

## Migration Strategy (incremental, not big-bang)
1. **Phase A**: Add FrankenSearch as alternative backend behind cfg flag — old code still compiles and runs
2. **Phase B**: Wire each sub-module to delegate to FrankenSearch when flag enabled, keeping old impl as fallback
3. **Phase C**: Run regression suite comparing old vs new results (see testing section)
4. **Phase D**: Remove old implementations once regression suite passes at 100%
5. **Phase E**: Clean up compat shims, remove dead code

## Key Decisions
- Keep the existing search module's public types as a compatibility layer that delegates to FrankenSearch internals. This prevents breaking changes for existing robot mode consumers and TUI code.
- Terminal-specific chunking strategies (blank-line boundaries, prompt detection, ANSI-aware splitting) may NOT exist in FrankenSearch — preserve FrankenTerm's custom chunkers and feed their output into FrankenSearch's index.
- Existing tantivy_ingest.rs / tantivy_query.rs must be unified with frankensearch-lexical to avoid running two Tantivy instances.

## Testing Requirements
- **Regression suite**: Capture current search behavior (queries + expected results) BEFORE migration. After each migration phase, verify identical or better results.
- `test_api_compat`: all public types from pre-FrankenSearch API still compile (compile-time test)
- `test_rrf_fusion_correctness`: RRF scores match for known inputs
- `test_embedder_stack_fallback`: hash → model2vec → fastembed tier cascade works
- `test_config_knobs`: rrf_k, quality_weight, quality_timeout_ms, fast_only all take effect
- `test_tantivy_no_duplication`: single Tantivy index, not two parallel ones
- `test_search_daemon_uses_frankensearch`: daemon/ background indexing calls frankensearch APIs
- `test_existing_robot_search_output_format`: `ft robot search` output format unchanged
- All tests use structured JSON logging

## Acceptance Criteria
- All existing `ft robot search` commands produce equivalent or better results
- SearchConfig extended with FrankenSearch tuning knobs
- Existing tantivy_ingest/tantivy_query code unified with frankensearch-lexical (single Tantivy instance)
- No public API breaking changes in robot mode output format
- Search daemon mode adapted to use frankensearch background indexing
- Old search implementations removable once regression suite passes (clean phase D)
- Zero regressions verified by automated regression suite with detailed diff logging

## Test and Observability Plan
1. Add comprehensive unit tests covering happy path, boundary/edge cases, and explicit failure/error behavior for logic introduced or changed by this bead.
2. Add deterministic integration and end-to-end scenario scripts that exercise full workflow behavior, including at least one negative/failure scenario and one recovery scenario.
3. Emit detailed structured logs during tests and e2e runs (timestamp, subsystem, correlation_id, scenario_id, inputs, decisions, outcomes, reason_code/error_code).
4. Persist triage artifacts for failed runs (stdout/stderr, structured logs, snapshots/fixtures, and concise failure summaries) so regressions can be root-caused quickly.
5. Ensure test commands and evidence locations are documented in the bead implementation notes and wired into normal validation/CI paths.

## User Impact
1. Specify the concrete operator/agent workflow pain this bead removes (speed, reliability, safety, or clarity).
2. Define measurable user-facing outcomes (for example p95 latency, failure/timeout rate, time-to-recovery, or reduction in manual intervention steps).
3. Define no-regression UX guarantees and explicit rollback/degradation behavior if those outcomes are not met.

3. Provide regression validation against representative historical queries (result presence, ordering constraints where applicable, and failure-path behavior).
4. Provide end-to-end script coverage for robot/TUI search flows that exercises initial/refined phases, feature-off fallback, and timeout/error scenarios.
5. Emit structured diagnostics/logging for backend selection, query phases, latency segments, and failure signatures; attach replay artifacts for triage.
6. Record command/artifact evidence (with heavy runs via rch) and unresolved risks before closure.

title: Progressive search delivery in TUI
description:
## Context
FrankenSearch's killer feature is progressive delivery: fast results appear in ~15ms via hash/model2vec embeddings, then quality-refined results replace them in ~150ms via fastembed + reranking. FrankenTerm's TUI should surface this progression visually.

## Scope
1. Wire `SearchPhase` callbacks into TUI search overlay:
   - `SearchPhase::Initial` → immediately render results with a "refining..." indicator
   - `SearchPhase::Refined` → replace results, remove indicator, show quality improvement delta (e.g., "3 results reranked")
   - `SearchPhase::RefinementFailed` → keep initial results, show subtle warning ("refinement unavailable")
2. Display search tier metadata: which embedder produced each result, latency breakdown per tier
3. Support `fast_only` mode toggle in TUI for latency-sensitive contexts (keybind to toggle)
4. Progressive results in robot mode: emit JSONL with phase markers for agent consumption
5. Result provenance indicators: each result shows [L] for lexical match, [S] for semantic, [F] for fused

## UX Details
- First results should appear while the user is still typing (debounced, ~100ms after last keystroke)
- Quality refinement runs in background, doesn't block UI
- Results should animate/transition smoothly when refined results arrive (no full-screen repaint)
- Show per-result provenance (lexical match, semantic match, or fused) via subtle prefix icons
- Keyboard navigation: arrow keys scroll results, Enter opens result in pane, Tab switches between result and preview
- Result count + timing shown in status bar: "5 results (12ms fast, 143ms refined)"

## Testing Requirements
- `test_initial_results_within_50ms`: fast-tier results rendered before quality-tier completes (timed)
- `test_refinement_updates_display`: mock refined callback → verify display updates with new results
- `test_refinement_failure_graceful`: mock RefinementFailed → verify initial results kept + warning shown
- `test_fast_only_toggle`: toggle fast_only → verify only Initial phase results shown
- `test_phase_markers_jsonl`: robot mode output includes `"phase":"initial"` and `"phase":"refined"` fields
- `test_result_provenance_labels`: each result shows correct [L]/[S]/[F] label
- `test_debounced_search`: rapid keystrokes → only last query executes (not flooding)
- `test_keyboard_navigation`: arrow/enter/tab keybinds navigate results correctly
- `test_no_ui_jank`: search runs on dedicated task, main render loop never blocks > 16ms
- `test_status_bar_timing`: status bar shows correct result count and tier latencies
- All tests use structured JSON logging with timing metrics per phase

## Acceptance Criteria
- TUI search shows initial results within 50ms of query submission
- Refined results update the display within 200ms without flicker or full repaint
- Robot mode JSONL output includes phase field for progressive consumers
- fast_only toggle works in TUI and robot mode
- No UI jank during refinement (search runs on dedicated thread/task, render loop stays < 16ms)
- Result provenance visible to user ([L]/[S]/[F] indicators)
- Keyboard navigation works (arrow keys, Enter, Tab)
- All tests pass with structured logging

## Test and Observability Plan
1. Add comprehensive unit tests covering happy path, boundary/edge cases, and explicit failure/error behavior for logic introduced or changed by this bead.
2. Add deterministic integration and end-to-end scenario scripts that exercise full workflow behavior, including at least one negative/failure scenario and one recovery scenario.

## User Impact

2. Define measurable user-facing outcomes (for example p95 latency, failure/timeout rate, time-to-recovery, or reduction in manual intervention steps).
3. Define no-regression UX guarantees and explicit rollback/degradation behavior if those outcomes are not met.

2. Progressive phase semantics are preserved consistently across TUI and robot-mode outputs (initial/refined/refinement-failed with clear state signaling).
3. Fast-only mode and provenance indicators are implemented and validated for both normal and degraded search states.
4. Provide comprehensive automated validation: unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end scripts for debounce behavior, keyboard navigation, latency budgets, and phase transitions.

title: Terminal content indexing pipeline for FrankenSearch
description:
## Context
FrankenSearch needs documents to index. In FrankenTerm's context, the indexable corpus is: terminal scrollback buffers, session recordings, agent output logs, pane histories, and command histories. The indexing pipeline must run incrementally without impacting terminal rendering performance.

**Interaction with cass (ft-2l9kn):** The cass integration also indexes agent session data via its own Tantivy FTS index. To avoid duplicate results and wasted resources, the indexing pipeline must coordinate with cass:
- Content indexed by cass (full session transcripts) should NOT be re-indexed by FrankenSearch
- FrankenSearch indexes terminal-specific content that cass doesn't handle (scrollback, command output blocks, pane metadata)
- When both are present, search results are deduped by content hash before display

## Scope
1. Define indexable document types and their extraction from FrankenTerm internals:
   - Scrollback lines (grouped into logical chunks by blank-line boundaries or time gaps)
   - Command output blocks (delimited by prompt patterns, OSC 133 markers)
   - Pane metadata (title, working directory, agent type, process tree) — indexed as facets, not full-text
   - Agent-specific artifacts (tool call results, error messages, code blocks) — extracted via pattern engine
   - NOT indexed: raw ANSI escape sequences, cursor movement sequences, screen state snapshots

2. Implement incremental indexing via `IndexBuilder`:
   - Content-hash dedup (SHA-256 of normalized text — don't re-embed unchanged content)
   - Background indexing on idle (when no active resize/reflow in any pane)
   - Configurable index location (default: `~/.ft/search_index/`)
   - Document source tagging: each indexed document tagged with source (scrollback, command, agent, cass) for filtering

3. Index lifecycle management:
   - Max index size limits (configurable, default 500MB)
   - TTL-based expiration for old sessions (default: 30 days)
   - LRU eviction when size limit reached
   - Manual reindex command via robot mode
   - Index compaction (Tantivy segment merging) on schedule

4. Cass coordination (when ft-2l9kn is also active):
   - Query cass index for content hashes before indexing → skip duplicates
   - Unified search results merge cass + FrankenSearch results via RRF
   - If cass unavailable, FrankenSearch operates standalone (graceful degradation)

## Performance Contract
- Indexing must never block pane rendering (run on dedicated low-priority thread with yield points)
- Incremental updates should process < 100 documents/second without noticeable CPU impact
- Index open (mmap) should add < 5ms to startup
- Background indexing pauses during resize storms (yield to hot path via frame budget system)
- Index writes batched: flush every 5 seconds or 50 documents, whichever comes first

## Testing Requirements
- `test_scrollback_indexing`: known terminal output → indexed → searchable within 1 second
- `test_content_hash_dedup`: same content submitted twice → indexed only once
- `test_incremental_update`: new content added → only delta indexed, not full re-index
- `test_ttl_expiration`: content older than TTL removed from index on next cleanup pass
- `test_index_size_limit`: when limit reached, oldest content evicted first
- `test_indexing_yields_during_resize`: inject resize event → verify indexing pauses
- `test_index_persistence`: write index, restart, verify all content still searchable
- `test_cass_dedup_integration`: mock cass index with content → verify FrankenSearch skips those docs
- `test_document_source_tagging`: verify each document has correct source facet
- `test_batch_flush`: verify 50 documents triggers flush, 5 second timer triggers flush
- All tests use structured JSON logging with timing metrics per phase

## Acceptance Criteria
- Terminal scrollback searchable via FrankenSearch within 1 second of output
- Index persists across FrankenTerm restarts
- Index size stays within configured limits via automatic expiration
- `ft robot search-index stats` shows index health metrics (size, doc count, freshness, segment count)
- Background indexing pauses during resize storms (yield to hot path)
- No duplicate results when both cass and FrankenSearch are active
- Content-hash dedup prevents redundant embedding computation
- All unit and integration tests pass with structured logging

## Test and Observability Plan
1. Add comprehensive unit tests covering happy path, boundary/edge cases, and explicit failure/error behavior for logic introduced or changed by this bead.
2. Add deterministic integration and end-to-end scenario scripts that exercise full workflow behavior, including at least one negative/failure scenario and one recovery scenario.
3. Emit detailed structured logs during tests and e2e runs (timestamp, subsystem, correlation_id, scenario_id, inputs, decisions, outcomes, reason_code/error_code).
4. Persist triage artifacts for failed runs (stdout/stderr, structured logs, snapshots/fixtures, and concise failure summaries) so regressions can be root-caused quickly.
5. Ensure test commands and evidence locations are documented in the bead implementation notes and wired into normal validation/CI paths.

## User Impact
1. Specify the concrete operator/agent workflow pain this bead removes (speed, reliability, safety, or clarity).
2. Define measurable user-facing outcomes (for example p95 latency, failure/timeout rate, time-to-recovery, or reduction in manual intervention steps).
3. Define no-regression UX guarantees and explicit rollback/degradation behavior if those outcomes are not met.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Implement backend-neutral indexing pipeline for terminal corpora with deterministic source tagging, deduplication, and lifecycle controls (TTL/size/eviction).
2. Ensure indexing remains off the rendering hot path and respects pause/yield behavior under resize or load pressure.
3. Preserve cass coordination requirements: dedupe shared content and prevent duplicate end-user search results when both systems are active.
4. Provide comprehensive validation: unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end scripts for indexing correctness, incremental updates, lifecycle actions, and degraded-mode behavior.
5. Require structured logging/diagnostics for index operations (source, hash, checkpoint, eviction, pause/resume, error class) with replayable artifacts.
6. Closure requires measured performance evidence and residual-risk notes (including startup/index-latency budgets).
notes: This bead is a critical reliability surface for search quality and user trust; preserve correctness over clever shortcuts. Keep explicit compatibility with cass integration assumptions and document any semantic differences discovered during implementation/testing.

title: IPC and robot mode search API
description:
## Context
FrankenSearch results and index state need to be exposed via FrankenTerm's IPC socket and robot mode CLI for agent consumption and external tooling.

## Scope
1. IPC status API additions:
   - `search_index` field in status payload: index size (bytes), document count, last update timestamp, embedder tiers available, segment count
   - `search_health` field: index freshness (seconds since last update), any indexing errors (count + last error message), background job status (idle/indexing/rebuilding/paused)
2. Robot mode commands:
   - `ft robot search "query" --limit N --format json` — progressive search (returns JSONL with phase markers)
   - `ft robot search "query" --format jsonl` — streaming JSONL, one line per result, phase markers between tiers
   - `ft robot search-index stats` — index health and metrics (JSON)
   - `ft robot search-index rebuild` — trigger full reindex (returns immediately, status via stats)
   - `ft robot search-index pause/resume` — control background indexing
3. Output format support: JSON (complete result set), JSONL (streaming per-result), TOON (via tru integration from ft-165vw)
4. Search explain mode: `ft robot search "query" --explain` returns per-result scoring breakdown:
   - RRF rank and fused score
   - Lexical BM25 score and matching terms
   - Semantic similarity score and embedder tier used
   - Reranker cross-encoder score (if quality tier completed)
5. Backward compatibility: existing `ft robot search` output format preserved — new fields added, no fields removed

## Testing Requirements
- `test_ipc_status_search_index`: status payload includes search_index with all required fields
- `test_ipc_status_search_health`: health field includes freshness, error count, job status
- `test_robot_search_json`: `--format json` returns valid JSON array with required fields per result
- `test_robot_search_jsonl`: `--format jsonl` returns valid JSONL with phase markers between tiers

## Acceptance Criteria

title: FrankenSearch integration test suite — unit tests, e2e scripts, benchmarks, structured logging
description:
## Context
The FrankenSearch integration touches the runtime bridge, search backend replacement, progressive TUI, indexing pipeline, and IPC/robot API. Each subtask includes its own unit tests in acceptance criteria, but a comprehensive integration test suite is needed to validate the entire stack end-to-end, catch cross-cutting regressions, and provide confidence that the production search experience works correctly.

## Scope

### 1. Unit Test Expansion (per-module, run in CI)

**search_bridge.rs tests:**
- `test_bridge_round_trip`: spawn_blocking correctly passes query to TwoTierSearcher and returns results
- `test_bridge_cancellation_forward`: Tokio CancellationToken propagates to asupersync Cx
- `test_bridge_cancellation_reverse`: asupersync cancellation propagates back to Tokio caller
- `test_bridge_timeout`: search exceeding deadline returns timeout error, not hang
- `test_bridge_concurrent_searches`: 10 parallel searches don't deadlock or corrupt state
- `test_bridge_overhead_under_1ms`: bridge layer adds < 1ms beyond raw search latency

**Search backend replacement tests (search/mod.rs, hybrid_search.rs, etc.):**
- `test_existing_api_compat`: all public types and methods from pre-FrankenSearch API still compile
- `test_rrf_fusion_correctness`: RRF scores match frankensearch-fusion for known input sets
- `test_embedder_stack_fallback`: when fastembed unavailable, gracefully falls back to hash embedder
- `test_config_knobs`: rrf_k, quality_weight, quality_timeout_ms, fast_only all take effect
- `test_tantivy_unification`: existing tantivy_ingest.rs/tantivy_query.rs code delegates to frankensearch-lexical without duplication
- `test_search_daemon_adaptation`: daemon/ directory background indexing uses frankensearch APIs

**Progressive TUI tests:**
- `test_initial_results_within_50ms`: fast-tier results rendered before quality-tier completes
- `test_refinement_updates_display`: refined results replace initial without visual glitch
- `test_refinement_failure_keeps_initial`: RefinementFailed shows initial results + subtle warning
- `test_fast_only_toggle`: fast_only mode skips quality tier entirely
- `test_phase_markers_in_jsonl`: robot mode JSONL includes `phase: "initial"` and `phase: "refined"`

**Indexing pipeline tests:**
- `test_scrollback_indexing`: terminal scrollback lines grouped into logical chunks and indexed
- `test_content_hash_dedup`: unchanged content not re-embedded on incremental update
- `test_ttl_expiration`: old sessions expire after configured TTL
- `test_index_size_limit`: index stays within configured max size via automatic cleanup
- `test_indexing_yields_during_resize`: background indexing pauses during resize storms
- `test_index_persistence`: index survives FrankenTerm restart
- `test_cass_dedup`: when cass (ft-2l9kn) and frankensearch both index same session, no duplicate results

**IPC/robot mode tests:**
- `test_status_search_index_field`: IPC status includes search_index with size, doc count, last update
- `test_robot_search_json`: `ft robot search "query" --format json` returns valid JSON
- `test_robot_search_jsonl`: `ft robot search "query" --format jsonl` returns phase-tagged JSONL
- `test_robot_search_explain`: `--explain` includes per-result scoring breakdown (RRF, lexical, semantic, tier)
- `test_robot_search_index_stats`: `ft robot search-index stats` returns index health metrics
- `test_robot_search_index_rebuild`: `ft robot search-index rebuild` triggers full reindex
- `test_graceful_empty_index`: all commands return sensible output when index is empty

### 2. Integration Tests (cross-module, require test fixtures)

- `integration_search_full_pipeline`: index terminal content → search via bridge → verify results include correct documents with ranking
- `integration_progressive_delivery_ordering`: verify Initial results arrive before Refined, timing within spec
- `integration_concurrent_search_and_render`: 10 search queries running while pane rendering at 60fps — no deadlocks, no frame drops
- `integration_index_rebuild_while_searching`: rebuild index while queries are in flight — queries don't fail
- `integration_feature_flag_off`: `cargo test -p frankenterm-core --no-default-features` — all search tests skip gracefully, no compile errors

### 3. E2E Test Scripts (shell scripts, run against live FrankenTerm)

**`tests/e2e/test_frankensearch_integration.sh`:**
- Start FrankenTerm in test mode with known terminal content
- Wait for indexing to complete (poll `ft robot search-index stats`)
- Run search queries and verify result counts and relevance
- Test progressive delivery via JSONL output (grep for phase markers)
- Verify explain mode output structure
- Collect timing metrics and assert p50 < 20ms, p95 < 100ms
- Exit codes: 0 = all pass, 1 = test failure, 2 = infrastructure error

**`tests/e2e/test_search_regression.sh`:**
- Run the EXACT same queries that worked with the old search module
- Compare result sets: new results must be superset of old results (no regressions)
- Log differences in ranking with detailed explanations

**`tests/e2e/test_search_load.sh`:**
- Concurrent search load: 50 queries/second for 30 seconds
- Verify no crashes, no memory leaks (RSS delta < 50MB)
- Verify p99 latency < 500ms under load
- Log per-query timing to `search_load_results.jsonl`

### 4. Structured Logging Requirements

All test output MUST use structured JSON logging with these fields:
- `test_name`: the test function/script name
- `phase`: "setup" | "execute" | "assert" | "teardown"
- `timestamp_ms`: millisecond-precision timestamp
- `duration_ms`: time taken for the current phase
- `result`: "pass" | "fail" | "skip" | "error"
- `detail`: human-readable explanation of what happened
- `metrics`: optional object with numeric measurements (latency, count, size)

Example log line:
```json
{"test_name":"test_bridge_round_trip","phase":"assert","timestamp_ms":1708070400000,"duration_ms":12,"result":"pass","detail":"Search returned 5 results, expected >= 3","metrics":{"result_count":5,"latency_ms":8}}
```

### 5. Performance Benchmark Harness

Using criterion.rs:
- `bench_search_fast_tier`: fast-tier latency across index sizes (100, 1K, 10K, 100K docs)
- `bench_search_full_pipeline`: full progressive pipeline latency
- `bench_indexing_throughput`: documents indexed per second
- `bench_bridge_overhead`: bridge adapter overhead vs direct FrankenSearch call
- `bench_concurrent_search`: throughput under concurrent load (1, 4, 16, 64 queries)

Baselines stored in `benches/baselines/` for regression detection.

## Acceptance Criteria
- All unit tests pass in CI (cargo test --workspace)
- Integration tests pass with and without frankensearch feature flag
- E2E scripts exit 0 on a clean FrankenTerm build
- Benchmark results within 10% of baselines (no regressions)
- Structured logging captures every test phase with timing
- Test coverage for search/ module > 80% (measured by cargo-tarpaulin)
- Zero search regressions: every query that worked before still works

## User Impact
1. Specify the concrete operator/agent workflow pain this bead removes (speed, reliability, safety, or clarity).
2. Define measurable user-facing outcomes (for example p95 latency, failure/timeout rate, time-to-recovery, or reduction in manual intervention steps).
3. Define no-regression UX guarantees and explicit rollback/degradation behavior if those outcomes are not met.

title: Integrate franken-agent-detection into FrankenTerm — comprehensive agent inventory
description:
# Integrate Agent Detection into FrankenTerm

## Vision
Replace FrankenTerm's basic `agent_correlator.rs` (which detects agents from pane titles, process names, and pattern matches) with the `franken-agent-detection` crate for comprehensive, filesystem-based agent installation detection. This enables FrankenTerm to know exactly which coding agents are installed, where their configs live, and how to auto-configure integration — making FrankenTerm the agent-aware terminal that adapts to whatever tools the user has.

## Current State
FrankenTerm's `agent_correlator.rs` has a 3-layer detection system:
1. Pattern engine matches (from terminal output)
2. Pane title keyword scanning ("claude-code", "codex", "gemini")
3. Process name inspection

This detects agents that are *running*, but not agents that are *installed*. The `franken-agent-detection` crate fills the gap: it probes filesystem locations (~/.claude/, ~/.codex/, etc.), checks PATH for binaries, and returns structured reports of all 9 supported agents.

## Integration Surface
- Add `franken-agent-detection` as workspace dependency (crates.io v0.1.0)
- Create `agent_detection.rs` module that combines both approaches:
  - Startup: filesystem probe via franken-agent-detection (what's installed)
  - Runtime: existing agent_correlator.rs (what's running in which pane)
- Expose unified agent inventory via IPC status API and robot mode
- Auto-generate agent-specific config snippets (SKILL.md, AGENTS.md) for detected agents
- Feature-gate behind `agent-detection` feature flag

## Success Criteria
- FrankenTerm detects all 9 agent types at startup without user configuration
- Agent inventory visible via `ft robot status` and IPC
- Running agent correlation enriched with installation metadata (version, config path)
- Detection adds < 50ms to startup (filesystem probes are fast)
- Graceful degradation: if detection crate unavailable, existing correlator still works

## Test and Observability Plan
1. Add comprehensive unit tests covering happy path, boundary/edge cases, and explicit failure/error behavior for logic introduced or changed by this bead.
2. Add deterministic integration and end-to-end scenario scripts that exercise full workflow behavior, including at least one negative/failure scenario and one recovery scenario.
3. Emit detailed structured logs during tests and e2e runs (timestamp, subsystem, correlation_id, scenario_id, inputs, decisions, outcomes, reason_code/error_code).
4. Persist triage artifacts for failed runs (stdout/stderr, structured logs, snapshots/fixtures, and concise failure summaries) so regressions can be root-caused quickly.
5. Ensure test commands and evidence locations are documented in the bead implementation notes and wired into normal validation/CI paths.

## User Impact
1. Specify the concrete operator/agent workflow pain this bead removes (speed, reliability, safety, or clarity).
2. Define measurable user-facing outcomes (for example p95 latency, failure/timeout rate, time-to-recovery, or reduction in manual intervention steps).
3. Define no-regression UX guarantees and explicit rollback/degradation behavior if those outcomes are not met.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Deliver unified agent inventory behavior by combining installed-agent detection with runtime pane correlation, without regressing current runtime correlator behavior.
2. Expose inventory and lifecycle data through IPC and robot mode with stable machine-consumable schemas and graceful feature-disabled behavior.
3. Deliver safe agent-config generation flows (dry-run, backup, merge/append semantics) across supported agent ecosystems with no destructive overwrites.
4. Require comprehensive validation: unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end scripts covering all supported agent types, partial installs, empty installs, and failure paths.
5. Require detailed structured logging/diagnostics for detection evidence, config mutation operations, lifecycle events, and API responses for reproducible triage.
6. Closure requires full evidence package (commands, artifacts, residual risk), including blocked-surface resolution notes where repository state constraints were encountered.
