# Task: Vendored version compatibility

## Goal
Prevent mysterious breakage by checking whether the running WezTerm is compatible with the vendored protocol.

## Deliverables
- Function to determine local WezTerm version.
- Embed vendored version/commit in build metadata.
- Compatibility classification:
  - matched
  - compatible (warn)
  - incompatible (disable vendored backend; suggest fix)
- Surface in `wa doctor` and `wa status --health`.

## Testing
- Unit tests:
  - parse representative local version strings (stable + nightly-ish)
  - compatibility classification matrix is deterministic
  - incompatible → vendored disabled (fallback to CLI) and warning message is stable

## Acceptance Criteria
- On mismatch, wa clearly explains what to do.

title: Vendored tests: feature build + compatibility gating + basic RPC fixtures
description:
# Task: Vendored tests (feature vendored)

## Goal
Ensure vendored mode does not rot.

Vendored mode is optional and higher-risk (we’re embedding upstream code). If it compiles but breaks at runtime, it becomes a maintenance trap.

## Test tiers
### 1) Build-level verification (always in CI)
- `cargo test --features vendored` (or at least `cargo check`) must succeed.
- Ensure the default (non-vendored) build still works.

### 2) Pure unit tests (offline)
- Version compatibility logic:
  - local wezterm version parsing
  - compatibility decisions are deterministic

- Client selection logic:
  - “vendored available” → prefer vendored
  - “vendored unavailable” → fall back to CLI client

### 3) Fixture-based protocol tests (offline)
- Where possible, test mux RPC framing using fixtures:
  - encode/decode round-trips
  - error cases (truncated frames, invalid message types)

### 4) Optional manual smoke
- On a dev machine with a real mux server, run a smoke command that:
  - connects
  - reads minimal pane metadata
  - exits cleanly

## Acceptance Criteria
- CI includes at least a vendored build/test step.
- Core selection + compatibility logic is unit-tested.
- Protocol handling is exercised with offline fixtures (no live mux required).


## Testing
- Meta-validation:
  - Add at least one intentionally-invalid RPC frame fixture to ensure error handling paths are tested.
  - Ensure CI runs both default and vendored test commands so regressions don’t hide behind feature flags.
close_reason: done

title: Vendoring ROI decision: CLI gaps + benchmarks + go/no-go
description:
# Task: Vendoring ROI decision (go/no-go)

## Goal
Decide whether WezTerm vendoring delivers enough value to justify the maintenance cost.

## Why
Vendoring increases complexity and build cost. We should only proceed if it meaningfully improves:
- output capture latency
- CPU usage
- fidelity (fewer gaps)

## Work items
- Benchmark CLI polling baseline (CPU, latency, gap rate) under realistic workloads.
- Identify concrete pain points that vendoring solves (e.g., streaming, zero-copy scrollback).
- Define success thresholds for vendored mode (e.g., 5x lower polling CPU, <50ms avg latency).

## Deliverables
- Go/no-go decision recorded in this bead.
- If go:
  - list of required vendored APIs
  - minimal supported WezTerm version window
- If no-go:
  - defer vendoring tasks and document reasons

## Testing
- Use existing benchmark harness (`wa-4vx.10.2`) to capture baseline numbers and include them in the decision.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Decision includes measurable evidence and clear thresholds.
notes: Provisional no-go pending real WezTerm CLI metrics; baseline + thresholds in benchmarks/vendoring_roi_decision.md

title: Vendoring maintenance plan: pin commit, embed commit metadata, CI vendored build+smoke
description:
# Task: Vendoring maintenance plan (pin commit + build metadata + CI job)

## Goal
If we enable `--features vendored`, make it maintainable and diagnosable by implementing the maintenance posture from PLAN.md Appendix H.

## Why
Vendoring WezTerm increases:
- build complexity
- upgrade burden
- risk of subtle compatibility breaks

Without explicit maintenance infrastructure, vendored mode becomes a “rotting optional feature”.

## Deliverables (Appendix H, made concrete)
1) **Pin to a commit hash**
   - Decide the mechanism:
     - git dependency pinned to commit, or
     - vendored subtree/submodule
   - Record the exact commit hash and update procedure.

2) **Embed vendored commit in build metadata**
   - `wa --version --verbose` includes:
     - vendored commit hash (when vendored feature enabled)
     - local wezterm version (if detectable)
   - `wa doctor` can compare local WezTerm against vendored compatibility info.

3) **Add CI coverage for vendored feature**
   - Add a CI job that:
     - builds `wa` with `--features vendored`
     - runs a minimal offline mux protocol smoke test (fixtures)
     - reports compilation breakage early

## Testing
- Unit tests:
  - build metadata includes vendored commit when feature enabled
  - `wa doctor` compatibility reporting is deterministic

- CI tests:
  - `cargo test --features vendored` (or `cargo check` + targeted tests) runs and is non-flaky

## Acceptance Criteria
- Vendored mode has an explicit, repeatable “update vendored commit” procedure.
- CI will catch vendored compilation breakage quickly.
- Users can report issues with enough metadata to know whether compatibility is the cause.
close_reason: done

title: [EPIC] Real-time output streaming: subscribe to pane deltas (vendored)
description:
# [EPIC] Real-time output streaming

## Mission
Move from polling-based capture to subscription-based capture when vendored WezTerm is available.

## Why
- Lower latency
- Less CPU
- Eliminates missed scrollback windows under heavy load

## Scope
- Subscribe to pane output events and feed them into the existing ingest/event bus.
- Preserve current polling path as fallback.

## Definition of done
- Vendored mode can stream deltas for a pane.
- Ingest can switch between polling and streaming based on capabilities.


## Success Criteria
- Real-time streaming of pane output is optional, performant, and does not regress ingest correctness.
- Backpressure and resource limits prevent runaway memory/CPU usage.
- Tests validate correctness under streaming and non-streaming modes.


## Testing
- Correctness tests:
  - Streaming mode must preserve the same seq/gap invariants as polling.
  - Compare streaming vs polling capture on the same fixture transcript (when possible) and assert equivalence.

- Backpressure tests:
  - Simulate slow consumers and ensure bounded queues drop/slow appropriately without unbounded memory.

## Acceptance Criteria
- All items in the following sections are satisfied: Success Criteria, Definition of Done.
- All Testing requirements pass (unit/integration/E2E) with the logging/artifacts described above.
- Any explicit dependencies for this bead are implemented and validated via tests or E2E artifacts.

## Test Framework Requirements
- **LabRuntime DPOR** (Dynamic Partial Order Reduction): Use LabRuntime's DPOR scheduler to test streaming concurrency invariants. Key scenarios:
  - Multiple panes streaming concurrently into the event bus — verify no interleaving corrupts per-pane sequence ordering.
  - Polling-to-streaming mode switch mid-capture — verify no gaps or duplicates at the transition boundary.
  - Backpressure activation under concurrent producers — verify bounded queue invariants hold regardless of scheduling order.
- **Criterion benchmarks** for stream throughput:
  - `bench_stream_ingest_throughput`: Measure bytes/sec for streaming ingest of a synthetic pane output (1 KB, 64 KB, 1 MB chunks).
  - `bench_stream_vs_poll_latency`: Compare end-to-end latency from pane output emission to event bus delivery for streaming vs polling modes.
  - `bench_backpressure_overhead`: Measure throughput degradation when backpressure engages (slow consumer scenario).
  - All benchmarks must run in CI and regressions >10% should trigger warnings.

## Cross-references
- **wa-283h4.5** (Reactive dataflow graph): The streaming subscription model in this epic feeds into the reactive dataflow graph's input nodes. Ensure the stream event format (PaneDelta, GAP, detection events) is compatible with the dataflow graph's expected input schema. Backpressure signals from the dataflow graph should propagate back to the streaming layer to avoid unbounded buffering between the two systems.

## Test and Observability Plan
1. Add comprehensive unit tests covering happy path, boundary/edge cases, and explicit failure/error behavior for logic introduced or changed by this bead.
2. Add deterministic integration and end-to-end scenario scripts that exercise full workflow behavior, including at least one negative/failure scenario and one recovery scenario.
3. Emit detailed structured logs during tests and e2e runs (timestamp, subsystem, correlation_id, scenario_id, inputs, decisions, outcomes, reason_code/error_code).
4. Persist triage artifacts for failed runs (stdout/stderr, structured logs, snapshots/fixtures, and concise failure summaries) so regressions can be root-caused quickly.
5. Ensure test commands and evidence locations are documented in the bead implementation notes and wired into normal validation/CI paths.

## User Impact
1. Specify the concrete operator/agent workflow pain this bead removes (speed, reliability, safety, or clarity).
2. Define measurable user-facing outcomes (for example p95 latency, failure/timeout rate, time-to-recovery, or reduction in manual intervention steps).
3. Define no-regression UX guarantees and explicit rollback/degradation behavior if those outcomes are not met.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Implement scoped streaming/agent capability with deterministic ordering and resilient reconnect/backpressure behavior.
2. Require comprehensive unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end scripts for happy path, race/interleaving cases, and failure/recovery modes.
3. Require structured diagnostics/logging for connection state, sequence tracking, persistence boundaries, and protocol errors with reproducible artifacts.
4. Heavy validation/benchmark/soak runs must execute via rch and be captured as evidence.
5. Closure requires explicit proof of correctness, performance envelopes, and operational safety.
notes: Distributed execution control point: preserve deterministic ordering and explicit failure semantics; no closure without replayable evidence artifacts.

title: Streaming design: event types, backpressure, integration with existing seq/gap model
description:
# Task: Streaming design

## Goal
Specify how streaming output integrates with wa’s segment/seq/gap invariants.

## Key constraints
- We must preserve monotonic per-pane `seq`.
- We must still emit explicit GAP events when discontinuities occur.
- Streaming must not overwhelm storage/event bus.

## Deliverables
- Definition of the streamed unit (bytes, lines, or “delta string”).
- Mapping to `OutputSegment` + seq assignment.
- Backpressure strategy:
  - bounded channels
  - drop policy (prefer emitting GAP over silent drop)

## Testing
- Property/invariant tests:
  - given an input stream with drops/out-of-order events, we either:
    - re-order safely, OR
    - emit a GAP deterministically (explicitly choose and lock down)

- Integration tests with a fake stream:
  - slow consumer behavior
  - bounded channel behavior
  - cancellation/reconnect paths do not leak resources

## Acceptance Criteria
- A reviewer can implement streaming ingestion from this issue alone.
- The design includes an explicit plan for invariant testing (seq monotonicity + gap semantics).
close_reason: done

title: Implement subscribe_output (vendored): stream pane output events as deltas
description:
# Task: Implement `subscribe_output` (vendored)

## Goal
In vendored mode, subscribe to pane output events and expose a stream of deltas that integrates with wa’s existing seq/gap model.

Polling scrollback works, but subscriptions enable:
- lower latency
- lower CPU
- better fidelity (fewer missed segments)

## Deliverables
- Vendored mux subscription wiring (connect → subscribe → receive events).
- Stream adapter that yields a typed event (proposed: `PaneDelta`).
- Cancellation/shutdown handling:
  - dropping the stream unsubscribes
  - process shutdown closes cleanly

## Backpressure & robustness
- The stream must not allow unbounded buffering.
  - bounded channel
  - drop policy or slow-consumer handling (explicitly choose and document)

- Handle reconnects/timeouts gracefully:
  - transient errors → reconnect with backoff
  - permanent errors → surface a structured error and fall back to polling (if caller chooses)

## Integration with seq/gap
- Define how subscription events map to:
  - seq numbers
  - gaps (if the stream reports dropped events)

## Testing strategy
- Offline unit tests with fixtures:
  - decode/encode subscription messages
  - simulate event stream and ensure adapter produces ordered deltas
  - simulate dropped/out-of-order events and ensure we emit a GAP or diagnostic

## Acceptance Criteria
- Can subscribe to a pane and receive deltas while a command runs.
- Slow consumer does not cause unbounded memory growth.
- Error paths are deterministic and do not panic.
close_reason: done

title: Integrate streaming tailers: prefer subscription when available; fallback to polling
description:
# Task: Integrate streaming tailers

## Goal
Teach the ingest system to choose between:
- polling tailers (CLI get-text)
- streaming tailers (vendored subscribe)

The objective is reduced CPU/latency without changing downstream semantics.

## Capability detection
At runtime, decide per workspace/domain:
- if subscription is supported and healthy → use streaming
- otherwise → use polling

The decision should be:
- deterministic
- observable in logs/health snapshot

## Semantics must match polling mode
Regardless of tailer type:
- segments are written with seq
- gaps are emitted on discontinuity
- pattern detection and workflows behave the same

## Failure & fallback behavior
- If streaming connection drops:
  - record a diagnostic event
  - fall back to polling with backoff

- If polling is too slow or misses data:
  - record explicit GAP events (existing invariant)

## Performance expectations
- Vendored streaming mode should show significantly lower polling load and better latency.
- Add counters to compare:
  - messages/sec
  - dropped events
  - gap rate

## Testing strategy
- Unit tests with a fake stream:
  - normal ordered stream → segments
  - dropped/out-of-order stream → GAP behavior
  - stream disconnect triggers fallback

## Acceptance Criteria
- In vendored mode, ingest runs with significantly lower polling load.
- In non-vendored mode, behavior remains unchanged.
- Streaming failures degrade gracefully (no crashes, clear diagnostics).
close_reason: done

# Task: Expose streaming subscriptions (optional)

## Goal
Allow agent integrations to subscribe to:
- pane output deltas
- event stream
without polling.

## Options
- MCP streaming resource (if supported)
- Web server SSE/WebSocket endpoint (feature web)

## Requirements
- Backpressure and rate limiting.
- Privacy: apply redaction rules where appropriate.

## Testing
- Unit/contract tests:
  - stream message schemas are stable
  - backpressure behavior is bounded and deterministic
  - redaction is applied (no raw transcript secrets)

- E2E tests (optional, but preferred if we ship this):
  - a client subscribes and receives a bounded stream of updates
  - disconnect/reconnect does not leak resources

## Acceptance Criteria
- A client can subscribe and receive incremental updates with bounded memory.

## Test Framework Requirements
- **Criterion benchmarks** for subscription latency:
  - `bench_subscription_first_message_latency`: Measure time from subscription establishment to delivery of the first delta message (target: <5ms for local, <50ms for SSE/WebSocket).
  - `bench_subscription_steady_state_throughput`: Measure messages/sec sustained delivery to a single subscriber under continuous pane output.
  - `bench_multi_subscriber_fanout`: Measure latency and throughput with 1, 10, and 50 concurrent subscribers on the same pane stream. Identify the scaling curve.
  - `bench_redaction_overhead`: Measure per-message cost of applying redaction rules during streaming delivery.
  - All benchmarks must be gated behind `--features streaming` and run in CI.
- **LabRuntime DPOR** for concurrent subscribers:
  - Verify that multiple subscribers receiving the same stream see identical message ordering (no subscriber gets a reordered view).
  - Test subscriber connect/disconnect races: a subscriber disconnects while a message is in-flight — verify no resource leaks (file descriptors, memory, channel slots).
  - Test concurrent subscribe + backpressure: one slow subscriber must not block delivery to other subscribers (fan-out isolation).
  - Test redaction consistency: under concurrent delivery, all subscribers see the same redacted content (no race between redaction and delivery).

title: [EPIC] Optional distributed mode: wa-agent + aggregator + wire protocol
description:
# [EPIC] Optional distributed mode

## Mission
Support multi-machine WezTerm setups by running a lightweight `wa-agent` near each remote mux server.

## Model
- `wa-agent` (remote): captures deltas/events locally and streams them to...
- `wa` aggregator (workstation): merges streams, persists to local SQLite, runs workflows.

## Guiding principles
- Keep the wire protocol small and deterministic.
- Prefer delta streaming over full scrollback dumps.
- Security by default (auth token, localhost bind unless configured).

## Definition of done
- A single remote `wa-agent` can connect to an aggregator and stream pane deltas/events.
- Aggregator persists the data and exposes it via CLI/robot/MCP.


## Success Criteria
- Distributed mode is optional, secure-by-default, and does not broaden the attack surface unintentionally.
- Aggregator/agent protocol is versioned, tested, and includes replay protection and safe bind defaults.
- Local-only mode remains the default with no required network listeners.


## Testing
- Protocol tests:
  - Encode/decode roundtrips for each message type; version negotiation behavior.

- Security tests:
  - Default bind is localhost; remote bind requires explicit dangerous flag.
  - Auth token required; missing/invalid token is rejected with stable error codes.

- E2E tests:
  - Agent→aggregator E2E validates persistence + visibility and produces artifacts (`wa-nu4.4.3.5`).

## Acceptance Criteria
- All items in the following sections are satisfied: Success Criteria, Definition of Done.
- All Testing requirements pass (unit/integration/E2E) with the logging/artifacts described above.
- Any explicit dependencies for this bead are implemented and validated via tests or E2E artifacts.

## Test Framework Requirements
- **LabRuntime DPOR** for distributed coordination:
  - Agent-to-aggregator connection establishment: verify that concurrent connection attempts from multiple agents are handled without deadlock or dropped connections regardless of scheduling order.
  - Message interleaving from multiple agents: verify per-domain ordering is preserved even when messages from different agents arrive in arbitrary interleavings.
  - Auth token handshake races: verify that a connection attempt with an invalid token concurrent with a valid connection does not corrupt the valid session's state.
  - Aggregator shutdown with active agents: verify graceful disconnection — agents detect the shutdown and enter reconnect-with-backoff without data loss for in-flight messages.
  - Version negotiation under concurrent connects: verify that agents with different protocol versions are correctly accepted or rejected without blocking other connections.

## Cross-references
- **wa-1360** (Mux server sharding): Distributed mode's agent placement and stream routing must align with the mux server sharding topology. Each `wa-agent` maps to one or more mux server shards; the aggregator must be aware of shard boundaries to correctly attribute pane data to domains. Shard rebalancing (adding/removing mux servers) must be coordinated with agent lifecycle — the aggregator should handle agents appearing/disappearing as shards migrate. Reuse the shard identity and routing metadata from wa-1360 in the distributed wire protocol.

## Test and Observability Plan
1. Add comprehensive unit tests covering happy path, boundary/edge cases, and explicit failure/error behavior for logic introduced or changed by this bead.
2. Add deterministic integration and end-to-end scenario scripts that exercise full workflow behavior, including at least one negative/failure scenario and one recovery scenario.
3. Emit detailed structured logs during tests and e2e runs (timestamp, subsystem, correlation_id, scenario_id, inputs, decisions, outcomes, reason_code/error_code).
4. Persist triage artifacts for failed runs (stdout/stderr, structured logs, snapshots/fixtures, and concise failure summaries) so regressions can be root-caused quickly.
5. Ensure test commands and evidence locations are documented in the bead implementation notes and wired into normal validation/CI paths.

description:
# Task: Implement `wa-agent`

## Goal
Create a lightweight daemon that runs near a mux server and streams:
- pane deltas
- detections
- gaps
- minimal metadata

## Design
- Capture engine:
  - default: polling tailers (CLI)
  - optional: streaming if vendored available
- Network:
  - connect to aggregator via configured URL
  - reconnect with backoff

## Safety
- Agent should be read-only unless explicitly given permission to perform pane-local actions.
- Network safety must follow the distributed security bead:
  - auth token handshake
  - never log tokens
  - bounded message rates / reconnect behavior

## Testing
- Unit tests:
  - wire protocol encode/decode integration
  - reconnect/backoff behavior is bounded and deterministic

- Integration tests (offline):
  - stream fixture deltas into a fake aggregator endpoint
  - assert messages are well-formed and redacted where needed

- E2E coverage:
  - full agent→aggregator behavior is covered by `wa-nu4.4.3.5`.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `wa-agent` can connect to aggregator and stream at least one pane's output deltas.

## Test Framework Requirements
- **Criterion benchmarks** for capture overhead:
  - `bench_agent_capture_cpu`: Measure CPU overhead of the agent's capture loop (polling mode) at idle, moderate (1 KB/s), and heavy (1 MB/s) pane output rates. Target: <2% CPU at idle, <10% at heavy.
  - `bench_agent_capture_memory`: Measure steady-state RSS of the agent process with 1, 10, and 50 monitored panes. Ensure memory scales linearly (no per-pane unbounded buffers).
  - `bench_agent_delta_serialization`: Measure time to serialize a PaneDelta message (varying payload sizes: 256B, 4KB, 64KB). This is the hot path for streaming throughput.
  - `bench_agent_network_send`: Measure end-to-end latency from capture to aggregator receipt over localhost (baseline for distributed latency expectations).
  - All benchmarks gated behind `--features distributed`.

## macOS: Process Monitoring Considerations
- On Linux, `wa-agent` can use `procfs` (`/proc/<pid>/stat`, `/proc/<pid>/fd/`) for lightweight monitoring of mux server health and resource usage. On macOS, `/proc` does not exist.
- macOS fallbacks:
  - Use `sysctl` (`kern.proc.pid`) or the `libproc` C API (`proc_pidinfo`, `proc_pidpath`) for process introspection.
  - Use `kevent`/`kqueue` with `EVFILT_PROC` for process lifecycle events (exit, fork) instead of polling `/proc`.
  - For file descriptor counting, use `proc_pidinfo(PROC_PIDLISTFDS)` instead of reading `/proc/<pid>/fd/`.
- Wrap platform-specific monitoring behind a `ProcessMonitor` trait with `LinuxProcessMonitor` and `MacosProcessMonitor` implementations. Use `#[cfg(target_os = "...")]` to select at compile time.
- Test both implementations in CI (Linux runner + macOS runner) to catch platform drift.

## User Impact
1. Specify the concrete operator/agent workflow pain this bead removes (speed, reliability, safety, or clarity).
2. Define measurable user-facing outcomes (for example p95 latency, failure/timeout rate, time-to-recovery, or reduction in manual intervention steps).
3. Define no-regression UX guarantees and explicit rollback/degradation behavior if those outcomes are not met.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Implement scoped streaming/agent capability with deterministic ordering and resilient reconnect/backpressure behavior.
2. Require comprehensive unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end scripts for happy path, race/interleaving cases, and failure/recovery modes.
3. Require structured diagnostics/logging for connection state, sequence tracking, persistence boundaries, and protocol errors with reproducible artifacts.
4. Heavy validation/benchmark/soak runs must execute via rch and be captured as evidence.
5. Closure requires explicit proof of correctness, performance envelopes, and operational safety.
notes: Distributed execution control point: preserve deterministic ordering and explicit failure semantics; no closure without replayable evidence artifacts.

description:
# Task: Aggregator mode

## Goal
Add an aggregator mode to `wa watch` that accepts remote streams and integrates them into the same pipeline as local capture.

## Responsibilities
- Accept connections from `wa-agent`.
- Merge streams (per-domain / per-pane) into the event bus.
- Persist segments/events to SQLite.
- Run workflows (and if an action must be pane-local, delegate back to the appropriate agent in future iterations).

## Security & safety
- Must enforce distributed security requirements (auth token, bind defaults, replay protection).
- Never accept unauthenticated traffic by default.

## Testing
- Unit tests:
  - per-pane ordering/merge behavior is deterministic
  - backpressure limits are enforced
  - malformed messages produce structured errors (no panics)

- Integration tests (offline):
  - accept a fake agent stream and ensure segments/events land in SQLite
  - ensure explicit gaps are preserved

- E2E coverage:
  - full agent→aggregator behavior is covered by `wa-nu4.4.3.5`.

## Acceptance Criteria
- With one `wa-agent` connected, `wa status` shows remote panes and `wa query` can search their output.

## Test Framework Requirements
- **Criterion benchmarks** for merge throughput:
  - `bench_aggregator_merge_single_agent`: Measure events/sec the aggregator can merge from a single agent stream (varying message sizes: 256B, 4KB, 64KB payloads). Target: >10K events/sec for small messages.
  - `bench_aggregator_merge_multi_agent`: Measure aggregate throughput with 1, 5, and 20 concurrent agent streams. Identify the scaling bottleneck (CPU, SQLite write lock, event bus contention).
  - `bench_aggregator_persist_latency`: Measure p50/p95/p99 latency from message receipt to SQLite commit. Target: p95 <10ms for single-agent workload.
  - `bench_aggregator_query_under_load`: Measure `wa query` response time while the aggregator is actively ingesting from multiple agents. Ensure ingest does not starve query responsiveness.
  - All benchmarks gated behind `--features distributed`.
- **LabRuntime DPOR** for concurrent stream merging:
  - Multiple agents sending to the same domain/pane concurrently: verify per-pane sequence ordering is deterministic regardless of arrival interleaving.
  - Concurrent ingest + query: verify that a `wa query` executing concurrently with active ingest sees a consistent snapshot (no torn reads or partial segments).
  - Concurrent ingest + persist: verify SQLite write batching does not lose messages when multiple agent streams commit concurrently (test with WAL mode contention).
  - Agent disconnect during active merge: verify in-flight data is either fully committed or cleanly rolled back — no partial segments persisted.

## Test and Observability Plan
1. Add comprehensive unit tests covering happy path, boundary/edge cases, and explicit failure/error behavior for logic introduced or changed by this bead.
2. Add deterministic integration and end-to-end scenario scripts that exercise full workflow behavior, including at least one negative/failure scenario and one recovery scenario.
3. Emit detailed structured logs during tests and e2e runs (timestamp, subsystem, correlation_id, scenario_id, inputs, decisions, outcomes, reason_code/error_code).
4. Persist triage artifacts for failed runs (stdout/stderr, structured logs, snapshots/fixtures, and concise failure summaries) so regressions can be root-caused quickly.
5. Ensure test commands and evidence locations are documented in the bead implementation notes and wired into normal validation/CI paths.

## User Impact
1. Specify the concrete operator/agent workflow pain this bead removes (speed, reliability, safety, or clarity).
2. Define measurable user-facing outcomes (for example p95 latency, failure/timeout rate, time-to-recovery, or reduction in manual intervention steps).
3. Define no-regression UX guarantees and explicit rollback/degradation behavior if those outcomes are not met.

title: Distributed security: auth token, bind defaults, replay protection (minimal)
description:
# Task: Distributed mode security

## Goal
Prevent accidental exposure when running aggregator/agent networking.

Distributed mode turns wa into a networked system; the default posture must be “safe and local”, with explicit opt-in for anything remotely reachable.

## Requirements
### Bind defaults
- Aggregator binds to localhost by default.
- Public bind requires an explicit, scary flag (e.g., `--dangerous-bind-any`) and prints a prominent warning.

### Authentication
- Simple shared auth token between agent and aggregator (v0):
  - sent in a header or the first message
  - constant-time compare
  - never logged

### Replay / injection resistance
- Basic replay protection:
  - monotonic sequence numbers per agent session
  - reject stale/duplicate sequences

- Rate limiting / connection limits:
  - cap concurrent connections
  - cap messages/sec per connection

### Redaction
- Aggregator logs and any exposed query surfaces must use wa’s redaction rules.

## Testing strategy
- Unit tests:
  - token verification rejects wrong/missing token
  - replay checks reject duplicate/stale sequence numbers

- Integration tests:
  - unauthenticated client cannot inject fake events/segments
  - authenticated client can stream
  - logs do not contain token values

## Acceptance Criteria
- An unauthenticated client cannot inject fake events/segments.
- Public bind is never the default.
- Replay/injection controls are present and test-covered.
close_reason: done

title: Distributed E2E tests: agent→aggregator stream, persistence, CLI visibility
description:
# Task: Distributed E2E tests (feature distributed)

## Goal
Validate distributed mode end-to-end so it can be trusted when enabled:
- agent → aggregator streaming
- persistence + indexing
- CLI/robot visibility of aggregated data

Distributed mode is optional, but if we ship it, it must not be flaky.

## E2E harness requirements
- Must run **offline** with no real WezTerm required.
- Prefer a deterministic "fake agent" producer that emits:
  - segments (PaneDelta)
  - explicit GAP events
  - detections/events
  - out-of-order or duplicated messages (to test robustness)

- Spin up an aggregator instance bound to localhost with an ephemeral port.
- Capture artifacts:
  - aggregator logs
  - agent logs
  - a small exported DB snapshot

## Test runner integration
- Must run via the shared E2E runner (`./scripts/e2e_test.sh`) and follow the harness artifacts contract.
- The runner should allow skipping this case when `--features distributed` is not enabled.

## Required scenarios
1) Happy path
   - agent streams a few segments
   - aggregator persists them
   - CLI/robot query surfaces can retrieve them

2) GAP preservation
   - agent emits a gap
   - aggregator records it
   - downstream queries reflect the discontinuity

3) Robustness
   - duplicated messages do not create duplicate persisted rows (or are deduped deterministically)
   - out-of-order messages either:
     - are re-ordered safely, OR
     - are recorded as a gap + diagnostic (explicitly choose and test)

4) Security baseline
   - auth token required when configured
   - logs + responses remain redacted

## Observability expectations
- Structured logs with correlation ids:
  - stream connection/session id
  - pane id
  - message counts
- On failure, E2E script prints where artifacts were written.

## Registry
- Register this case in the E2E case registry (`wa-4vx.10.20`).
- Mark it as **non-default** unless `--features distributed` (or equivalent) is enabled.

## Logging
- Follow the standard E2E harness logging contract (`wa-4vx.10.6`) and runner (`wa-4vx.10.11`).
- Emit per-step start/end markers with timestamps + durations.
- Include case name and pane ids in every log line.
- Redact secrets (device codes, tokens) in logs and artifacts.

## Acceptance Criteria
- An E2E script (or `cargo test --features distributed`) can spin up fake agent + aggregator and assert:
  - segments arrive
  - gaps are preserved
  - detections/events arrive
  - aggregated data is visible via CLI/robot query
- Failures produce actionable logs + artifacts.


## Testing
- Meta-validation:
  - Add a negative security scenario: missing/invalid auth token must be rejected and logged (redacted) with stable error codes.
  - Assert required artifacts exist (agent logs, aggregator logs, DB snapshot/export) before declaring PASS.

## Docker Compose Test Infrastructure
- The distributed E2E harness should use a `docker-compose.yml` to orchestrate the test topology:
  - **Service: fake-agent** (one or more instances): Runs the deterministic fake agent producer, configured to emit the required scenarios (happy path, GAP events, duplicates, out-of-order).
  - **Service: aggregator**: Runs `wa watch --aggregator` bound to an ephemeral port on the compose network.
  - **Service: test-runner**: Executes assertions against the aggregator's CLI/robot query interface after the agents have streamed their payloads.
- Use Docker Compose `depends_on` with health checks to sequence startup (aggregator healthy before agents connect).
- Artifact collection: mount a shared volume for logs and DB snapshots; the test-runner service copies artifacts to the host on completion (success or failure).
- Compose profiles: use `--profile distributed` so these services are not started by default (mirrors the `--features distributed` gate).

## macOS Docker Considerations
- **Docker Desktop for Mac** runs Docker inside a Linux VM, which affects this harness:
  - **Networking**: Inter-container networking works identically, but host-to-container port mapping uses the Docker Desktop VM's network stack. Use `docker compose port` to discover mapped ports rather than hardcoding.
  - **File system performance**: Shared volumes between macOS host and containers are slow. Use named volumes for the shared artifact directory and copy artifacts to the host only at the end of the test run.
  - **Apple Silicon (arm64)**: Ensure all container images in the compose file support `linux/arm64`. If any image is amd64-only, use `platform: linux/amd64` explicitly and accept the Rosetta 2 emulation overhead (document expected slowdown).
  - **Resource limits**: The default Docker Desktop resource allocation (2 CPU, 2 GB RAM) may be insufficient for running multiple agent containers + aggregator concurrently. Document minimum requirements (4 CPU, 4 GB RAM) and detect/warn at harness startup.
- CI matrix should run these E2E tests on both a native Linux runner and a macOS runner to catch platform-specific Docker behavior differences.

title: Distributed mode scope decision (when multi-machine coordination is needed)
description:
# Task: Distributed mode scope decision (when multi-machine coordination is needed)

## Goal
Resolve PLAN.md Open Question #6: **when do we actually need cross-machine wa instances to communicate?**

This is a decision gate: we should not invest in distributed mode unless there is a clear, measured user benefit.

## Why this matters (user value)
Distributed mode adds:
- operational burden (deploying and updating `wa-agent`)
- security surface area (network listeners, auth tokens)
- additional failure modes

If users do not need it yet, we should defer and keep the core system simpler and more reliable.

## Inputs to evaluate
1. **Scale triggers**
   - Number of remote domains/panes where CLI polling becomes slow or flaky.
   - Average tail latency and gap rates with current CLI/Lua approaches.

2. **User-story triggers**
   - Does any priority user story *require* cross-machine aggregation (e.g., H1 across many hosts)?
   - Are there cases where local-only wa cannot observe all panes reliably?

3. **Reliability/operations**
   - Does a single workstation failure represent an unacceptable single point of failure?
   - Do we need to keep local capture alive when aggregator is offline?

4. **Security/constraints**
   - Are there environments where outbound agent→aggregator streaming is forbidden?
   - Are there compliance constraints that require local-only capture?

## Work items
- Collect baseline metrics from the CLI/Lua-only mode:
  - capture latency
  - gap rate
  - CPU usage on busy mux servers
- Define **thresholds** that justify distributed mode, e.g.:
  - N domains/panes beyond which latency or gap rate exceeds target.
  - Latency SLO violation (e.g., > 250ms p95) under normal load.
- Decide **go/no-go** for distributed mode in the next release cycle and document:
  - timeline (v0.2? later?)
  - minimal MVP scope if “go”
  - deferral rationale if “no-go”

## Deliverables
- Decision note recorded in this bead with measurable thresholds and timeline.
- If “go”:
  - update distributed epic to reflect MVP scope and prerequisites.
- If “no-go”:
  - document the specific triggers that would cause a re-evaluation.

## Testing / validation
- Use existing perf/metrics harnesses (e.g., `wa-4vx.10.2`, `wa-nu4.3.4.2`) to gather baseline numbers.
- Evidence should be reproducible (logs or summary table in the decision note).

## Acceptance Criteria
- Decision is documented with thresholds tied to measurable data.
- The decision explicitly references user-story impact (what it enables or why it’s unnecessary).
- Re-evaluation triggers are clear and actionable.

title: Coordination primitives: multi-pane selection, group locks, safe broadcast semantics
description:
# Task: Coordination primitives

## Goal
Define the primitives required for safe multi-pane workflows ("swarm" behavior) without turning wa into a chaos machine.

Multi-pane automation is powerful but risky: we need deterministic selection, locking, and per-pane auditing.

## Concepts
### Pane groups
- Define grouping strategies:
  - by domain
  - by inferred agent
  - by project (cwd-based)
- Group selection must be deterministic and explainable.

### Group locks
- Build on per-pane workflow locks to support multi-pane coordination:
  - lock acquisition across N panes is all-or-nothing (or explicitly partial with clear reporting)
  - timeouts and deadlock avoidance

### Safe broadcast semantics
- Observe each pane first.
- Only act on panes that pass preconditions (prompt state, no gap, not alt-screen, etc.).
- Execute actions with policy gating + rate limiting.
- Record per-pane results:
  - allowed/denied
  - verification success/failure
  - timing

## Testing strategy
- Unit tests with synthetic panes:
  - group selection and determinism
  - lock acquisition behavior
  - partial failure reporting

## Acceptance Criteria
- A workflow can target N panes and produce an auditable per-pane outcome.
- Preconditions prevent “spray and pray” broadcasting.

title: Implement `wa why` command: explain any recent policy decision
description:
# Task: Implement `wa why` command

## Goal
Create a dedicated CLI command that explains any recent policy decision with full context.

## Why This Matters
When wa denies a send or takes unexpected action, users need to understand why. The `wa why` command provides that answer instantly without diving into logs.

## Command Interface
```bash
# Explain the most recent denial
$ wa why denied

# Explain a specific decision by ID
$ wa why denied --decision-id abc123

# Explain denial for a specific pane
$ wa why denied --pane 3

# Explain a workflow decision
$ wa why workflow-skipped --workflow handle_compaction

# JSON output for automation
$ wa why denied --pane 3 --format json
```

## Output Format
```
Decision: DENY
Type: SendText
Target: Pane 3 (claude_code @ /home/user/project)
Timestamp: 2026-01-18T14:32:01Z

Reason: Pane is in AltScreen mode
Rule: safety.alt_screen_block (severity: hard_deny)

Evidence:
  - AltScreen flag: true (detected at 14:31:55)
  - Last normal mode: 14:28:12
  - Pane title: "vim AGENTS.md"

Rationale:
  Sending input while AltScreen is active can corrupt TUI applications
  or cause unintended side effects. This is a safety guard.

To proceed:
  1. Wait for pane to exit AltScreen (close vim/less/etc.)
  2. Check pane state: wa status --pane 3
  3. If you truly need to override, use the allow-once approval flow:
     - rerun the original action to get an allow-once code
     - approve it: wa approve <code>
     - retry the action
```

## Implementation

### 1. Decision Context Storage
Extend the audit trail to store full decision context (see `wa-7wk`):
- conditions/capabilities
- rules evaluated
- determining rule
- evidence collected

### 2. Explanation Templates
Map `(rule_id, decision)` → explanation template:
```rust
struct ExplanationTemplate {
    reason: &'static str,
    rationale: &'static str,
    to_proceed: Vec<&'static str>,
}

static EXPLANATIONS: phf::Map<&str, ExplanationTemplate> = phf_map! {
    "safety.alt_screen_block:deny" => ExplanationTemplate {
        reason: "Pane is in AltScreen mode",
        rationale: "Sending input while AltScreen is active can corrupt TUI applications...",
        to_proceed: vec![
            "Wait for pane to exit AltScreen (close vim/less/etc.)",
            "Check pane state: wa status --pane {pane_id}",
            "If needed, use allow-once approvals: wa approve <code>",
        ],
    },
    // ... more templates
};
```

### 3. Query Interface
```rust
fn explain_decision(
    storage: &StorageHandle,
    decision_id: Option<&str>,
    pane_id: Option<PaneId>,
    decision_type: DecisionType,
) -> Result<Explanation, Error>;
```

### 4. CLI Integration
```rust
#[derive(Parser)]
struct WhyArgs {
    #[clap(subcommand)]
    decision_type: DecisionType,

    #[clap(long)]
    decision_id: Option<String>,

    #[clap(long)]
    pane: Option<PaneId>,

    #[clap(long, default_value = "text")]
    format: OutputFormat,
}
```

## Testing
- Unit tests: Each rule has a valid explanation template
- Integration tests: `wa why` returns expected explanations for known scenarios
- Template tests: All templates have placeholders filled correctly
- UX tests: Explanations are understandable (user testing)

## Acceptance Criteria
- `wa why denied` explains the most recent denial
- `wa why denied --pane 3` explains denial for specific pane
- All policy rules have explanation templates
- Output includes evidence, rationale, and "To proceed" steps
- JSON output is available for automation

title: E2E script: RequireApproval → wa approve allow-once → send succeeds (audited)
description:
# Task: E2E script — approval allow-once

## Goal
Validate the full RequireApproval UX loop:
1) an action requires approval
2) wa returns a structured allow-once payload
3) a human grants approval via `wa approve`
4) the action succeeds on retry
5) the whole flow is auditable and redacted

This is the critical "human-in-the-loop" bridge that keeps wa safe and ergonomic.

## Scenario
- Use a policy config that forces RequireApproval for SendText in a safe situation (so this test is deterministic).
- Spawn a dummy pane that echoes received input.

Steps
1. Attempt a send (`wa send` or `wa robot send`): expect RequireApproval.
2. Extract `allow_once_code` from the output.
3. Run `wa approve <code> --yes`.
4. Retry the same send: expect Allow and successful injection.
5. Verify audit trail contains:
   - initial require-approval decision
   - approval grant
   - successful retry
   - redacted summaries (no raw secret-like input)

## Assertions
- RequireApproval returns a stable allow-once payload.
- Approval is scoped (wrong pane/action/workspace does not match).
- Retry succeeds only for the matching fingerprint.

## Artifacts
- Effective config used.
- Robot/human command outputs.
- Audit export JSONL (or query output).

## Registry
- Register this case in the E2E case registry (`wa-4vx.10.20`), including prerequisites and default inclusion status.
- Ensure `./scripts/e2e_test.sh --all` includes this case (or mark non-default with justification).

## Logging
- Follow the standard E2E harness logging contract (`wa-4vx.10.6`) and runner (`wa-4vx.10.11`).
- Emit per-step start/end markers with timestamps + durations.
- Include case name and pane ids in every log line.
- Redact secrets (device codes, tokens) in logs and artifacts.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Script is deterministic.
- On failure, artifacts clearly distinguish:
  - policy decision bug
  - approval storage/lookup bug
  - audit/redaction bug


## Testing
- Meta-validation:
  - Add a negative assertion: use the allow-once code against a different pane/workspace and ensure it is rejected.
  - If approvals have TTL, assert that an expired token is rejected (or explicitly document if TTL is not implemented).

- Artifact validation:
  - Assert audit artifacts include three distinct records (require-approval, approve, allowed retry) and are fully redacted.

# `wa timeline` command (ASCII timeline)

## Purpose
Display a unified event timeline in the terminal with an ASCII visualization and optional correlation markers.

```bash
wa timeline [--last <duration>] [--pane <id>] [--type <event-type>] [--format {auto|plain|json}] [-v|-vv]
```

title: SQLite tables for snapshot storage and scrollback dedup
description:
## Goal
Extend wa's existing SQLite database (schema v20+) to store mux snapshots persistently, with efficient querying and retention management.

## Background
wa already has a mature SQLite storage layer with WAL mode, schema versioning, 13+ tables including panes, output_segments, events, agent_sessions, etc. The snapshot storage should follow the same patterns: epoch-ms timestamps, proper indexing, and retention policies.

## Design
1. New table `mux_snapshots`:
   - id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY
   - snapshot_id TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE (UUID)
   - created_at INTEGER NOT NULL (epoch ms)
   - trigger TEXT NOT NULL ('periodic', 'manual', 'pre_restart', 'pre_upgrade')
   - mux_server_pid INTEGER
   - wezterm_version TEXT
   - wa_version TEXT
   - window_count INTEGER
   - tab_count INTEGER
   - pane_count INTEGER
   - snapshot_json TEXT NOT NULL (full MuxSnapshot as JSON)
   - snapshot_size_bytes INTEGER
   - checksum TEXT (SHA-256 of snapshot_json for integrity)

2. New table `snapshot_scrollbacks`:
   - id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY
   - snapshot_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES mux_snapshots(snapshot_id)
   - pane_id INTEGER NOT NULL
   - content_hash TEXT NOT NULL (for dedup across snapshots)
   - content TEXT NOT NULL (escaped terminal output)
   - line_count INTEGER
   - byte_count INTEGER
   - UNIQUE(snapshot_id, pane_id)

3. Content-addressed scrollback dedup:
   - If two consecutive snapshots have the same scrollback hash for a pane, only store it once
   - Reference by content_hash to avoid duplicating multi-MB scrollback buffers

4. Retention policy:
   - Keep last N snapshots (configurable, default 10)
   - Keep all snapshots from last 24 hours
   - Keep at least 1 snapshot per day for last 7 days
   - Configurable via wa.toml [snapshots] section

5. Schema migration:
   - Increment schema version to 21 (or next available)
   - Add migration in storage.rs following existing patterns

## Acceptance Criteria
- Tables created on schema upgrade
- Insert and query snapshots with proper indexing
- Scrollback dedup verified (same content only stored once)
- Retention cleanup works correctly
- Migration from v20 to v21 is clean

## Benchmark & Property Testing Requirements

### Criterion Benchmarks
Add `benches/snapshot_sqlite.rs` using criterion:
- **insert_latency**: Benchmark inserting a full MuxSnapshot (50 panes, 5000 lines each) into the mux_snapshots and snapshot_scrollbacks tables. Measure wall-clock time and I/O bytes. Target: <500ms for a typical 50-pane snapshot.
- **query_latest_snapshot**: Benchmark querying the most recent snapshot by created_at. Target: <5ms with proper indexing.
- **query_by_trigger**: Benchmark querying snapshots filtered by trigger type. Target: <10ms.
- **dedup_savings**: Benchmark insert time when content_hash matches an existing row (dedup path) vs fresh insert. Measure storage savings for 10 consecutive snapshots where 80% of panes have unchanged scrollback.
- **retention_cleanup**: Benchmark the retention cleanup query (DELETE old snapshots) with 100, 500, 1000 snapshots in the table.

### Proptest
Add `tests/proptest_snapshot_sqlite.rs`:
- **schema_migration_correctness**: For any arbitrary initial database state (proptest generates random existing rows in pre-migration tables), assert that migration to v21 preserves all existing data and creates new tables without errors. Run the migration, then verify all pre-existing rows are intact and new tables exist with correct schema.
- **retention_policy_invariants**: For any sequence of snapshot inserts with arbitrary timestamps and trigger types (proptest generates), assert that after cleanup: (a) at most N snapshots remain, (b) all snapshots from the last 24 hours are retained, (c) at least 1 snapshot per day for the last 7 days is retained.
- **dedup_correctness**: For any sequence of (snapshot_id, pane_id, content) triples where some share the same content, assert that only one copy of each unique content exists in storage, and all references resolve correctly.

## Cross-References
- **wa-283h4.2** (WAL snapshots): The WAL (Write-Ahead Log) snapshot system provides a complementary persistence mechanism. While wa-nz6 stores discrete point-in-time snapshots, WAL snapshots capture a continuous log of state changes. The two systems should share the same SQLite database and coordinate schema versions. WAL snapshots can reference bd-nz6's snapshot_id as a "checkpoint" -- the WAL only needs to store deltas since the last full snapshot, dramatically reducing WAL size.

title: [EPIC] Universal mux I/O flight recorder + hybrid lexical/semantic search
description:
# [EPIC] Universal Mux I/O Flight Recorder + Hybrid Search (FrankenSQLite + Tantivy + Semantic)

## Vision
Build a **flight recorder** for FrankenTerm that captures **all text entering and leaving the mux server** in an ultra-performant append-only pipeline, then exposes fast, trustworthy, hybrid lexical/semantic retrieval for operators and agents.

This epic is intentionally broader than simple logging. It defines a full system:
1. Capture/tap points for ingress and egress text
2. Durable append-only write path under high concurrency
3. Indexing and retrieval architecture (lexical + semantic)
4. Query/API surfaces for humans and robots
5. Reliability, observability, and rollout safety

## Why this matters
- Multi-agent terminal swarms generate high-volume, high-value forensic data.
- Current observability is good for event/state workflows, but not yet a true end-to-end immutable transcript plane optimized for forensic replay and hybrid retrieval.
- A robust flight recorder increases debugging speed, incident response quality, postmortem accuracy, and model/operator feedback loops.

## Design intent
- **Performance first**: append-only, batched writes, minimal per-event overhead.
- **Correctness first**: total ordering/causality metadata sufficient for replay and audit.
- **Durability first**: resilient write path (including exploration of FrankenSQLite multi-writer and WAL self-healing capabilities).
- **Search first**: Tantivy-backed lexical retrieval plus semantic retrieval and rank fusion.
- **Operator first**: stable CLI/robot/MCP interfaces and runbooks.

## Research grounding
Implementation must be informed by close study/adaptation patterns from:
- `/dp/frankensqlite`
- `/dp/coding_agent_session_search` (cass)
- `/dp/xf`

## Non-goals (for this epic)
- Replacing all existing storage paths in one unsafe big-bang migration.
- Shipping semantic retrieval without lexical fallback and measurable quality baselines.
- Adding unbounded retention without explicit cost/retention controls.

## Deliverables
- Full bead graph (research -> architecture -> implementation -> validation -> rollout)
- Feature-gated implementation plan with rollback path
- Search quality/perf test strategy and success thresholds
- Operator docs and migration guidance

## Success criteria
- Flight recorder captures ingress+egress text with stable ordering metadata.
- Append-only writer sustains swarm-scale load without destabilizing watcher/runtime.
- Lexical and hybrid search return correct results with measurable latency/quality targets.
- End-to-end system is testable, observable, and safe to roll out incrementally.

## Acceptance criteria
- All child tracks are completed or explicitly deferred with rationale.
- Dependency graph is acyclic and implementation-ready for swarm execution.
- Every major component includes unit/integration/e2e/load tests and failure-mode coverage.
close_reason: All 8 tracks (1-8) CLOSED. Flight recorder epic complete.

title: Capture track: canonical ingress/egress event schema + mux tap semantics
description:
## Track objective
Define and implement the canonical flight-recorder event model and capture tap points for **all mux ingress/egress text** with deterministic ordering metadata.

## Why this track exists
If capture semantics are ambiguous, durability and search become untrustworthy. This track establishes the contract for what is captured, in what order, and with what context.

## Deliverables
- Event schema (ingress/egress/control markers/metadata)
- Tap-point implementation plan for mux boundaries
- Causality/sequence model across panes and workflows
- Backpressure/failure semantics for capture stage

## Acceptance criteria
- Event schema is versioned, testable, and replay-compatible.
- Capture contract is explicit enough for independent indexing/search teams to implement against it.

title: Define versioned recorder event schema for ingress/egress mux text
description:
## Goal
Define a versioned canonical event schema for mux ingress/egress text capture, including metadata needed for replay, search filtering, and causality analysis.

## Background
Schema ambiguity will invalidate downstream indexing and replay. This bead establishes the ground-truth contract.

## Scope
- Define event types (ingress text, egress output, control markers, lifecycle markers).
- Define required metadata (pane/session/workflow correlation IDs, timestamps, sequence numbers, source).
- Define schema evolution/versioning rules and compatibility tests.

## Deliverables
- Recorder event schema spec and serialization contract.
- JSON-schema or equivalent testable schema artifact.

## Acceptance criteria
- Schema is precise enough for independent producer/consumer implementation.
- Evolution rules cover additive and breaking changes explicitly.

Implement ingress capture tap points (text/actions entering mux/panes) with minimal overhead and explicit source attribution.

Ingress visibility is required for full forensic replay and for understanding operator/agent actions leading to outcomes.

- Identify ingress boundaries and hook locations.
- Capture payload + metadata in canonical schema.
- Ensure capture path does not break policy gating behavior.

## Deliverables
- Ingress capture implementation plan + instrumentation tests.
- Validation that policy decisions and ingress logs remain consistent.

## Acceptance criteria
- Ingress events are captured for all supported injection paths.
- Overhead budget for ingress capture is documented and met in benchmarks.

description:
## Goal
Implement egress capture tap points (pane/mux output leaving runtime paths) with contiguous segment semantics and explicit gap markers.

## Background
Egress capture is the primary data source for replay and search; it must preserve ordering and discontinuity semantics.

## Scope
- Hook egress at the authoritative output pipeline.
- Emit explicit discontinuity markers where continuity cannot be guaranteed.
- Preserve compatibility with existing ingest/pattern detection semantics.

## Deliverables
- Egress capture instrumentation with segment/gap semantics.
- Regression tests for continuity/gap behavior.

## Acceptance criteria
- Egress events are complete for observed panes.
- Gap semantics are explicit and machine-detectable.

title: Define deterministic sequence + correlation model for replayable causality
description:
## Goal
Define deterministic sequence and correlation rules across ingress/egress streams so replay/search can reconstruct causality.

## Background
Raw timestamps alone are insufficient under concurrency. We need deterministic ordering semantics and correlation keys.

## Scope
- Define sequence assignment rules per pane and global merge strategy.
- Define correlation metadata (pane UUID/session/workflow/action linkage).
- Define clock-skew and race-handling behavior.

## Deliverables
- Ordering/correlation specification.
- Determinism and replay correctness test plan.

## Acceptance criteria
- Ordering rules are unambiguous and test-assertable.
- Replay results are stable across repeated runs on same input.

title: Define capture-stage redaction policy and deterministic implementation boundaries
description:
## Goal
Specify and implement capture-stage redaction boundaries so sensitive tokens are protected without destroying search/replay utility.

## Background
A full recorder introduces privacy/security risk. Redaction policy must be explicit early, not bolted on later.

## Scope
- Define sensitive-pattern classes and redaction modes.
- Define where redaction is applied (before persist, before index, before query response).
- Define auditability for redaction actions.

## Deliverables
- Redaction policy and implementation requirements.
- Tests for deterministic redaction behavior and false-positive guardrails.

## Acceptance criteria
- Sensitive fields are consistently protected across storage/index/API layers.
- Redaction behavior is measurable and tunable.

title: Specify and validate capture backpressure/overflow behavior under swarm load
description:
## Goal
Define capture-path backpressure/failure semantics and verify behavior under overload so recorder does not destabilize core watcher operations.

## Background
Recorder capture must fail safely under stress; silent degradation is unacceptable.

## Scope
- Define queueing and overflow policy (drop/slow/spool) with rationale.
- Define telemetry and alerting conditions.
- Validate with overload and fault injection tests.

## Deliverables
- Backpressure policy doc and implementation plan.
- Overload test scenarios with expected outcomes.

## Acceptance criteria
- Overload behavior is deterministic and observable.
- Core watcher stability is preserved under recorder stress.

title: Storage track: append-only writer path + backend abstraction + FrankenSQLite integration
description:
## Track objective
Build the append-only persistence path for flight-recorder events, including backend abstraction, high-throughput writer path, and FrankenSQLite integration path with safe fallback.

## Why this track exists
Logging quality is bounded by write-path reliability and throughput. This track ensures durability under load while preserving rollout safety.

## Deliverables
- Storage abstraction for recorder log backends
- Baseline backend (for immediate bring-up)
- FrankenSQLite backend plan/integration path
- Crash recovery/replay and corruption handling strategy

## Acceptance criteria
- Sustained append throughput targets are met under concurrent writer load.
- Failure modes are explicit and exercised in automated tests.
close_reason: All 6 children closed: storage abstraction (3.1), append-only writer (3.2), FrankenSQLite backend (3.3), crash-safe checkpointing (3.4), retention lifecycle (3.5), pipeline telemetry (3.6). Full storage track complete.

title: Define recorder storage abstraction and backend-gated configuration
description:
## Context
The recorder must support multiple storage backends during rollout, including an immediate low-risk path and an advanced FrankenSQLite-backed path. We need a stable contract before implementation to avoid coupling capture, storage internals, and query/index pipelines.

## Scope
Define a versioned `RecorderStorage` abstraction (append, flush, checkpoint/read cursor, health, lag metrics) plus config/feature-gate surfaces selecting backend at runtime.

## Deliverables
- Trait/interface boundary and data contracts (event envelope + batch semantics)
- Backend selection config model with explicit default/fallback behavior
- Failure taxonomy and retry contract (retryable vs terminal)
- ADR notes on why this interface is shaped for high-throughput append-only ingestion

## Why this matters
A narrow, explicit storage contract prevents premature lock-in and lets us ship incrementally without rewriting capture or query layers.

## Acceptance
- Interface is sufficient for both local append-log backend and FrankenSQLite backend
- Error and durability semantics are explicit and testable
- Feature flags/config behavior are documented and deterministic

title: Implement ultra-fast append-only writer hot path for recorder events
description:
## Context
Flight recorder ingestion must remain ultra-low-overhead under swarm-scale burst traffic. The initial backend should be a minimal, append-only write path with predictable latency and minimal allocations.

## Scope
Implement the hot-path append writer (batched writes, bounded queues, durable flush policy) for canonical recorder events.

## Deliverables
- Append-only log writer implementation with batching and backpressure signals
- Tunable flush cadence/size thresholds with sane defaults
- Monotonic offset assignment and persisted write checkpoints
- Unit/integration tests for ordering and durability behavior

## Why this matters
This is the performance-critical spine of the recorder. If this path regresses runtime responsiveness, the feature fails regardless of search quality.

## Acceptance
- Sustains target ingest throughput without destabilizing watcher loop
- Maintains append ordering guarantees and crash-safe durability semantics
- Produces stable offsets consumable by indexers/replay tools

comments.text: Execution/reconciliation complete in this checkout: append-only writer hot path is implemented in crates/frankenterm-core/src/recorder_storage.rs with RecorderStorage contract implementation (AppendLogRecorderStorage), batched append path, bounded in-flight admission with QueueFull signaling, idempotent batch_id handling, deterministic offsets, persisted state/checkpoint metadata, and torn-tail valid-prefix recovery scan/truncate on startup. title: Integrate FrankenSQLite backend adapter for concurrent durable recorder writes
description:
## Context
User intent explicitly calls out evaluating/adapting `/dp/frankensqlite` (multi-writer WAL + self-healing ideas) for durable high-concurrency logging.

## Scope
Design and implement a FrankenSQLite-backed recorder adapter behind `RecorderStorage`, including concurrency, WAL settings, and corruption/recovery policy boundaries.

## Deliverables
- Adapter implementation mapping recorder event batches to FrankenSQLite schema
- Concurrency model (writer sharding, lock strategy, or queueing) documented and benchmarked
- WAL tuning + self-healing strategy notes (what is adopted vs deferred)
- Validation tests for correctness under concurrent writer stress

## Why this matters
This is the highest-upside durability/performance path and the main mechanism for learning from frankensqlite in production-adjacent conditions.

## Acceptance
- Adapter passes contract tests from storage abstraction
- Concurrency behavior is reproducible and does not violate ordering invariants
- Recovery behavior is documented with explicit operator expectations

title: Implement crash-safe checkpointing and deterministic replay cursor semantics
description:
## Context
Indexer and replay systems require reliable continuation after process restarts/crashes. We need explicit checkpoints and idempotent resume semantics from storage.

## Scope
Implement write/checkpoint metadata and restart replay protocol so downstream consumers can resume from last committed offset without duplication or gaps.

## Deliverables
- Durable checkpoint format and atomic update protocol
- Resume/read APIs for indexers and replayers
- Duplicate suppression strategy where at-least-once replay is unavoidable
- Crash/restart integration tests

## Why this matters
Without deterministic replay/resume semantics, indexing quality and forensic trustworthiness degrade quickly.

## Acceptance
- Restart from crash resumes at deterministic point
- Replay APIs provide no silent gap behavior
- Duplicate handling strategy is explicit and tested
close_reason: Duplicate of wa-oegrb.3.4 (canonical).

comments.text: Implemented missing replay/checkpoint semantics in crates/frankenterm-core/src/recorder_storage.rs: added ReplayCursor/ReplayBatch/ReplayResumePlan contract types, trait surface (plan_resume/replay_batch), append-log replay reader with deterministic ordinal cursoring and torn-tail-safe behavior, and crash/restart resume tests. Also wired health() to include pipeline metrics default to satisfy expanded health schema. Validation: CARGO_TARGET_DIR=target_gentlesnow cargo check -p frankenterm-core --all-targets (passes); CARGO_TARGET_DIR=target_gentlesnow cargo test -p frankenterm-core recorder_storage -- --nocapture (8 recorder_storage tests passed, including new resume/replay tests).

title: Define retention, partitioning, and archival lifecycle for append-only recorder data
description:
## Context
Full-fidelity recorder data can grow rapidly. Retention and partitioning choices must be first-class so we do not accumulate unbounded costs or operational risk.

## Scope
Define and implement retention windows, partition strategy (time/size), and archival/export hooks for append log segments.

## Deliverables
- Retention policy model (default + override scopes)
- Segment lifecycle logic (active, sealed, archived, purged)
- Tooling hooks for safe archival/export
- Tests proving retention operations preserve invariants and auditability

## Why this matters
Cost and operability determine whether this feature can remain always-on in real swarm usage.

## Acceptance
- Retention behavior is deterministic and observable
- Purge/archive operations do not corrupt offset continuity semantics
- Operators can reason about storage growth via documented policy
close_reason: 39-test recorder_retention module: sensitivity tiers T1/T2/T3, segment lifecycle, configurable retention windows, T3 accelerated purge, sweep-based transitions, checkpoint hold enforcement

title: Add deep storage-pipeline telemetry, diagnostics, and SLO-oriented metrics
description:
## Context
The writer path is mission-critical; without deep telemetry we cannot tune or safely roll out. We need first-class metrics and tracing for throughput, lag, failures, and durability state.

## Scope
Instrument storage pipeline with metrics/events/logging suitable for SLOs and incident triage.

## Deliverables
- Metrics for append rate, batch size, queue depth, flush latency, error classes, replay lag
- Structured diagnostics for backend health and checkpoint progression
- Alert recommendations for critical degradation patterns
- Documentation mapping metrics to likely remediation actions

## Why this matters
Observability is necessary both for performance tuning and for proving recorder trustworthiness in incidents.

## Acceptance
- Critical failure/lag states are externally visible
- Metrics are stable enough for automated thresholds
- Documentation allows operators to diagnose common failure modes
close_reason: 36-test storage_telemetry module: latency histograms, throughput counters, EWMA rate, health tiers, SLO tracking, diagnostics

title: Indexing track: Tantivy lexical indexing, incremental ingestion, rebuild tooling
description:
## Track objective
Design and implement lexical indexing over recorder logs using Tantivy with near-real-time incremental ingestion and robust rebuild/repair workflows.

## Why this track exists
The recorder only creates value if data is rapidly discoverable. Lexical search is the baseline reliability layer and must remain available regardless of semantic subsystem state.

## Deliverables
- Tantivy schema and analyzer strategy
- Incremental indexer pipeline from append-only log
- Query semantics for phrase, boolean, field filters, time windows
- Rebuild/checkpoint/repair tools

## Acceptance criteria
- Lexical search latency and correctness targets are documented and test-enforced.
- Index can be rebuilt from append-only logs without data ambiguity.
close_reason: Duplicate of wa-oegrb.4 (canonical).

title: Design versioned Tantivy schema for recorder text + metadata filters
description:
## Context
Lexical retrieval quality and index stability depend on getting schema decisions right early (field structure, analyzers, stored vs indexed fields, offset references, metadata filters).

## Scope
Design the canonical Tantivy schema for recorder events, including text fields, normalized metadata, and time/agent/pane filters.

## Deliverables
- Versioned Tantivy schema definition with migration notes
- Field-by-field rationale (why indexed/stored/tokenized)
- Analyzer/tokenizer strategy tuned for terminal text (commands, stack traces, mixed symbols)
- Golden tests for schema compatibility and queryability

## Why this matters
Schema drift or poor tokenization destroys search quality and makes reindexing expensive.

## Acceptance
- Schema supports required filters and retrieval use-cases
- Analyzer choices are justified with examples
- Versioning strategy is documented for future migrations
notes: Delivered Tantivy lexical schema contract in docs/flight-recorder/tantivy-schema-v1.md, including field-by-field schema, tokenizer strategy for terminal text/symbols, migration/rebuild semantics, and golden compatibility/queryability test plan. Linked contract from ADR and cross-project extraction matrix for downstream implementation beads.

title: Implement incremental Tantivy ingestion from append-log checkpoints
description:
## Context
Recorder writes are append-only; indexer must consume offsets incrementally with deterministic resume behavior and bounded lag.

## Scope
Implement incremental index ingestion from recorder checkpoints, including idempotent retries and commit cadence controls.

## Deliverables
- Offset-driven incremental indexer pipeline
- Checkpoint coordination with storage replay cursors
- Commit/flush policy for freshness vs throughput tradeoffs
- Integration tests for restart/resume without data loss

## Why this matters
Incremental indexing is the bridge between high-throughput logging and usable near-real-time search.

## Acceptance
- Indexer resumes deterministically after restarts
- No silent drops/duplication under normal retry paths
- Lag is measurable and bounded under target load
close_reason: Work completed via wa-oegrb counterpart (same deliverables, code committed and tested)

title: Tune Tantivy commit/merge policy for sustained recorder ingest and query latency
description:
## Context
Tantivy segment management strongly affects write amplification and query latency. We need explicit merge and commit strategies aligned with recorder workload.

## Scope
Tune and codify segment lifecycle policy (commit frequency, merge heuristics, memory budgets) for terminal transcript data.

## Deliverables
- Merge policy configuration and rationale
- Benchmarked commit/merge profiles for common load regimes
- Operational toggles for safe runtime tuning
- Tests/benchmarks guarding against pathological segment explosion

## Why this matters
Poor segment strategy can make a correct index unusably slow or expensive.

## Acceptance
- Query latency and ingest throughput remain within target envelopes
- Segment growth remains bounded/predictable
- Policy is tunable without code surgery

title: Implement deterministic reindex/backfill tooling from recorder source-of-truth log
description:
## Context
We need deterministic rebuild/backfill tooling for schema evolution, corruption recovery, and historical imports.

## Scope
Create tooling to rebuild lexical index from recorder log ranges, with progress reporting and safety checks.

## Deliverables
- Full reindex command path with resumable checkpoints
- Partial/range backfill support by time/offset
- Integrity checks comparing index docs to source offsets
- Operator runbook for rebuild scenarios

## Why this matters
Without robust rebuild tooling, index incidents become high-risk and long-duration.

## Acceptance
- Rebuild can be run safely on large datasets
- Progress and completion criteria are explicit
- Integrity validation detects missing/corrupt ranges

title: Build lexical query service over Tantivy with stable filters/ranking/snippets
description:
## Context
Hybrid search still depends on high-quality lexical retrieval as both baseline and fallback. Query behavior must be explicit, testable, and stable.

## Scope
Implement lexical query service (filters, ranking, snippets/highlights, pagination) over the Tantivy index.

## Deliverables
- Query API for lexical search with deterministic sorting/pagination
- Filter support (time, pane, session, agent, direction, tags)
- Highlight/snippet strategy suitable for terminal text
- Relevance regression tests and fixture corpus

## Why this matters
Lexical search is the reliability anchor; semantic rankers should enhance, not replace, this foundation.

## Acceptance
- Lexical results are accurate and predictable
- Filters and pagination semantics are stable
- Fixture-based tests protect behavior from regressions

title: Create lexical quality harness with golden queries, relevance assertions, and latency budgets
description:
## Context
Search correctness can silently degrade with tokenizer, schema, or ranking changes. We need explicit evaluation harnesses tied to expected outcomes.

## Scope
Establish lexical search quality harness (golden query set + relevance assertions + latency checks).

## Deliverables
- Golden query dataset derived from realistic terminal workflows
- Relevance assertions (must-hit docs, ordering tolerances)
- Latency budget checks per query class
- CI wiring for regression detection

## Why this matters
A formal harness converts subjective “search feels off” complaints into actionable, reproducible failures.

## Acceptance
- Harness runs in CI/local and fails on quality regressions
- Query corpus covers critical forensic/operator scenarios
- Metrics are baseline-tracked for future improvements

title: Semantic track: embeddings + vector retrieval + hybrid rank fusion
description:
## Track objective
Implement semantic retrieval and hybrid lexical+semantic ranking over recorder data, reusing validated patterns from cass/xf where appropriate.

## Why this track exists
Pure lexical search misses semantically similar incidents and prior solutions. Hybrid ranking materially improves operator and agent recall in incident/debug workflows.

## Deliverables
- Embedding/chunking strategy for recorder corpus
- Vector retrieval subsystem and ANN strategy
- Rank-fusion strategy combining lexical and semantic evidence
- Offline relevance evaluation corpus and metrics

## Acceptance criteria
- Hybrid ranking behavior is deterministic enough to test and tune.
- Semantic subsystem can degrade gracefully without breaking lexical search.

title: Define embedding provider interface and model-governance strategy
description:
## Context
Semantic retrieval needs a model/provider strategy that balances quality, latency, cost, privacy, and offline operability. This must be explicit before implementation.

## Scope
Define embedding provider interface, model selection rubric, and deployment modes (local/remote) for recorder search.

## Deliverables
- Embedding abstraction API with pluggable providers
- Model selection matrix (quality/latency/cost/privacy tradeoffs)
- Normalization/versioning strategy for embedding vectors
- Operational policy for outages and fallback behavior

## Why this matters
Semantic quality depends as much on model governance as algorithm design. Unclear provider rules create unstable, expensive systems.

## Acceptance
- Provider interface supports swapping implementations without query-layer changes
- Selection rationale is documented and reproducible
- Fallback behavior is deterministic when embeddings unavailable

This satisfies acceptance requirements for wa-oegrb.5.1 and unblocks wa-oegrb.5.2/wa-oegrb.5.3.

title: Implement context-aware chunking/windowing policy for semantic embeddings
description:
## Context
Terminal streams are noisy and irregular. Effective semantic retrieval requires principled chunking/windowing, not naive line-level embeddings.

## Scope
Design and implement chunking policy that preserves context boundaries (session/pane/direction/time) while keeping embedding size manageable.

## Deliverables
- Chunking/windowing algorithm and tunable parameters
- Boundary rules for commands, outputs, errors, and prompt transitions
- Metadata linkage from chunk -> source offsets for replay/audit
- Tests on edge cases (very long outputs, tiny fragments, mixed directions)

## Why this matters
Bad chunking degrades semantic recall/precision and undermines trust in hybrid results.

## Acceptance
- Chunking policy yields reproducible chunks across reindex runs
- Chunk metadata fully traces back to source log offsets
- Edge-case tests demonstrate robust boundary handling

title: Build vector retrieval storage pipeline aligned with recorder/index lifecycle
description:
## Context
We need a durable vector retrieval layer integrated with recorder/index lifecycle, including updates, deletes/retention handling, and checkpoint alignment.

## Scope
Implement vector index storage/retrieval path and lifecycle management aligned with recorder offsets and lexical index updates.

## Deliverables
- Vector persistence layer and nearest-neighbor query path
- Upsert/update protocol tied to chunk identity/version
- Retention-aware cleanup strategy (delete/tombstone/rebuild)
- Consistency checks between vector and lexical stores

## Why this matters
Hybrid search fails if vector and lexical stores drift or lifecycle behavior is undefined.

## Acceptance
- Vector retrieval is deterministic for fixed index/model versions
- Lifecycle operations preserve referential integrity to recorder offsets
- Drift detection mechanisms are implemented and testable
